Operate CALIBER

Reference profile

How to run CALIBER as the reference deployment: the one shape that refuses to start on an unsafe setting, every requirement with its variable and reason, and a configuration that passes.

OperatorReferenceBETA
PrerequisitesA PostgreSQL database and a way to set environment variables for the CALIBER process
Reviewed 2026-10-30 · current main branch docs contract

Use this page to run CALIBER as the reference deployment: one supported shape that refuses to start while any of the settings below is unsafe. It is the deployment the EGI reference architecture's claims (governed action, safe restart, evidence) are made about; docs/architecture/adr/0001-reference-profile.md defines the whole shape, and this page lists what the process itself enforces today.

Turn it on#

Set CALIBER_PROFILE=reference. The default, development, starts with whatever is configured and behaves exactly as before. Under reference, create_app checks the configuration before it opens the database or creates the bootstrap account, so a refused start leaves nothing behind, and it lists every violation at once:

reference profile refused (2 violations):
- database_url is a SQLite file; set CALIBER_DATABASE_URL=<a PostgreSQL URL> for the reference profile [sqlite_database]
- csrf_enabled is false; set CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED=true for the reference profile [csrf_disabled]

Each line ends with the violation's stable code in brackets. A line names the setting and the variable to change, never the value that was configured.

An unknown profile name is a configuration error. GET /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/readiness carries a profile field, so an operator can see which rules the running process was started under.

The messages in the refusal name the setting and the variable to change. The table is checked by caliber/tests/test_profile.py: a rule that is not listed here, or a row without a rule, fails the build.

MCP allowlists (B12.3b, #746)#

CALIBER_MCP_STDIO_COMMAND_ALLOWLIST (default ${PYTHON}, the interpreter running CALIBER) and CALIBER_MCP_REMOTE_HOST_ALLOWLIST (default localhost,127.0.0.1,::1) decide which MCP servers the gateway will start or reach. An allowlisted stdio command is arbitrary code on the CALIBER host and an allowlisted remote host is an endpoint nobody reviewed, and the dispatcher admits an MCP call (connector mcp-tool, Governed MCP tools), never a server. So the Beta profile lists no MCP command or host: caliber.profile.REFERENCE_MCP_ALLOWLIST is an empty tuple (ADR 0001, amendment of 2026-10-31), and under CALIBER_PROFILE=reference a process whose either allowlist holds any entry refuses to start with the code mcp_allowlist_not_in_profile. The shipped defaults are entries the profile does not list, so a reference deployment sets both variables to the empty string explicitly:

reference profile refused (1 violation):
- mcp_remote_host_allowlist lists an MCP command or host the reference profile does not allow (it allows none); set CALIBER_MCP_REMOTE_HOST_ALLOWLIST to empty for the reference profile [mcp_allowlist_not_in_profile]

Recovery: set the variable named in the line to the empty string (CALIBER_MCP_REMOTE_HOST_ALLOWLIST=). Leaving it unset does not help: the unset value is the non-empty default, which is refused too. When both allowlists offend, one line names both variables. The message never quotes an entry. Blank items (,, spaces) are not entries.

  • What an empty allowlist means at run time. The gateway already refuses a server whose command or host is not allowlisted (mcp_server_not_ready), so with both lists empty no MCP server is reachable in a reference deployment, including the first-party PostgreSQL database servers (EP-114). That is the intent for the Beta: the exact dispatcher contract of a server must be supported before an entry is added to the tuple, which is an ADR change, not a setting.
  • The development profile is unchanged. It never runs this check; the defaults and any entries keep working there.
  • Oracle. caliber/tests/test_profile.py (each code, ordering, messages, the requirements table) and the scenario caliber/tests/egi_scenarios/test_b12_mcp_startup_rule.py, which starts real reference processes: each unlisted entry exits the process before it serves, and the same environment with both lists empty answers its health route.
  • Not covered here. The rule reads the two settings only. It does not inspect the registered server records, the administrator's tool_policies (an unclassified tool is already refused by the policy gate in both profiles), the other allowlists (CALIBER_MCP_STDIO_PYTHON_MODULE_ALLOWLIST, CALIBER_MCP_MANAGED_SIDECAR_HOSTS: they only narrow a command or host that the two lists already admit), or OpenAPI integration settings.
  • The shipped compose stack is a development deployment. It does not set CALIBER_PROFILE and it passes the two variables through ${VAR:-default}, which treats an empty value as unset, so it cannot express "empty" for a reference run. Start a reference deployment from its own environment, as in A configuration that passes.

What it also does at runtime#

Beyond refusing to start, the reference profile bounds every request body: a body above CALIBER_REFERENCE_MAX_BODY_BYTES (default 1 MiB) is answered 413 with {"reason": "request_too_large", "max_bytes": N}, whether the client declared a large Content-Length or streamed the body without one (or understated it). The check is the outermost layer, so an oversized request is refused before authentication, CSRF or routing reads it. A request at exactly the limit is accepted, and the development profile installs no limit.

Two kinds of request have a limit of their own, because their routes accept more than 1 MiB. The larger limit applies; the default is never lower than a route's own:

requestlimitsetting
multipart/form-data (skill zips, attachments, workspace imports, storage objects)256 MiBCALIBER_REFERENCE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES; raise it together with CALIBER_WORKFLOW_STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (250 MiB), which each route still enforces, tighter, afterwards
the GitHub webhook routeCALIBER_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES (2 MiB)the route's own setting; the global 1 MiB never lowers it

A refusal carries x-request-id (the caller's, or one generated) and writes one warning log line naming the method, path and size. The body is refused, not drained, so a client that keeps sending a very large body may see a connection reset rather than the 413.

Governed webhook and API-request nodes#

Manifest-backed webhook and api_request nodes use the registered private http effect backend. Before a request is sent, the runtime records an immutable proposal containing the node occurrence, URL, method, headers, timeout and body. Dispatch then rechecks the exact bound approval and the captured execution-owner lease in one transaction, emits the durable dispatch event, and only then calls the private transport. The path does not call a public CALIBER route or recursively invoke the OpenAPI execution surface. Egress is checked before the proposal is submitted and by the default client at connection time.

The generic HTTP backend cannot assume that every endpoint supports durable idempotency or a lookup-by-key API. It therefore emits Idempotency-Key from the proposal's stable logical key, but requires the runtime caller to provide an authoritative receipt verifier for the endpoint. The verifier must read the downstream's own state and return receipt facts matching the proposal's connector, resource, intent hash and attempt. A missing verifier, missing exact approval or missing lease is refused before transport; a response that cannot be verified does not become committed and remains recoverable as an unknown effect. The platform makes no universal exactly-once claim for arbitrary HTTP services.

In the reference profile a manifest-backed plan without this governed context is refused rather than falling back to the raw sender. Outside the reference profile it is not refused: see Profiles and a missing governed context. Legacy plans without a workflow manifest retain the existing _perform_guarded_effect ledger behavior and do not create an effect proposal. The runtime integration that owns a run must bind the context with the run id, exact approval provider, live execution-owner lease and endpoint-specific verifier. Since #1051 the worker does bind it in the reference profile (see The worker binds the governed path), but with no verifier for the generic http connector (#1055) a webhook or API-request node is refused no_authoritative_verifier before its proposal is recorded.

Governed registered tools (B04.3)#

A workflow tool node that names a registered Python tool is routed by the tool's registry row, read from the database for the tool being run: its name, owner, version, module, callable and declared side-effect level. The manifest binding, an exported bundle and the model do not decide it (IRToolBinding and ToolRegistryEntry carry no owner, so there is nothing in them to forge). A plan is governed when it is wired to the registry (an identity reader) or to an authority (a governed context); the table below lists every place the runtime builds a plan and which it is. OpenAPI bindings are routed the same way by Governed OpenAPI tools, and MCP bindings by Governed MCP tools.

the registry row isthe tool node
a CALIBER built-in (@caliber, version 1.0, its own module and callable) the protected-effect inventory refuses (EP-055: read_text_file, list_folder_files, grep_files, regex_search; sandbox_python)refused before it is bound or called: registered tool '<name>' refused: unsupported_effect_path; nothing is recorded
a CALIBER built-in classified read (and declared read)runs inline, as before
any other CALIBER built-inproposed, approved and dispatched at the inventory class (or the declared class when stricter)
a row that reuses a built-in's reserved name without being the seed's own row, a tool with no readable row, or an unrecognised declared levelclassified irreversible_write, the fail-closed class, and dispatched; never inline
an administrator-registered tool declared readruns inline, as before
an administrator-registered tool declared write or external_actionproposed, approved and dispatched; the proposal records irreversible_write because the inventory does not list it; the recorded class is always the stricter of the inventory's class and the class the row's declared level implies
a row whose module, callable or backend differs from the bindingrefused: registered tool '<name>' does not match its registry row

A protected call follows the same boundary as the governed HTTP nodes: the runtime records an immutable proposal (connector: registered_tool, resource registered-tool/<name>/<version>, the tool's arguments and input), asks the run's authorization provider for the exact approval and the captured execution-owner lease, and dispatch rechecks both in one transaction, consumes the approval and writes the dispatch event before the private registered_tool backend calls the bound tool. The tool is called with the arguments recorded in the proposal, not with what the caller still holds, and never retried (the binding's max_retries is ignored for a governed call): a tool that raises or times out leaves the proposal unknown for the reconciler. A local callable has no downstream key to replay, so the platform makes no exactly-once claim; it guarantees at most one claim per logical effect, and re-executing a finished node does not call the tool again. The registered_tool backend is a pinned entry of the reference profile's trusted connector table (REFERENCE_CONNECTORS): its implementation, capability record (no key to replay, no lookup) and settings (invoker, receipt_verifier) are admitted, and it accepts the risks write_not_exactly_once and key_retention_unconfirmed by name. As for HTTP, the run's context must supply an authoritative receipt_verifier; a response it cannot verify does not become committed.

Every refusal is a ToolExecutionError carrying a stable code and no argument, input or tool output:

registered tool effect proposal refused: bad_field              # arguments or input too large or not plain JSON
registered tool effect authorization was not granted           # no exact approval: the proposal stays `proposed`
registered tool effect authorization failed: ValueError         # the provider raised; only the type is reported
registered tool effect dispatch refused: proposal_not_approved  # not approved, or the node already ran
registered tool effect did not commit: ambiguous:unclassified_error  # the tool raised: effect unknown, not retried
'tool_node' requires a governed effect context to run protected registered tool 'open_ticket'
registered tool 'open_ticket' identity could not be read: ConnectionError

Recovery: a proposed effect needs an exact approval, after which the run can be resumed or resubmitted (the proposal is reused for the same node occurrence, so the tool still runs once); an unknown effect is settled by the reconciler (B05) or an operator, never by re-running the node; a manifest-backed deployment whose run owner has not bound a governed context must keep protected registered tools out of its workflows in the reference profile, because it refuses them there (read-class tools are unaffected; outside the reference profile see Profiles and a missing governed context). Every construction site of a runtime plan (RuntimePlan() in the code, and what it does with a protected registry tool:

plan built byused forregistry readerprotected registry tool
promoter.build_planworker runs, synchronous version runs, sub-workflows, Aria previewsbounda worker run of an admitted reference-profile run gets a governed context (#1051) and the tool is refused no_authoritative_verifier before it is recorded; every other build_plan plan (synchronous, sub-workflow, preview) has none: refused in the reference profile, legacy guarded path in development (#1068); a preview stubs it
refinement._replay (via orchestrator/workflow_stages.py::run_workflow_eval)candidate evaluationbound by the stagerefused (typed, nothing recorded); read-class tools run
calibration._replay_calibration_manifest (via evaluate_workflow_calibration_candidates in the stage)calibration replaybound by the stagerefused; read-class tools run
promoter deploy-gate replayrelease gate evaluationnone, but preview=Truestubbed, never run for real
export_runtime.execute_exported_workflowstandalone exportsnone (no registry to read)not governed: called directly
a caller that builds a plan itself (tests, SDK embedding)anynone unless it passes onenot governed: called directly

The two evaluation replays used to call a candidate manifest's write tools for real (found in review of B04.3); they now refuse them, so a workflow whose protected tool must be exercised by an evaluation or calibration needs that tool replaced by a read-class stand-in until the replay can run under a governed context (#1051). The module-import paths stay inventory rows EP-015, EP-016 and EP-019, refused by #774.

Two limits. An administrator-registered tool declared read is trusted as read-class: its declared level is part of the definition the deployment bundle pins and re-verifies before a run (deployment_bundle.tool_snapshot), but the platform does not observe what its code does, so register a tool that writes with write or external_action. And model-chosen tool calls inside an agent step are not routed by this change (B04.6, B04.7); OpenAPI tool nodes are routed by Governed OpenAPI tools and MCP tools by Governed MCP tools.

No migration, no new setting and no new route; rolling back is reverting the change (a registered_tool proposal already recorded remains readable and reconcilable).

Governed OpenAPI tools (B04.4)#

A workflow tool node bound to a tool published from an OpenAPI integration (execution_backend: openapi_http) is routed by the tool's registry row, as a registered Python tool is, and by the operation that row selects. Two things the registry holds decide the class, and the stricter wins: the row's declared side_effect_level and the method of the operation its own backend_config describes (a tool pack's operation is chosen by the call's operation input from the row's list of bound operations, never from the binding). The manifest binding, an exported bundle and the model decide nothing: the binding's backend_config and input_schema must equal the row's, or the node is refused.

the row and its operationthe tool node
GET, HEAD or OPTIONS, declared readruns inline, as before: no proposal, no approval
GET, HEAD or OPTIONS, declared write or external_actionproposed, approved and dispatched (the declared level floors the class)
POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, whatever the level (an under-declared read included)proposed, approved and dispatched: a method that is not a read method is at least a reversible_write
a built-in's reserved name, or an unrecognised levelclassified irreversible_write and dispatched; never inline
a tool with no readable row, a row that is not an OpenAPI tool, or an operation the row does not bindrefused before anything is recorded or sent
a binding whose configuration or schema differs from the rowrefused: registered tool '<name>' does not match its registry row
a protected call in a plan with no governed context, or replaced by an injected callablerefused: nothing is recorded or sent
a protected method reaching the public OpenAPI entry from anywhere else (an export, a model-chosen call, Aria, an ungoverned plan)refused before anything is prepared or sent: unsupported_effect_path

The proposal (connector: openapi-http, always recorded irreversible_write, because the inventory does not list a registered tool) holds the resource openapi/<METHOD> <server><path template>, built from the row, and the arguments {"tool", "version", "input"}. Dispatch rechecks the exact approval and the captured execution-owner lease in one transaction, consumes the approval and writes the dispatch event before the private openapi_http backend sends. That backend sends through the private raw transport: it rebuilds the request from the row and the recorded arguments, requires the result to be the recorded resource (method, server and path) and sends nothing otherwise, so what is sent is what the approver saw, and it can never reach the dispatcher or the public entry again.

The public entry reads; the private transport sends. execute_openapi_http_tool (and bind_openapi_http_tool, which wraps it) is the public entry of the OpenAPI executor. It sends only an operation whose method reads (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS): any other method is refused with unsupported_effect_path before the input is validated, a secret is resolved or anything is sent, so no caller of it can perform a protected effect without a recorded, approved proposal. The method is read from the tool's configuration (a pack's operation is chosen by the input), never from a claim. A configuration that resolves to no operation gets the executor's ordinary configuration refusal instead. The send itself is the module-private _send_raw, which only the dispatcher's private backends (document request and openapi_http) and the executor module itself may name; the two development-profile compatibility entries over it are named in the sections below. It never calls the public entry, so a dispatched effect cannot re-enter the dispatcher or the public path. tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py fails when any other production module names _send_raw (test_the_private_raw_transport_is_named_only_by_pinned_modules) or the public entry (test_the_raw_openapi_executor_is_named_only_by_pinned_callers). A read-method tool is still classified by the registry row before it reaches the public entry (a GET declared write is dispatched), and Aria checks a tool's declared level itself.

Everything that can be refused without sending is refused before the proposal is recorded, so no approval is requested or spent for a call that cannot be made: the input against the row's schema, the server (a plain http(s) origin with no credentials, query or fragment, because its text is persisted in the resource), the egress policy for the request URL and for an OAuth token URL, an unsupported auth kind, a caller-supplied idempotency key and a conflicting precondition. No secret is resolved and nothing is sent at that point; the transport applies the egress policy again when it connects.

Keys, preconditions and retries.

  • When the row binds an idempotency key header, the platform owns the key: the transport sends the proposal's stable logical key, and an idempotency_key input or a header_params entry for that header is refused (openapi_key_override_refused), never sent next to it.
  • When the row binds a precondition header (for example If-Match), the expected_resource_version input and a header_params entry must agree (openapi_precondition_conflict). The value is recorded once, as the proposal's expected_resource_version (so the approval is bound to it and the approver's check compares it with the current version), and the transport sends it as the bound header. A recorded precondition the row cannot send is refused, never dropped.
  • The transport retries only when the request really carries an emitted key: a row with no key header is sent once, even for a method the executor would otherwise retry (PUT, DELETE). With a key, the executor's own bounded retry (the row's max_attempts, at most 5) repeats the same key within one dispatch. The dispatcher does not redrive an ambiguous effect after that dispatch, and the binding's max_retries is ignored for a governed call. The in-dispatch retry is an accepted risk, not a guarantee: the capability record leaves key scope and retention unconfirmed, so a downstream that does not honour the key can commit twice. Leave max_attempts at 1 unless the downstream is known to replay a key.

Headers, and what is stored. header_params may not set a method-override header (X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method, X-Method-Override) or a framing or hop-by-hop header (Host, Content-Length, Content-Encoding, Transfer-Encoding, Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Connection, Proxy-Authorization, TE, Trailer, Upgrade, Expect; case-insensitive): classification uses the row's method, and a downstream that honours an override would turn a read into a write. The check applies to every call of the executor, an inline GET included, and is refused as openapi_header_forbidden (a governed call, before the proposal) or as an executor error that names no header (an inline call). It does not cover a method override carried in a query parameter or a body field a particular downstream might honour. The input is recorded verbatim: body, header_params, query_params and path_params are stored in the proposal's args.input (caliber_effect_proposals) and shown to the approver, so credentials belong in the row's auth_binding (a secret reference resolved at send time), never in the call's input. The proposal never records the auth binding.

What an answer proves. The openapi-http capability record promises nothing about a downstream: no key scope or retention, no lookup by key, no documented rejection status. So a 2xx is a claim that the run's authoritative receipt_verifier must confirm (an unconfirmed claim stays unknown), and every other answer, a 4xx included, is unknown rather than failed. A connection dropped or timed out after the downstream committed is unknown: the node does not run again, the reconciler has no lookup binding for this connector and leaves it (not_bound), and only the verifier, a receipt callback or an operator can settle it. The connector is a pinned entry of REFERENCE_CONNECTORS (backend kind openapi_http, settings operation and receipt_verifier, accepted risks write_not_exactly_once and key_retention_unconfirmed).

Every refusal is a ToolExecutionError with a stable code and no argument, input, header, URL or response body:

OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_egress_blocked         # the request or token URL fails the egress policy
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_input_invalid          # input breaks the row's schema, or a path parameter is missing
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_key_override_refused   # a caller-supplied idempotency key for a row that binds one
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_precondition_conflict  # If-Match and expected_resource_version disagree, or are blank
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_config_invalid         # the row's server or path cannot be used (credentials, query, scheme)
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_auth_unsupported       # the row binds an auth kind the executor does not support
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_header_forbidden       # header_params sets a method-override, framing or hop-by-hop header
OpenAPI tool 'tickets' refused: openapi_operation_unresolved    # a pack operation the row does not bind
OpenAPI tool 'tickets' refused: unsupported_effect_path         # no readable OpenAPI row for the tool
unsupported_effect_path: a protected OpenAPI call is sent only by the effect dispatcher   # a non-read method at the public entry
OpenAPI effect authorization was not granted                    # no exact approval: the proposal stays `proposed`
OpenAPI effect dispatch refused: proposal_not_approved          # not approved, or the node already ran
OpenAPI effect did not commit: ambiguous:http_503               # unknown: the answer proves nothing, nothing is resent
OpenAPI effect did not commit: receipt_unverified               # a 2xx the verifier could not confirm: unknown
'tool_node' requires a governed effect context to run protected OpenAPI tool 'open_ticket'

Recovery: a refusal before the proposal needs the input, the row or the egress allowlist corrected (nothing was recorded). A proposed effect needs an exact approval, after which the run can be resumed (the proposal is reused for the same node occurrence). An unknown effect is settled by the receipt verifier, a receipt callback or an operator (see the recovery runbook), never by running the node again.

After the approval. The backend rebuilds the request from the row and the recorded arguments and checks it again, the egress policy included. Any failure at that point (a recorded proposal that is not the row's operation, or a destination that stopped passing the egress policy since the proposal, a transient DNS or allowlist change included) sends nothing and settles the proposal failed with the reason not_sent; the dispatch's internal refusal code is not surfaced, and the approval is already consumed: ask for a new proposal (run the node again after fixing the cause).

Not routed through the dispatcher, and what they can do now (B04.4b). Model-chosen tool calls inside an agent step (B04.6, #768), the Aria assistant's published-tool call (inventory EP-034: there is no workflow run to propose into; owned by #1063), standalone exports and plans a caller builds itself (#1051: build_plan binds the registry reader but no governed context, so a in the reference profile a deployed workflow's protected OpenAPI nodes are refused (the worker's context has no verifier for the connector yet, #1055, #1051), and outside it they run inline through a named legacy entry, see Profiles and a missing governed context; read-class GET nodes always run) all reach the public entry, which refuses a protected method with unsupported_effect_path. So none of them can perform an OpenAPI write any more: they can read, and a write needs the governed route above. This is a behavior change for an Aria deployment in build mode with auto_all or full_autonomy approval, which no longer offers a write or external-action tool to the model (it could only fail), for a tool declared read whose operation is a POST (refused rather than sent), and for a standalone export whose tool writes. The operator's draft preview route (EP-033) is read-only in the reference profile (#1072): it sends through the public entry, so a draft whose operation is not a read (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) is refused, see Draft preview is read-only. The callers of the public entry are pinned by tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py::test_the_raw_openapi_executor_is_named_only_by_pinned_callers, so a new one fails until it is routed or pinned with a reason.

Configuration, migration and rollback. No new setting, no route and no migration. The two names openapi_http and openapi-http become reserved tool names like the other connectors (409 reserved_tool_name); a tool already registered under one is untrusted and unaffected. Reverting the change restores the direct call (a proposal already recorded remains readable).

The worker binds the governed path (#1051)#

In the reference profile the workflow-run worker builds the governed contexts for an admitted run it owns, from state the server holds (caliber.effects.governed_context). Nothing a request, a manifest, a tool call or a model supplies becomes authority, and a trusted input that is missing is a refusal, never an implicit allow.

trusted inputwhere it comes from
the execution-owner leasea provider the lifespan binds to the process's ExecutionRoleController (WorkflowRunWorker.bind_lease_provider), read at the moment an effect is dispatched and compared in the claim and in every settlement write. No lease: lease_unavailable, nothing is claimed
the approver's authoritythe decision route records who decided (decided_by and the quorum). The scopes a dispatch attests are derived then from the configured user lists (CALIBER_ADMIN_USERS, CALIBER_APPROVER_USERS, CALIBER_OPERATOR_USERS) for every one of those approvers and intersected, so a scope revoked since the decision is gone (role_revoked) and a quorum is as strong as its weakest approver. Project role, membership, the requester and the initiator are re-derived by the commit recheck itself, as before
the requesterthe run's initiator, run.created_by, read from the run row (an approval request names it; the approver must be someone else)
which tools may be proposed throughCALIBER_AGENT_STEP_TOOL_BACKENDS, keyed by the tool's registry identity (name, version), never by a local name in a manifest
the downstream an effect is sent tothe base_url of the connector's binding in CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS for the run's project: the address the reconciler asks, so an effect is never sent where it cannot be looked up. No binding: connector_unbound, refused before anything is claimed
step limits and the run's token budgetthe operator's ceilings (CALIBER_AGENT_STEP_MAX_*) and CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS

An agent step, end to end. An agent node bound to a mapped tool runs as a governed step; every other agent node runs as before (a governed step has no text output, so only an agent built to propose is governed). The scripted or real model proposes a protected action: the platform binds it to the inventory, records one proposed effect and the approval request bound to that exact intent, and the run parks waiting_approval on that request. A person other than the initiator decides it over HTTP (POST /workflow-runs/{id}/approval/approve). A decision does not wake the run (it records the human decision and nothing else); an operator resumes it (POST /workflow-runs/{id}/resume), which is the one point where the run runs again. The node finds its proposal instead of asking the model again, and the producer's dispatch_approved crosses the dispatcher: the approval is consumed and the dispatch claimed in one transaction under the lease before the downstream is called, the downstream is sent the proposal's stable key exactly once, and the receipt is read back by the connector's own lookup by key. committed completes the node; anything short of it (an ambiguous answer, a receipt that could not be read back, a worker killed after the send) leaves the proposal dispatched or unknown and the run waiting_effect, which the reconciler settles by key and then wakes. A rejected request is final (approval_rejected); an expired one is asked again; a revoked approver, a lost lease or an unbound connector fails the node with its fixed code and sends nothing.

What each plan shape gets. legacy_guarded_effects stays, so the development profile is unchanged.

plangoverned context
a worker run, admitted, reference profilethe effect context, and the step context when an agent node is bound to a mapped tool
the same, with an agent bound to a mapped tool but no lease binding, no initiator, no usable manifest digest or a configuration that does not parsethe run fails (governed_context_unavailable) before the model is asked: never a legacy agent
the same, but the run was not admittedthe run fails (run_not_admitted) if an agent in it can reach a mapped tool; otherwise nothing is bound and a protected node is refused for want of a context
a worker run in the development profilenothing bound: the legacy path of Profiles and a missing governed context
a synchronous version run and the sub-workflows of a worker run (build_plan outside the worker's own run)no owner lease in the process that builds the plan, so no context: a protected node is refused in the reference profile and takes the legacy path in development, exactly as before. An agent in such a plan that is bound to a mapped tool, or whose handoffs can reach one, directly or through other agents, is refused when it runs (agent '<id>' can reach a tool the operator mapped to a governed backend, and this plan has no governed step for it): build_plan records the agents bound to a mapped tool (RuntimePlan.agents_requiring_governance, reference profile only) and the interpreter checks each agent's handoff closure, cycle-safe
an evaluation, a gate replay or an Aria previewrun as previews (preview=True): protected tools are stubbed, so the refusal above does not apply to them
refinement and calibration replays (the stage tells the replay which agents are mapped, agents_requiring_governance)not previews: this change makes a mapped agent (or one that hands off to one) refused in the replay, so evaluating or calibrating a workflow whose agent is bound to a mapped tool scores an error in the reference profile (give the replay a manifest without the mapped agent); what a replay does with a protected registry tool is the registered-tools table above, and protected model-chosen tool calls in replays are #1079's
the deploy-gate replayunchanged: a preview, protected tools stubbed
standalone exports and plans a caller builds itselfunchanged: not governed

A workflow node (webhook, API request, registered tool, OpenAPI tool, MCP tool) is bound to the context and refused. The context the worker binds has the whole mechanism (a proposal, an approval request bound to the exact intent, a park behind it, a dispatch under the lease), but it names no backend it can verify: the generic http, registered_tool, openapi_http and mcp connectors have no lookup by key the platform can call, so an outcome it could not read back would end unknown and park the run with no way out (#1055). Such a node is therefore refused before its proposal is recorded, so no approval is asked for or spent on it:

HTTP effect refused: no_authoritative_verifier
registered tool effect refused: no_authoritative_verifier
OpenAPI effect refused: no_authoritative_verifier
MCP effect refused: no_authoritative_verifier

A verifier for a backend (effect_context(authority, verifiers={...})) is what makes it reachable; until #1055 settles which connectors have one, the only backend a production run reaches is document_request, through a governed agent step. A protected MCP tool call (B04.5) goes through the same context and is refused the same way.

Limits, stated plainly.

  • A governed workflow effect, or a governed agent, inside a fan-out, loop, error boundary, handoff or parallel branch cannot park the run: the run is refused up front (agents) or fails (effects).
  • The legacy requires_approval gate of a tool node still asks first, with its own node-level request; a governed effect then asks the exact-intent question, so such a node is approved twice.
  • A proposal that names a resource version is sent only through a connector whose downstream enforces the precondition atomically with the write (document_request does: a stale version is the downstream's 412, a definitive rejection). The platform has no read of its own for another connector's target, so a versioned proposal for any other connector is version_unverifiable.
  • A revoked approver, a lease that is gone before the claim, or a connector with no binding ends the run failed with the proposal still proposed; a downstream that rejects ends it with the proposal failed. Settling the proposal of an ended run and withdrawing an approved, unconsumed decision are #1074. A refusal or an error that arrives after the downstream was called (settling refused because the lease moved on, a verifier that raised) is not a failure of the run: the proposal is read again, an open one (dispatched, unknown) parks the run waiting_effect for the reconciler and a committed one completes the node.
  • Model-chosen tool calls of an agent that is not governed are not routed (#768). An agent that is bound to a mapped tool, or can reach one through handoffs, is either governed (the worker's own graph) or refused in every plan build_plan and the refinement and calibration replays build outside a preview; a plan a caller builds by hand and passes no agents_requiring_governance is not covered (it is not governed either: see the table).
  • If the store is down at both the settlement and the re-read that follows a failed dispatch, the run fails store_failed; the proposal is still the reconciler's (it was claimed, so it is dispatched or unknown and is settled by key).
  • CALIBER_AGENT_STEP_TOOL_BACKENDS outside the reference profile is ignored and logged at startup (there is no lease to dispatch under).

No migration. The new setting is CALIBER_AGENT_STEP_TOOL_BACKENDS (default []: no agent is governed, and a reference profile with the default behaves as before). Rolling back is reverting the change; a recorded proposal stays readable and reconcilable.

Draft preview is read-only (#1072)#

The operator's draft preview (POST /openapi-integrations/{id}/tool-drafts/{draft_id}/preview, inventory EP-033) fires one real upstream request for an unpublished draft. It is gated by the caliber.admin or caliber.operator scope, the project action resource.execute and the draft's allow_in_preview flag, and it is audited, but allow_in_preview is set by the same operator who fires the call. A write sent through it would therefore be self-approvable: no second person, no proposal, no lease and no receipt.

  • Reference profile (and a process with no config, which is treated as the reference profile). Preview sends through the public entry, so it sends only a read: a draft whose operation is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS previews as before, and any other method is refused before the input is validated, a secret is resolved or anything is sent. The answer is 409 with reason_code unsupported_effect_path and a fixed message that names no method, server, path, draft or input value. The refusal is audited as preview_openapi_tool_draft with error: unsupported_effect_path; no request left the platform. A write goes through a published tool in a workflow, where the dispatcher proposes, approves and sends it.
  • Development profile. Unchanged: preview sends any method through the named legacy entry execute_legacy_openapi_draft_preview, still gated by allow_in_preview and audited. It is a compatibility exemption for a laptop, not the governed path, and the reference profile never reaches it.

tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py pins both names: the route may name the public entry (RAW_OPENAPI_CALLERS) and the legacy entry (LEGACY_PREVIEW_CALLERS), and no production module outside the dispatcher and the executor names the private _send_raw (RAW_TRANSPORT_CALLERS lost the route). There is no new setting, route or migration. A deployment that previewed a write in the reference profile now gets the 409; read previews are unaffected.

Governed MCP tools (B04.5)#

An MCP server is untrusted: its tool names, descriptions, annotations such as readOnlyHint, and results are data the platform reads, never a classification. A workflow tool node bound to an MCP tool and an MCP node are therefore classified from three things CALIBER itself holds, for exactly the tool being called:

  1. the MCP server record (caliber_mcp_servers: transport, command or URI, arguments, the names of its environment variables and headers), read from the database for the run's identity, never from the manifest binding or the model;
  2. the tool policy an administrator wrote (tool_policies: allowed, side_effect_level, requires_approval), which the policy gate already requires to be explicit and complete: a tool the server lists but nobody classified is refused, not guessed at; and
  3. the protected-effect inventory (EP-114), which applies to the first-party PostgreSQL MCP server only, and only under the reference profile (#774 owns the switch for every inventory row). That server is recognised from the record and the deployment settings, never from the tool names a server reports: a stdio server that runs the CALIBER interpreter with -m caliber.mcp_servers.db, or a remote server whose host the operator listed in CALIBER_MCP_MANAGED_SIDECAR_HOSTS (the shipped compose stack runs the three first-party database servers as such sidecars). That setting attests an isolation boundary, not an identity, so a third-party server on an attested sidecar host is treated as the first-party one too and its tools named like EP-114's are refused (the conservative direction): list only hosts that run the first-party servers if that matters. A server on any other host, however it names its tools, is third-party and is classified by its own administrator's policy.
the server record, policy and inventory saythe tool node or MCP node
side_effect_level: read (an approval-requiring read keeps the workflow binding's own approval gate)runs inline, as before: no proposal
writeproposed, approved and dispatched; recorded irreversible_write (the inventory does not list a third-party MCP tool)
external_actionproposed, approved and dispatched; recorded irreversible_write
the server lists the tool but there is no complete policy for it, the policy is invalid or has allowed: false, the tool is not in the discovered list, or the server is not ready (status, transport, allowlist, blocked address)refused with a stable code before anything is recorded or sent
a write tool of the first-party database server (EP-114), whatever the administrator classified it as, under the reference profilerefused: unsupported_effect_path (the development profile classifies it by the policy like any tool)
a server the run's identity cannot read, or a timeout the connector does not acceptrefused: mcp_server_unavailable, mcp_timeout_invalid
a protected call in a plan with no governed context (reference profile; the development profile runs it inline as before, see below), or replaced by an injected callablerefused: nothing is recorded or sent

The binding's declared side_effect_level and a server's readOnlyHint decide nothing: a binding that claims read cannot make an administrator's write inline, and a server that claims a tool is read-only does not change it.

The proposal (connector: mcp-tool) holds the resource mcp/<server_id>/<tool> and the arguments {"server_id", "tool", "server_digest", "arguments"}. server_digest binds the server record and the three classification fields the decision was made from (no credential value: the names of the environment variables and headers and the authentication type are in it, a rotated token is not). Dispatch rechecks the exact approval and the captured execution-owner lease in one transaction, consumes the approval and writes the dispatch event before the private mcp backend sends. That backend reads the server record again and classifies the call again: the recorded server, tool, resource and digest must be the trusted call's, and the call must still be protected, so an administrator who blocked, reclassified or edited the server after the approval was requested is seen, and nothing is sent (the proposal is settled failed, reason not_sent, and the approval is already consumed: ask for a new proposal). The recorded arguments are what is sent.

Execution policy is preserved, and checked again. The backend sends through the gateway's own transport, so the tool-policy gate, the stdio command, module and environment checks, the isolation wrapper, the remote-host allowlist and the resolved-address check all run again at dispatch, and a rate limit is consumed by the call that really goes out (an exceeded limit is proven_not_sent: failed, approval spent). The address check is made when the connection is prepared, not pinned to the connection: a DNS answer that changes between that check and the connect is an existing limit this change does not close.

What an MCP server can confirm: nothing the platform can rely on. MCP has no idempotency key, no precondition and no lookup by key, so the mcp-tool capability record promises nothing and the connector is a pinned entry of REFERENCE_CONNECTORS (backend kind mcp, settings call and receipt_verifier, accepted risks write_not_exactly_once and key_retention_unconfirmed).

  • A returned result is a claim. It becomes committed only when the run's receipt_verifier returns facts for this proposal; otherwise the proposal stays unknown (receipt_unverified). Most MCP servers cannot read their own effects back through a channel the platform trusts, so a deployment that wants committed needs a verifier that asks the system of record by something the workflow put in the call's arguments (the platform sends the server no key).
  • Anything that may have reached the server and did not return a result is unknown, not failed: a timeout, a dropped session, an MCP error, and a result the server marks is_error (an untrusted server can say a call failed that ran). Only a failure the gateway proves came before the request (policy, egress, command allowlist, a session that never opened, a rate limit) is failed. The call is sent once: the dispatcher does not redrive an ambiguous effect, the binding's max_retries is ignored for a governed call, and the reconciler has no lookup for this connector (not_bound), so an unknown MCP effect is settled by the verifier, a receipt callback or an operator.
  • The result is untrusted data. It must be plain JSON of at most 256 KiB and 32 levels of nesting; anything else is unknown (ambiguous:result_out_of_bounds) and is neither stored nor returned. The returned object is a JSON round trip, so nothing of the server's making survives into a record or a response. No credential is read into a record: the proposal holds the arguments and the digest, never the server's environment, headers or authentication.

Under the reference profile the gateway entry points refuse a protected call. invoke_tool_sync and invoke_tool_by_server_id_sync (what the runtime's MCP-bound callables, MCP nodes and exported workflows call) run only a tool whose trusted classification is read, and raise EffectRefused (mcp_effect_requires_proposal; unsupported_effect_path for a first-party database write tool) for every other, with nothing sent. Under the development profile (the default) they let a protected call through, as before the dispatcher (#1068; development is an allow-list, so any other profile refuses): that inline call has no proposal, exact-intent approval, lease or receipt and is not the governed path (see "Profiles and a missing governed context" below). The one caller of the ungated transport (invoke_tool_raw_sync) is the dispatcher's mcp backend; tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py pins every module that names the gateway, so a new caller fails until it is routed or pinned with a reason. The operator's discover, test and playground routes use the async transport directly (EP-038 to EP-040, exempt: they are not agent-reachable and need the operator scope).

Every refusal is a ToolExecutionError with a stable code and no argument, URL, header or result:

MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_tool_unclassified      # listed by the server, no complete administrator policy
MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_tool_not_discovered    # not in the discovered list (run discover-tools)
MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_tool_not_allowed       # the policy says allowed: false
MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_server_not_ready       # status, transport, allowlist or address blocks the server
MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_tools_not_discovered   # nothing discovered yet (run test-connection and discover-tools)
MCP tool 'insert_rows' refused: unsupported_effect_path    # a first-party database write tool (EP-114)
MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_server_unavailable     # the record cannot be read by the run's identity
MCP tool 'issue_write' refused: mcp_timeout_invalid        # the node's timeout is not a finite number of seconds, at most 300
MCP node 'n' refused for 'srv'/'tool': mcp_effect_requires_proposal   # a caller-built plan reached the gateway with a write
MCP effect authorization was not granted                   # no exact approval: the proposal stays `proposed`
MCP effect dispatch refused: proposal_not_approved         # not approved, or the node already ran
MCP effect dispatch refused: connector_config_not_admitted # the backend settings are not the pinned ones
MCP effect did not commit: not_sent                        # failed: a policy, egress or session failure before the request
MCP effect did not commit: ambiguous:may_have_been_sent    # unknown: the request may have reached the server; nothing is resent
MCP effect did not commit: ambiguous:result_out_of_bounds  # unknown: the answer was not bounded plain JSON
MCP effect did not commit: receipt_unverified              # a result the verifier could not confirm: unknown
'tool_node' requires a governed effect context to run protected MCP tool 'issue_write'

Recovery: a refusal before the proposal needs the policy, the server record or the allowlist corrected (nothing was recorded), for example PATCH /mcp-servers/{server_id}/tools/{tool_name}/policy with an explicit allowed, side_effect_level and requires_approval. A proposed effect needs an exact approval, after which the run can be resumed. A failed effect needs a new proposal. An unknown effect is settled by the receipt verifier, a receipt callback or an operator (see the recovery runbook), never by running the node again: check the server's own system of record first.

Behaviour changes to plan for. What happens to a protected MCP call depends on the profile (the classification itself does not):

the callreference profiledevelopment profile (the default)
MCP node or tool node, an authority is bound (governed_effects)proposed, approved, dispatched, but only for a server the gateway can reach: the reference profile requires both MCP allowlists empty, so no server is reachable yet (MCP allowlists)proposed, approved, dispatched
MCP node or tool node in a build_plan plan, no authority bound (#1051)refused: requires a governed effect context to run protected MCP toolruns inline, as before B04.5, behind the node's own approval gate: not governed (legacy_guarded_effects)
a model-chosen call inside an agent step, a caller-built plan, a generated exportrefused by the gateway entry point (EffectRefused; a model sees an error marker) until B04.6 (#768) proposes itruns inline, as before: not governed
a first-party database write tool (EP-114)refused: unsupported_effect_pathclassified by the administrator's policy like any tool
an unclassified, blocked, undiscovered or not-ready toolrefused (both profiles)refused (both profiles)

An operator can still call any tool from the playground (EP-039/040, exempt).

Not covered by this change: a governed path for the development profile (it keeps the alpha inline call until #1051), model-selected calls (B04.6, #768), the refusal switch for every inventory row marked refuse (B04.7, #774), a key channel to MCP servers that could use one, pinning the resolved address to the connection, and a governed context for deployed workflows (#1051).

Configuration, migration and rollback. No new setting, no route and no migration. The names mcp and mcp-tool become reserved tool names like the other connectors (409 reserved_tool_name). Reverting the change restores the direct call (a proposal already recorded remains readable).

Profiles and a missing governed context (#1068)#

build_plan (worker runs, synchronous version runs, sub-workflows) binds the registry reader but no execution-owner lease and no exact-intent approval provider. Since #1051 the worker binds a GovernedEffectContext after build_plan for an admitted run in the reference profile (The worker binds the governed path); the plans build_plan returns to every other caller still have none, and this section is what they do. The dispatcher routing of B04.2, B04.3 and B04.4 made every protected node of a manifest-backed plan fail for that reason in every profile, which broke the shipped cookbook labs (03, 04, 05, 07, 08, 09, 16 and 19) on main. The decision, from ADR 0001 ("Features outside the shape keep working in development", "The profile never silently falls back to a weaker control"), the B04.2 scope ("keep _perform_guarded_effect for runs without a manifest (legacy)") and #774 (the refusals are config.profile == "reference"): the refusal is a reference-profile control, not a development-profile one. build_plan therefore sets RuntimePlan.legacy_guarded_effects from the profile, and a protected node with no governed context behaves like this:

nodereference profile (CALIBER_PROFILE=reference)development profile (the default)
webhook or API-request node, no contextrefused: '<node>' requires a governed effect context for manifest HTTP execution_perform_guarded_effect: egress policy, then the legacy effect ledger (at most one send per run, node and input across a restart; a definitive failure is retryable, an ambiguous one is reported indeterminate)
protected registered tool, no contextrefused: '<node>' requires a governed effect context to run protected registered tool '<name>'runs inline, as before B04.3, behind the node's own approval gate (requires_approval); no ledger, as before
protected OpenAPI tool, no contextrefused: '<node>' requires a governed effect context to run protected OpenAPI tool '<name>'runs inline, as before B04.4, behind the node's own approval gate, through the named legacy entry bind_legacy_openapi_http_tool (the private raw transport; the public entry still refuses a protected method)
protected MCP tool or MCP node, no context (B04.5)refused: '<node>' requires a governed effect context to run protected MCP tool '<name>'runs inline through the gateway entry point, as before B04.5, behind the node's own approval gate; unclassified and blocked tools are still refused
read-class tool, GET OpenAPI node or read-class MCP toolruns inlineruns inline (unchanged)
any node, a context is boundgoverned pathgoverned path: a bound context is never bypassed and a refusal from it is final

What the development path does not guarantee. It is not the governed path and gives none of its guarantees: no persisted proposal, no exact-intent approval (the node's own approval is a legacy gate that approves "this node may run", not "this exact request"), no distinct-approver check at the effect, no execution-owner lease recheck, no receipt, no registered_tool/http/openapi_http connector admission, no reconciler. The HTTP path keeps the legacy ledger's at-most-once claim; the tool paths have only what they had before the dispatcher. Nothing about it is a Beta or reference claim (ADR 0001: features outside the shape stay out of Beta claims), and the operator effects view labels such rows legacy_ledger, not proposals.

What stays refused in every profile. Only the "no governed context" refusal is profile-dependent. Everything else in the route still applies in both: the built-ins the inventory refuses (EP-055 host-file tools, sandbox_python: unsupported_effect_path), a binding that is not its registry row, an unreadable registry, a tool with no readable OpenAPI row, an OpenAPI call replaced by an injected callable once governed, egress policy, and the preflight checks. A model-chosen OpenAPI call and Aria's published-tool call are not tool nodes, so they never take the legacy entry: in both profiles they use the public executor entry, which refuses a protected method (unsupported_effect_path). Calibration and refinement build RuntimePlan directly, so their flag is False and a candidate manifest's protected tools are refused there. The evaluation route (routes/evaluations.py) calls build_plan, so in the development profile its plan carries the flag; that is harmless, because a preview blocks HTTP nodes and the governed tool routes return None in a preview (a replay does not reach the legacy path, and the legacy OpenAPI entry is never bound for a preview).

How the switch is made. RuntimePlan.legacy_guarded_effects defaults to False (fail-closed), so a plan built by any caller other than build_plan and every reference-profile plan refuses. build_plan sets it to config.profile == "development", an allow-list, so a profile added later is fail-closed until it is listed; a missing config is the development profile, as everywhere else in build_plan. One helper, _legacy_effects_allowed(plan) (the flag and no bound context), is the only place the runtime decides it, for the HTTP, registered-tool and OpenAPI routes and for the legacy OpenAPI binding. bind_legacy_openapi_http_tool is named only by workflows/runtime.py (pinned by tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py::test_the_development_profile_legacy_entry_is_named_only_by_the_runtime). There is no setting, environment variable, route or migration, and no approval hook: nothing returns True for an authorization.

Cookbook labs. The labs run the development profile and create manifest-backed plans, so they depend on this path: the worker binds the governed context (#1051) in the reference profile only. Their UI specs depended on a second profile-blind rule: the console's Run control (#968) required an approved workspace release and environment for every project workflow, which the development server does not require, so its Run button stayed disabled. The console now offers and requires the pair only when GET /capabilities reports workflow_runs.lineage_required (true exactly where the server refuses a run without lineage: the reference profile). The Cookbook labs workflow now also runs on pull requests that touch the workflow runtime, the effect dispatcher, integrations, policy, the run worker and routes, profile.py and config.py, and on every push to main that touches them (it takes about fifty minutes, so it is not a required check).

Moving off it. #1051 wired the context in the worker (an authorization provider, the execution-owner lease, park and resume while an approval is pending), for the reference profile only: the development profile has no execution-owner lease to dispatch under, and no generic connector has an authoritative receipt verifier yet (#1055). legacy_guarded_effects is therefore not removed: it goes when the development profile can dispatch under a lease and the workflow connectors can be verified. A deployment that needs the exact-intent guarantees must run CALIBER_PROFILE=reference, where a protected workflow node is refused rather than sent without them.

Memory is owned, derived and read-mostly#

Until the owned memory lifecycle (M20: retention, legal hold, deletion) exists, the reference profile does not offer free-form durable memory (B12 memory, #667). The /memory API and the in-run memory tools behave as follows:

  • No free-form partition. agent_id must name an agent or workflow, and run_id a workflow run, that the caller can see; user_id must be the caller's own identity, admins included. A scope value that is present but not a non-empty string is a 400, not ignored. A run id alone is refused (403).
  • The partition is pinned to the caller. With an agent_id, the memory is the caller's own within that agent or workflow (the server adds user_id); with none, it is the caller's own namespace, qualified by the active project (<project>:<user>). A client never chooses whose memory a read or write reaches, and metadata may not carry user_id, agent_id, run_id or actor_id (400), because mem0 filters on those stored fields.
  • One refusal, no disclosure. A partition that does not exist, one that belongs to another project or user, and a label that names nothing all answer 404 memory partition not found; no id is echoed.
  • Writes are verbatim. POST /memory requires infer=false (403 otherwise), because LLM-inferred writes create durable facts nobody owns; and startup refuses CALIBER_MEMORY_INFER=true while memory is enabled (table above).
  • No bulk deletion. DELETE /memory answers 403: deleting memory needs the lifecycle's retention and legal-hold rules.
  • Bounded reads. top_k is capped at 100.
  • In-run tools. memory_search, memory_add, memory_list and list_entities act on the run initiator's memory within the workflow (the initiator is set by the server, never by the model); a run with no initiator gets no memory tools.
  • Same rules below the route. The service layer refuses bulk delete, inferred writes, run-only partitions and partition keys in metadata (MemoryLifecycleUnavailableError). It does not itself check that an agent_id or user_id belongs to the caller: the route and the in-run tool binding do that and are the only callers.

The development profile keeps the previous behaviour. The service uses mem0 2.x's supported scope contract for search and list: entity identifiers are passed in the filters mapping, not as top-level arguments. add and delete_all retain mem0's entity-keyword API, while list_entities already passes its scope as filters. This keeps the installed mem0 release and the service wrapper on the same boundary without changing the reference profile's ownership or lifecycle refusals.

Trace payload visibility in review surfaces#

Reference-profile trace visibility and trace-payload visibility are separate decisions. A caller may see a trace or a review queue without being allowed to read request, response, span input, span output, or governed trace attributes. For a project-owned experiment, the current project owner and editor roles may read those payloads; viewers and reviewers do not. An administrator without membership in the owning project is not an implicit payload reader.

The observability trace detail route and the review-queue alignment-example route use the same fail-closed contract: non-payload identifiers, status, timing, review question answers, provenance, and assessment identifiers remain, while governed request/response values are replaced with stable [redacted:<field>] placeholders. The queue detail route itself contains item identifiers and review metadata only; it does not grant payload access.

POST /eval-datasets/{dataset_id}/examples/from-trace first resolves trace identity and visibility without mapping payloads. It then requires trace.payload.read before copying the source request or response. A visible trace without that permission receives 403, a foreign or unknown trace receives the same 404 as a missing trace, and neither refusal changes the dataset version or inserts an example. Supplying explicit input or expected values does not bypass the source-trace authorization check. An authorized example records the from-trace and source trace tags.

The development profile retains its earlier behavior; these payload gates are part of the reference-profile contract.

Governed effect spans: the ids that link a trace to its rows (B11.3a, #737)#

A governed effect crosses four persisted records: the effect proposal, the policy decision that authorised the run, the runtime approval that was consumed, and the effect itself, which is its verified receipt. The spans of that path name those rows, so an operator can go from a trace to the database without reading any payload. The module is caliber.observability.span_attributes; B11.3b (#745) reads the same attributes back as a causal chain.

Span (type)Opened byAttributes it can carry
effect.approval.commit_check (CHAIN)approval_valid_at_commitcaliber.proposal_id once the locked proposal is read; caliber.approval_id once the request is bound to that proposal's exact intent, policy and evidence; caliber.decision_id from the run's current policy decision, only when every check passed
effect.dispatch (TOOL)dispatchcaliber.proposal_id from the proposal read; caliber.approval_id and caliber.decision_id from the validator's answer; caliber.effect_id after the settlement has committed
effect.receipt.write (CHAIN)record_receiptcaliber.proposal_id; the proposal's recorded approval (caliber.approval_id for an exact-intent approval, caliber.decision_id for a policy decision); caliber.effect_id once the receipt is stored in the caller's transaction

run_tags(ctx, node_id=..., proposal_id=..., decision_id=..., approval_id=..., effect_id=...) accepts the same four ids for a caller that has read them from a row, and emits each as caliber.<name> only when given.

An id is a link only if a row backs it. An attribute is absent, never blank or guessed, when the platform has not read that row: a proposal that never reached a verified receipt has no caliber.effect_id (unknown and failed included), the receipt-write span has no caliber.decision_id for an exact-intent approval (the proposal row does not store it), and the approval id a caller passes to dispatch is a claim until the validator has bound it to the proposal, so a refused dispatch never carries it. caliber.effect_id is the receipt id: the platform's only record that the downstream effect happened and was read back.

What can reach a span. Four keys, one allow-list, no payload:

  • Only the four keys above, caliber.refusal_code and the tracer's own caliber.status, caliber.error_type and caliber.error are set on these spans. No URL, argument, request, response, scope, approver, evidence hash or exception message is ever an attribute.
  • A value must be a plain string that is an opaque identifier: ASCII letters, digits, ., _, :, -, starting with a letter, at most 128 characters. Anything else (a number, an email address, whitespace, a path, a longer string) is dropped, not truncated: a truncated id would name a different row.
  • A workflow manifest cannot assert a link. Its mlflow.trace_group_tags are merged into the run tags first, and the five reserved keys are removed from them, so a tag named caliber.proposal_id is ignored.
  • A failure inside one of these spans is recorded as the exception type and, only when it is a platform refusal (ProposalError, EffectRefused, ApprovalCommitRefused), its stable caliber.refusal_code such as stale_version; the code of any other exception is not copied. The exception is re-raised after the span has closed, so MLflow's own exception event, which keeps the message, never sees it on these three spans. The re-raised exception still passes through any enclosing span (the workflow node span, trace_run), where MLflow records its message as it did before this change.
  • Tracing never changes the outcome of an effect: a redactor or tracer failure while setting one of these attributes is logged at debug level and the attribute is absent (the value is never sent unredacted).

Who can see them. The ids, caliber.refusal_code and the existing run, node and job ids are on profile.SAFE_SPAN_ATTRIBUTES, so a caller who may see a trace but not read its payload (B11.4b, above) sees them; every other span attribute stays [redacted:attributes.<key>], which includes caliber.error. An id does not widen who can open a trace: the trace, and then the row, still follow experiment and project visibility. caliber.approval_id is also the name of an existing release tag (AP-..., a prompt-version approval, see the prompts architecture page); on these spans it is always a runtime approval (RAP-...), told apart by the span name.

Refusal and recovery, with exact examples.

  • A stale approval. The recheck finds the resource moved on. The effect.approval.commit_check span has caliber.proposal_id, caliber.approval_id, caliber.refusal_code = stale_version and caliber.status = failed, and no caliber.decision_id; effect.dispatch has caliber.proposal_id and the same code. Nothing was sent, the approval is unconsumed and the proposal is still proposed. Recovery: request a new approval for the current resource version.
  • An approval id that is not this run's. The recheck answers not_found; no span carries that id, only the proposal (read from the row) and the code. Recovery: use the id returned when the request was created.
  • A lease lost after the effect was sent. effect.dispatch has the proposal, approval and decision (the claim had committed), caliber.refusal_code = lease_lost and no caliber.effect_id; no receipt exists and the proposal stays dispatched. Recovery is unchanged: the reconciler asks the downstream by key under the new lease.
  • An answer nobody could verify (an ambiguous transport result, or a 2xx the downstream's own query did not confirm). The proposal becomes unknown; effect.dispatch completes without caliber.effect_id. A missing effect id is the signal, not an error.

Not covered, said plainly. The node span of a workflow run does not carry these ids (the dispatcher's own spans do, and the same ids are in the database); the legacy effect-ledger path used by a plan with no governed context emits none; and the receipt-write span describes a write: if the caller's transaction is rolled back afterwards, the dispatch span, which names the effect only after commit, is the authority. Tracing is inert unless MLflow is installed and tracing is enabled, and an exporter failure never changes what the effect does.

Configuration, migration and rollback. No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. The spans open inside the transaction that holds the approval locks, but make no database call of their own. Rolling back is reverting the change; traces already recorded keep their attributes.

Reading the links back: GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/causal-links (B11.3b, #745)#

The spans above name rows; this endpoint returns the rows. It answers, for one run, with the persisted records that connect it to its governed effects, by id, digest, state and timestamp only, so a reviewer (or the evidence package of B14) can follow run -> manifest -> step context -> proposal -> approval -> decision -> receipt without reading a payload. It is read-only and is implemented by caliber.observability.causal_links (read_causal_links), which takes an already-authorized run row and never an id from a request.

Who may call it. The same access as reading the run (a run you cannot see is 404) plus a role in the run's project (read: viewer, reviewer, editor or owner), evaluated on every request from the caller's current membership. A caller who can see the run but has no role in its project, a caller from another project, a platform administrator with no project role (caliber.admin is not a project role) and an unknown id all get the same 404 (workflow run '<id>' not found), and a malformed parameter from such a caller is also that 404, never a 400. Nothing in the query string (a project, a second run id) widens access. A run with no project is gated by its workflow's visibility alone, as the admission manifest is.

Sections and paging. section is effects (the default), context_manifests or policy_decisions; only that list is filled and the other two are []. limit is 1 to 200 (default 50). cursor is the opaque next_cursor of the previous page (the id of its last row); while has_more is true pass it back. Pages are keyset pages ordered by (timestamp, id), so rows that share a timestamp are neither skipped nor repeated, and a cursor that names no row of this run, or is not one this API issued, is 400 cursor is invalid (a cursor from another run opens nothing). A page costs a fixed number of queries (the run manifest, the page, and one lookup each for contexts, approvals, decisions and receipts), not one per effect.

What an effect shows. For each proposal: proposal_id, node_id, occurrence_id, node_step_id, state, connector, connector_version, effect_class, intent_hash and the two timestamps, then four links, each with a status and, when it is not simply linked, a stable code. The statuses: linked (a row of this run), not_required (the record shows the link is not on this effect's path), pending (the effect is still in flight, so the row is expected to appear), missing (the chain needs a row, the effect is settled or the stored id names nothing, and there is none: a broken chain) and unrecorded (the platform does not store this link against the effect, so it can be neither followed nor called broken). In-flight work is never missing:

LinklinkedOther statuses and codes
context_manifestthe latest context manifest of this node occurrence (highest attempt, then highest revision), by id, revision, attempt and digestunrecorded / no_context_manifest_for_node_step (a step that is not an agent step has none, and the proposal does not say which kind of step it came from, so its absence is neither followable nor proven broken)
approvalan exact-intent approval request the proposal records, bound to this proposal in this run: ids, digests, request status, superseded_by, requested, decided, expires and consumed timestampsnot_required / approved_by_policy_decision; pending / approval_not_consumed (a request exists but the dispatcher has not consumed it; its id and status are shown), approval_not_requested; not_required / failed_before_approval (settled failed with no approval ever recorded); missing / approval_row_missing (the stored approval id names no row bound to this proposal in this run)
decisionthe policy decision that authorised the effect, by id and run: the one a policy-approved read names, or, for an exact-intent effect consumed since migration 0134, the commit-time decision stored on its approval request. Id, action, result, reason codes, policy version, input hash, evaluated-atunrecorded / decision_recorded_per_run_only (an exact-intent effect consumed before 0134, below); pending / not_approved_yet; not_required / failed_before_approval; missing / decision_row_missing (the stored decision id names no decision of this run)
effectthe verified receipt: effect_id (the receipt id, the id caliber.effect_id carries), attempt, receipt and response digests, verified-at, and committed (true when the proposal records that receipt as the one that settled it)pending with not_dispatched, outcome_pending, outcome_unknown or reconciled_without_receipt, by the proposal's state (the effect is not settled); not_required / failed_without_receipt (settled failed: nothing was verified and nothing will be); missing / receipt_row_missing (settled committed, which requires a receipt, but no receipt row is there)

missing_links lists only the missing links (a broken chain) and unrecorded_links the unrecorded ones, so a complete chain (missing_links == []) is distinguishable from a broken one, and a healthy exact-intent effect consumed since migration 0134 has missing_links == [] and a linked decision (unrecorded_links names only context_manifest for a non-agent step; one consumed earlier also names decision). An absent effect_id is the marker for an effect that has no verified receipt, in the API as on the span; it is never filled in from a neighbouring row, a timestamp or the proposal's state.

span_attributes is the caliber.* attribute map that the effect's resolved rows support, built by the same allow-list function (causal_attributes). It is a derived union, not what any one span carries: each span binds only the ids it had read when it closed (the receipt span binds the proposal's recorded approval ref even if that row is gone). The commit-time decision_id of an exact-intent effect is listed when its approval request stored it and the decision row resolved for this run; for an effect consumed before 0134 it is not listed (the dispatch span still carries it). An id is listed only when its row resolved for this run. Nothing is read from the tracing backend, so it cannot confirm that a trace was exported.

Digests. manifest_digest (run and context manifests), receipt_digest and a policy decision's input_hash are bare lowercase SHA-256 hex (64 characters). intent_hash, evidence_hash, policy_digest and response_digest are sha256:-prefixed (71 characters). They are stored in those forms and returned unchanged; compare like with like.

The decision of an exact-intent approval (B11.3c, #1061). The commit-time check (approval_valid_at_commit) records a run decision (resource.execute on workflow:<id>, the run authority) and the dispatch span names it. Since migration 0134 the dispatcher also stores that decision's id on the approval request it consumes (caliber_runtime_approval_requests.commit_decision_id), in the same claim transaction and the same UPDATE that sets consumed_at, from the ApprovalCommit the validator returned; a refused or rolled-back dispatch leaves neither. The proposal's frozen columns are not touched. The API resolves the id by run (and the request by proposal, as for approval), so for an exact-intent effect consumed after 0134 decision is linked with the decision's fields, caliber.decision_id is in span_attributes, and the id equals the PolicyDecision row in section=policy_decisions and the span's caliber.decision_id. A stored id that names no decision of this run is missing / decision_row_missing.

The database enforces the write (PostgreSQL and SQLite triggers): an INSERT cannot carry the column; an UPDATE may set it only from NULL, to a non-empty value, on a bound request whose consumed_at moves from NULL to a value in that same UPDATE; once set, neither it nor consumed_at can change. There is no backfill. A request consumed before 0134 keeps NULL, its effect's decision stays unrecorded / decision_recorded_per_run_only and its caliber.decision_id is not in span_attributes; the run's decisions are still listed per run (section=policy_decisions), and the API does not pair them by time. A consumer such as the evidence package (B14.1, #818) should treat decision: unrecorded on an exact-intent effect as "run authority asserted per run only" for those older effects: include the run's policy_decisions section and do not fail the chain or invent a pairing. The approval request's approval_request v1 contract is unchanged (the column is lifecycle state, like consumed_at, not part of what the approver is asked), and the causal-links response schema gains no field: the decision link already carries the decision's fields.

Whole-run markers. run_manifest is linked (id, schema version, digest, creation time; the manifest body stays at /admission-manifest), legacy (legacy_run_has_no_manifest: a run admitted before manifests has none and never will) or missing (manifest_row_missing: an admitted run whose row is not there). acceptance and evidence_package are {status: not_available, code: acceptance_record_not_available | evidence_package_not_available}: those records (B09, B14) do not exist yet and are never synthesized. trace_id is the run's stored trace id, a pointer only.

What it never returns.
