So is a deadlock in which the decision is the victim (SQLSTATE 40P01, a writer that takes the run and request rows in the opposite order) and, on SQLite, the busy timeout (database is locked, which surfaces at the decision's first write because SQLite has no row locks); the mapping covers the whole decision session (_decision_session), and any other database error is not mapped. Clock. Expiry is judged by the application clock (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) read after the run lock is won, the same clock that wrote expires_at (so a request is never judged by two clocks); at the claim it is the dispatcher's now (defaulting to the same clock). The database clock is deliberately not used (ownership.database_now is "never for deciding expiry"): nodes that share a database need synchronized clocks, and a request is honoured or refused by the node's clock to within its skew, which is why the window is half-open and the tests pin the microsecond. The dispatcher then rechecks the exact intent, evidence, policy, version and every approver's current authority in its claim transaction (run, proposal, request locks, under the lease the execution owner captured): each approver of the quorum must still hold the project approve action and not be the run's initiator or the requester, and the quorum (approval_count) must be met by approvers who remain authorized (role_revoked / self_approval otherwise, not_approved when the recorded approvers are fewer than the quorum). The platform scopes are one set the producer attests for the approving principals; membership and role are read per approver. Known limitation: the platform scopes of earlier approvers of a quorum are not re-derived at the claim. They were checked when each approved (the decision route), and at the claim only the last approver's attested scopes are applied (the one set the producer passes); a scope an earlier approver lost after deciding is not seen, while a lost project role or membership is. It sets consumed_at in the same commit as proposed -> approved -> dispatched and the outbox row, so concurrent dispatchers consume once. If the process dies after that commit and before the remote call, the durable dispatched row and outbox entry remain recoverable; a retry reads the proposal state (already_dispatched) and does not send again. The same UPDATE stores the commit-time policy decision's id on the request (commit_decision_id, migration 0134; see the causal-links section), so a refused or rolled-back claim leaves neither the consumption nor the id. A decision does not wake the run. It stays waiting_approval until POST .../resume (operator scope) requeues it. Limits. An approved decision that dispatch has not consumed cannot be withdrawn, other than by revoking the approver's project role (the claim rechecks it) or by superseding the request; rejecting a bound request fails the run but leaves its proposal proposed, and no reaper settles proposals of ended runs. Both are tracked in #1074.
from caliber.effects.dispatcher import EffectRefused, admit_backend, dispatch, submit_proposal

proposal = submit_proposal(
    session,
    workflow_run_id=run_id,
    node_id="ask",
    occurrence_id=occurrence_id,
    action=proposed_action,
    admission=admit_backend("document_request"),  # a kind your own code chose; see "Trusted connector admission"
)
session.commit()
try:
    result = dispatch(
        session_factory,
        proposal.proposal_id,
        approval_id=runtime_approval_id,
        approver_scopes={"caliber.approver"},
        lease=execution_lease,
        backend_kind="document_request",
        backend_config={"base_url": downstream_url},
        approval_validator=approval_valid_at_commit,
    )
except EffectRefused as refused:
    # Stable code only; re-read the proposal and approval before deciding whether to retry.
    logger.info("effect refused: %s", refused.code)

If the private transport returns proven_not_sent or a definitive rejection, the proposal settles failed. A committed HTTP response is only a claim: the connector verifier must return a receipt matching the logical key and intent before the proposal becomes committed. A timeout, process loss or verifier failure leaves a recoverable dispatched/unknown record; do not call dispatch again with a new occurrence. Hold the execution lease and use the reconciler's lookup-by-key path to settle it, or retry after a lease_lost refusal with a fresh lease and a fresh read.

  • Fenced by the lease (B05.5a, #734). Every move into or out of dispatched (dispatching, and committing, failing or marking unknown) must carry lease=, the Lease the owner captured when it acquired the execution-owner lease (see below), with lease.owner_id == owner_id. In the same transaction as the write (and, in settle_dispatch, the receipt), caliber.ownership.assert_fenced compares the persisted owner and fencing token for equality and the expiry against the database's clock; on PostgreSQL the lease row stays locked until the transaction ends, so a takeover waits for the settle instead of overtaking it. No lease is evidence_required (and a value that is not a Lease is bad_field); another owner's lease is stale_owner; a lease that is expired, taken over (an older token), never issued (a future token) or not the execution-owner lease at all (another lease name) is lease_lost. A fence that could not be asked (the database failed, timed out, or was serialized away) is store_failed, not lease_lost: roll back and retry from a fresh read. Each refusal records nothing: a stale worker cannot commit, cannot fail, and cannot even mark the attempt unknown itself, and a receipt it was about to record is rolled back with the refused move. The attempt stays dispatched for the reconciler (below), which asks the downstream by key under the new lease. A repeat of the owner's move is fenced too: applied=False tells a worker "recorded, this attempt is yours", and a worker that lost its lease must not hear that and go on to send the effect (it is lease_lost). Recovery: re-read proposal_state; if it is still dispatched under another owner, do nothing and let the reconciler find it; never re-dispatch. Moves that are not the owner's (approved, reconciled, the callback's commit) are not fenced by it, and neither is record_receipt on its own: a receipt is a verified statement about the downstream, and only settle_dispatch (receipt and state move together, lease first, then receipt, then proposal) is the owner's commit path. Moving a dispatched proposal under a different owner's lease, which the reconciler must do, is not possible here by design (stale_owner): it has its own entry point, abandon_dispatch (below).
from caliber.effects.records import StaleVersion, proposal_state, transition

state = proposal_state(session, proposal_id)
try:
    transition(
        session,
        proposal_id,
        "dispatched",
        expected_version=state.version,
        owner_id=lease.owner_id,
        attempt=1,
        lease=lease,  # captured at acquire(); expired or taken over means ProposalError "lease_lost" and nothing recorded
    )
    session.commit()
except StaleVersion as stale:
    session.rollback()  # someone else moved it: re-read stale.current_state and decide again
  • Limits. The occurrence id is allocated and persisted by the caller before the effect is attempted; this module records it and cannot tell whether a caller reused one wrongly. deployment is this installation's one configured organization (ADR 0001). Connector capability, receipts and reconciliation remain separate services below.

Trusted connector admission (B12.3a, #738)#

A private transport is admitted by what CALIBER can check about the code that will send, never by a name. The pinned record is caliber.profile.REFERENCE_CONNECTORS (ADR 0001, "trusted connectors only"); caliber.effects.dispatcher.admit_backend(kind) compares the transport registered under kind with it, and caliber.effects.admission holds the pure rules.

what is boundhow it is checkedrefused with
the connector id and versionthe registration must name the record's connector and connector_versionconnector_not_admitted
the implementationmodule:qualname of the registered transport's class (or function), read from the object: a subclass, a lookalike class or a bare function is a different implementationconnector_implementation_mismatch
the capability recordthe registration carries a ConnectorCapability and its digest() equals the pinned one; every risk it carries (write_not_exactly_once, key_retention_unconfirmed) must be listed in the record's accepted_risksconnector_capability_unproven (none, not a record, or an unaccepted risk), connector_capability_mismatch (another digest: a changed promise is a new digest)
the wire configurationthe digest of what the transport sends with (for the document-request connector: the submit and lookup operations, the key header and the accepted resource shape) equals the pinned oneconnector_configuration_mismatch
the settings handed to dispatchonly the record's config_keys, every required_config_keys present, each value bounded: a base_url is http(s) with a host, a valid port, and no userinfo, whitespace, control characters, query or fragment; max_attempts is 1 to 5; timeout_seconds is finite, above 0 and at most 300connector_config_not_admitted

The reference profile admits five connectors: document_request (connector document-request, version 1: the Beta reference connector, which has a stable key, a precondition and a lookup by key; its key retention is unconfirmed, and that risk is accepted by name), the generic http transport that governed webhook and API nodes use (it promises no exactly-once behaviour, so every effect through it needs the caller's own receipt verifier), the registered_tool transport of governed registered tools, and the openapi_http transport of governed OpenAPI tools (connector openapi-http; settings operation and receipt_verifier; it promises nothing about the downstream either), and the mcp transport of governed MCP tools (connector mcp-tool; settings call and receipt_verifier; no key, precondition or lookup, so a result is only a claim). The dispatcher refuses everything else: host-file exports, PostgreSQL MCP writes (EP-114) and any transport added to BACKENDS without a reviewed record. The mcp record admits the MCP transport for a classified call, not a server: the stdio command and remote-host allowlists still decide which servers can be reached. Each has no record in the table, so a proposal or dispatch that goes through the dispatcher is unsupported_backend (no registration) or connector_not_admitted (registered, not pinned), and the host-file and database-write tools are also unsupported_effect_path through the protected-effect inventory (EP-055, EP-114).

What is not gated yet. Only the dispatcher is gated. The paths that would reach host files or a database write do not go through it today, so these tools still execute outside the dispatcher until the later B04 and B12 work: model-selected calls in B04.6 (#768), where a protected MCP tool a model chooses is meanwhile refused by the gateway entry point (B04.5); the raising of unsupported_in_reference_profile for every inventory row marked refuse, which is what stops the host-file tools (EP-055) and the first-party database MCP write tools (EP-114) at run time, in B04.7 (#774); and (landed in B12.3b, #746) the startup refusal of any MCP stdio command or remote host on the two allowlists (MCP allowlists), which leaves no MCP server reachable in a reference deployment. Until the other two land, a reference deployment must not wire the host-file tools into a workflow (see "Refused until explicitly supported" below).

Where it is enforced:

  • submit_proposal requires admission=admit_backend(kind). A proposal that only names a connector (in an action, a manifest, a tool call or a model's output) is refused with connector_not_admitted before a row is written, so no approval is requested for it. The admission is re-verified against the live registry on every submit, and the intent's connector and version must be the admitted ones. Call admit_backend with a kind your own code chose, never one that came from data.
  • dispatch admits the transport itself, before the claim. A transport nobody pinned, or settings it does not accept, is refused with the proposal still proposed, its approval unconsumed and no connector called. The transport's identity digests (implementation, capability and configuration, never settings or payloads) are written into the effect.proposal.dispatched outbox event as connector_admission.
  • A user tool cannot pose as a connector. Tool registration (POST /tools) and the assistant's tool publisher refuse the names document_request, document-request, http, registered_tool, openapi_http, openapi-http, mcp and mcp-tool (and their tool.<name>.vN and case variants) with 409 reserved_tool_name, like a built-in's name. A tool already registered under such a name before this rule is not rewritten; it is untrusted, is never classified as a connector, and is flagged once by the reserved-name audit (flag_reserved_tool_name, plus one ERROR log per process that names the connector, not a built-in). Upgrade impact: no new version can be registered under such a name (409 reserved_tool_name), so a deployment with a tool called http (the most likely collision) registers it again under a different name, repoints the workflows that use it, then archives the old row.

Refusal and recovery (every code is stable and carries no payload, setting or URL):

codemeaningrecovery
unsupported_backendno transport is registered under that kinduse a registered kind; an MCP, host-file or database-write path is not supported in the reference profile
connector_not_admittedno pinned record for the transport, or the proposal names a connector the admission does not coversubmit with admission=admit_backend(<the kind that carries this connector>); an unpinned transport needs a reviewed record in REFERENCE_CONNECTORS
connector_implementation_mismatchthe registered transport is not the pinned implementationrestore the shipped transport; do not subclass or replace it
connector_capability_unproven / connector_capability_mismatchno capability record, an unaccepted risk, or a changed promiserestore the record; a changed promise is a code change that updates the pin in review
connector_configuration_mismatchthe transport's wire configuration is not the pinned onerestore the shipped configuration
connector_config_not_admittedbackend_config has an unknown or missing key or an out-of-bounds valuepass only base_url (and optionally max_attempts, timeout_seconds) for document_request; sender and receipt_verifier for http; invoker and receipt_verifier for registered_tool; operation (an OpenApiOperation built from the tool's registry row, never a name or a dict) and receipt_verifier for openapi_http; call (an McpToolCall the runtime built, never a name or a dict) and receipt_verifier for mcp
from caliber.effects.dispatcher import UnsupportedEffectPath, admit_backend

try:
    admission = admit_backend("document_request")
except UnsupportedEffectPath as refused:
    logger.error("connector not admitted: %s", refused.code)  # e.g. connector_implementation_mismatch

What admission is not:

  • Identity, not integrity. The pins say which code and which declared shape were reviewed. A class that forges its __module__ and __qualname__, or a registry entry replaced by in-process code that also controls profile.py, is admitted: code running inside the server process is trusted and is outside this control's threat model. The "configuration digest" covers the declared wire constants (operations, key header, accepted resource shape), not what the transport's code does with them, and the capability digest covers the documented promise, not a measurement of it. Behaviour is covered by the connector tests, not by the pin.
  • Data cannot mint an admission, code can. A manifest, a tool name, a client request or a model's output cannot produce an AdmittedConnector. submit_proposal re-verifies the value it is given against the live registry; an equal object built by hand from the public table passes that check (it carries no secret). That is harmless, because only trusted code reaches it and the object grants nothing a call to admit_backend would not, but it is not an unforgeable capability.
  • The address is not pinned. The pin binds the transport's code and shape, not the downstream's address. The address a dispatch uses is validated for shape only (http or https, a host, a valid port, no userinfo, whitespace or control characters, query or fragment: a pure check with no name resolution) and the executor still applies the egress policy at send time; binding it to the CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS entry the reconciler asks for belongs with the callers that wire the connector (B04.3 and later).

Configuration and rollback: no new setting and no migration. Reverting the change restores the unchecked registry lookup; proposals already recorded are unaffected.

Connectors: what they promise and what an answer proves#

Before the dispatcher (B04.1) sends an effect it needs two things that are not guesses (B05.3, #711; caliber/src/caliber/effects/connectors/): a capability record saying what the connector has been shown to do, and a typed outcome for each request that is never more optimistic than the evidence.

  • The capability record (ConnectorCapability): the stable-key header and its scope (downstream, resource or unknown) and retention (unbounded, bounded with seconds, or unconfirmed), what the connector answers when a key is reused for a different request and when a precondition is stale, the 4xx statuses it documents as "refused, nothing committed" (definitive_rejection_statuses), whether it can be asked "did my key commit?" and how consistent that is, and whether a "not found" proves the effect can never happen (absence_proves_noncommit, which also needs a lookup that reads its own writes). A contradictory record is refused when it is built, and digest() is the sha256: that connector admission binds (a changed promise is a new digest). carries_a_write_exactly_once is true only for a connector with a key of known scope that refuses conflicts, a lookup by key of known consistency and a precondition; whether its retention is confirmed is separate (retention_confirmed), and admission must require it or record the accepted risk. The document-request record (effects/connectors/document_request.py::CAPABILITY) is what its fixture shows through the real executor: Idempotency-Key; the same key replays (201 then 200) and commits once, before the precondition is checked (a retry after the commit is a 200, not a 412); the same key for a different request is 422; If-Match carries the case's integer version and a stale one is 412; the lookup (GET /document-requests?idempotency_key=) reads its own writes. Two claims are argued from the fixture's code, not measured, and are the ones to confirm against the real system: the key is one namespace for the whole downstream (the fixture holds one case), and a 404 does not prove non-commit (a request in flight at the downstream may still commit; no tombstone, no cancel), so absence_proves_noncommit is false. Key retention is unconfirmed (the fixture never expires a key).
  • The four outcomes (TransportOutcome) from classify_status / classify_result (a tool result) with the capability: proven_not_sent (see classify_error: the request never reached the downstream: refused before it was built, blocked by the egress policy, or every attempt failed to connect; recorded as not happened), definitive_rejection (a 4xx that the capability documents as a refusal, on the first and only dispatch: it committed nothing; recorded as failed), committed_receipt (200, 201 or 204: the downstream says it committed or replayed a commit; a claim that becomes committed only when its receipt is verified, B05.4) and ambiguous (everything else: a 4xx the capability does not name such as a gateway's 401 or 413 or a 409 "in progress", a 408, a 202 "accepted for later processing", a redirect, a 5xx, a dropped connection or a timeout after the request may have left, an error nobody classified; the proposal becomes unknown). A documented 4xx is also ambiguous when something earlier could have committed: an earlier attempt by the executor's own retry loop that may have reached the downstream (the result carries earlier_attempts_may_have_been_sent), or an earlier dispatch of the same effect the call cannot see (earlier_dispatch_possible=True, for a recovery after a crash), because a stale precondition on the retry is then caused by that commit. interpret_lookup(capability, status) returns answered (a 2xx: the downstream answered; what it holds is verified against the intent by B05.4), not_committed (a 404, only for a connector that proves absence) or unknown.
  • What the OpenAPI executor now reports and refuses (integrations/openapi/executor.py): OpenApiExecutionError carries never_sent, attempts, and attempt_log; every exception raised before a request is built carries never_sent=True. never_sent is true only if the request is known never to have reached the downstream, and false if any attempt may have (a dropped read, a read or write timeout, a 5xx that was then retried into a connection failure). A POST is retried only if its request carries exactly one idempotency key (from idempotency_key or header_params, header name matched case-insensitively): a bound header with no key behind it no longer enables retries; two different keys, or a blank key header, are refused rather than sent or dropped; a path parameter of . or .. is refused. For imported operations, the derived schema exposes idempotency_key and expected_resource_version as canonical fields and removes the bound Idempotency-Key/If-Match parameters from free-form header_params; conflicting canonical and header-map values are refused before dispatch. Results include attempt_log, replay_disposition, and receipt_disposition; the last is unverified until the connector lookup/receipt layer proves the downstream record matches the proposal. submit_input refuses a key that is not 1 to 255 printable ASCII characters without surrounding whitespace and a case_id that is not one safe path segment, before any request is built.

The dispatcher's private document_request backend does the following; it sends through the private raw transport (_send_raw), because the public execute_openapi_http_tool refuses a POST (unsupported_effect_path). Application code does not call it: a write is a proposal.

from caliber.effects.connectors import classify_error, classify_result
from caliber.effects.connectors.document_request import CAPABILITY, submit_config, submit_input
from caliber.integrations.openapi.executor import OpenApiExecutionError, _send_raw

try:
    result = _send_raw(
        execution_config=submit_config(server_url),
        input_schema=None,
        input_data=submit_input(
            case_id=case_id, idempotency_key=proposal_key, expected_resource_version=7, body={"document_type": "pay_statement"}
        ),
    )
    outcome = classify_result(result, capability=CAPABILITY).outcome  # committed_receipt, definitive_rejection or ambiguous
except OpenApiExecutionError as error:
    outcome = classify_error(error).outcome  # proven_not_sent, or ambiguous: the effect may have happened
  • Remaining boundary. #990 completes the executor/import plumbing: the dedicated canonical fields, import-persisted binding and retry limits, conflict refusal, and per-attempt/replay metadata are now available. The connector's submit_input still puts the key and version on the request itself, so the B04.1 dispatcher does not depend on the derived schema. Verified receipts and the reconciler remain B05.4 and B05.5; an executor 2xx or replay_candidate is not by itself proof of a committed receipt.

Receipts: committed only with proof (B05.4a, #717)#

A 2xx answer from a downstream is a claim. caliber.effects.receipts (table caliber_effect_receipts, migration 0125) turns it into a receipt only after the platform has asked the downstream's own query and what came back is this proposal's effect.

  • What a receipt is checked against. ReceiptFacts (what the connector read back) must carry the proposal's logical key as the stored idempotency key, hash (as the intent rebuilt from the stored request) to the proposal's intent_hash, name the proposal's connector, connector version and target resource, and answer the dispatch attempt the proposal recorded. A mismatch is refused with the names of the fields that differ (ReceiptMismatch, code receipt_mismatch), never their values. The document-request connector's facts_from_lookup also requires, when the proposal expected a case version, that the stored version is exactly one more; a lookup that answers 404, a 5xx, a body that is not a stored request, another case or another document type gives no facts (and is not a failure).
  • Immutable, one per attempt, not borrowable. A receipt is the canonical receipt v1 record and its SHA-256, refused for update or delete by database triggers (and on PostgreSQL a CHECK ties the digest to the bytes); read_receipt recomputes the record from the columns and checks it against its proposal (key, intent, attempt, connector, target), so a row edited in place is receipt_corrupt (rewriting the columns and the bytes together would not be detected: there is no MAC, a limit of every immutable table here). The same facts delivered twice are one receipt (created=False; the response digest is not compared, because it hashes the whole lookup body, which can gain a field between deliveries, and the first one stays recorded); a different request id or resource version for the same attempt, or a downstream request id that already belongs to another proposal or attempt, are receipt_conflict and never replace the first. A receipt can be recorded while the proposal is dispatched, unknown or reconciled, not before it was dispatched and not after it settled (receipt_state).
  • committed needs a receipt, and failed cannot have one. transition(..., COMMITTED, receipt_id=...) verifies the receipt exists, was read back (query), and answers this proposal's attempt, key and intent (receipt_refused otherwise); the id is recorded on the proposal, and the database refuses a move to committed whose receipt_id is empty, does not exist or is another proposal's or attempt's. Once a verified receipt exists the proposal cannot be moved to failed (receipt_exists; the database refuses it too): failed is final, and the downstream's own query said it committed. The database also refuses a receipt for a proposal that is not dispatched, unknown or reconciled.
  • Settling a dispatch. settle_dispatch(session, proposal_id, outcome=..., verify=..., lease=...) first checks the proposal is still dispatched at expected_version, held by this owner and attempt, under this owner's lease (another owner or attempt is refused before a query is made and records nothing; whether the lease is still held is decided at the write, never before the query, so the lease row is not locked across the network call; a repeat of a settle that already happened is stale_version), then records what one attempt proved, the receipt and the commit as one unit (a refused commit keeps no receipt; if verify raises the proposal stays dispatched): a committed_receipt claim runs verify() (the authoritative query) and commits with the receipt if it confirms, and otherwise leaves the proposal unknown (receipt_unverified): a 404 or a mismatching stored request never certifies a failure, because a downstream that does not know a key yet may still process it; a definitive_rejection is failed (rejected:<code>), proven_not_sent is failed (not_sent) and ambiguous is unknown (ambiguous:<code>).
from caliber.effects.connectors.document_request import facts_from_lookup
from caliber.effects.receipts import settle_dispatch
from caliber.effects.records import proposal_state, proposal_view

view = proposal_view(session, proposal_id)

def verify():
    found = lookup_by_key(view.logical_key)  # the connector's query: {"status_code": ..., "json": ...}
    return facts_from_lookup(view, lookup_status=found["status_code"], lookup_body=found["json"])

settled = settle_dispatch(
    session,
    proposal_id,
    expected_version=proposal_state(session, proposal_id).version,
    owner_id=owner_id,
    attempt=attempt,
    lease=lease,  # the lease the owner captured; fenced in this transaction (B05.4a/B05.5a)
    outcome=outcome,  # from classify_result / classify_error
    verify=verify,
)
  • What this does and does not prove. record_receipt can only compare the facts it is handed with the proposal, so a receipt is as sound as the connector verifier that built them from the downstream's answer. For document-request, facts_from_lookup confirms the stored key, case, document type and (when the proposal expected a version) a stored version exactly one more, which holds only for a proposal built with document_request.build_intent: its arguments are exactly {"document_type": ...}, because that is all the downstream stores; a proposal with other arguments would commit downstream and then stay unknown. The proposal's effect class and expected version come from the proposal itself, so only the key, case, document type and version are checked against the downstream's data. Under REPEATABLE READ PostgreSQL refuses a competing insert as a serialization failure (store_failed): roll back and retry from a fresh read.
  • Not here. The reconciler for unknown and abandoned dispatched proposals is below. The dispatcher delegates to these capability and receipt contracts; it does not infer a commit from an HTTP status alone.

Reconciler: only the owner asks about unknown and abandoned effects (B05.5b, #742)#

An effect with no recorded outcome is unknown, and an attempt whose dispatcher died or lost its lease while it was dispatched is abandoned: it may have been sent. Neither is ever dispatched again (there is no edge from unknown back to dispatched). caliber.effects.reconcile settles them the one way ADR 0003 allows: by asking the downstream by the original logical key, and believing only what it can prove.

  • Owner-only. reconcile_pass(factory, lease=..., targets=..., lookup=...) needs the Lease the execution owner captured, and every write re-compares it in the transaction that writes (fence_owner: exact owner and fencing token, database clock). No question is asked on a lease that is gone. A pass whose lease is taken over stops with ProposalError lease_lost; what it already settled stays settled and the new owner's pass takes the rest. The loop that runs the pass on an interval is below.
  • Abandoned means a prior lease. Migration 0126 records dispatch_token (the fencing token the owner held) with every dispatch. A dispatched proposal is abandoned exactly when its token is lower than the token of the lease the reconciler holds; abandon_dispatch then records unknown with reason abandoned_dispatch (under the reconciler's lease; not_abandoned for a dispatch under the current lease, which is in flight in this very process and is left alone unless the caller gives in_flight_seconds, see below, or one with no recorded token, which proves nothing). A dispatch under another token is also never a repeat of the dispatch before it.
  • Only authoritative terminal evidence moves it. The lookup runs outside any transaction, against the connector's own query, at the base_url of the CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS binding for that connector and project (so it goes through the egress policy), and is read by the connector's capability record (interpret_lookup):
    The downstream saysRecordedOutcome
    a stored request that is this proposal's effect (key, intent, target, expected version)verified receipt, reconciled, committed; one audit entrycommitted
    404 from a connector that proves absence final (tombstone or honoured cancel, reads its own writes)reconciled, failed (absence_proven)failed
    404 from any other connector (document-request included): delayed visibility, or a request still in flightnothingunknown
    5xx, 401 or any other statusnothingunknown (detail http_<code>)
    a 2xx whose body is not this proposal's effect (unreadable, or another request under the key)nothingunverified
    cannot be reached, or no binding for this connector and projectnothinglookup_failed / not_bound

    A proposal that another actor moved while the downstream was asked is moved and is not overwritten (the write is conditioned on the version that was read).

  • Unknown blocks what depends on it. The runtime asks plan.effect_gate before every node, at the top of every attempt of its retries and before a guardrail re-runs the agents feeding it, with the node and everything it may depend on: every node upstream of it by edge, and the inline children of each of those (a for_each / loop / error_boundary target, a boundary's compensate_with, an agent's handoff targets), which have no edges of their own. While an effect any of them asked for is dispatched, unknown or reconciled, the node does not run and the runtime returns a durable waiting_effect checkpoint (effect_reconciliation) containing the node inputs, proposal id, logical key and intent digest. The queued-run worker persists the run as waiting_effect with error_code=effect_reconciliation; it does not turn the refusal into a terminal failure or run the gated node. The refusal is never absorbed: a fan-out item, a loop iteration, an error boundary or its compensation does not turn it into the item's own error.
  • A parked run resumes as the same occurrence. After the reconciler or an authoritative receipt callback settles every proposal named in the checkpoint as committed or failed, the platform atomically changes that same run from waiting_effect to queued and records workflow.run.effect_resumed. The worker resumes from the checkpointed gated node, preserving the original run id, logical key and intent digest; it never creates a new logical occurrence or dispatches the proposal again. A proposal that remains dispatched, unknown or reconciled keeps the run parked. Manual POST /workflow-runs/{run_id}/resume and retry are refused while it is waiting_effect; only authoritative settlement wakes it. The proposal and run reason are visible in the parked_runs collection returned by GET /system/effects?source=proposal.
from caliber.effects.callbacks import parse_bindings
from caliber.effects.reconcile import reconcile_pass, targets_from_bindings

targets = targets_from_bindings(parse_bindings(config.effect_callback_connectors))
for result in reconcile_pass(session_factory, lease=lease, targets=targets):
    print(result.proposal_id, result.outcome, result.state)  # committed | failed | unknown | unverified | lookup_failed | not_bound | in_flight | moved
  • Timeout example (V08). The connector's timeout fires after the request went out (ambiguous, recorded unknown with reason ambiguous:may_have_been_sent; not failed, the downstream may have committed, and not committed, nobody read a receipt). The dependent run is parked at an effect_reconciliation checkpoint, nothing can dispatch the proposal again (illegal_transition from unknown to dispatched), and the next reconciler pass finds the stored request by the original key, commits it with a verified receipt and wakes the same run. Resuming the checkpoint produces one downstream mutation throughout (tests/egi_scenarios/test_v08_timeout_retry.py).
  • Refusals and recovery. lease_lost: you are no longer the owner, stop and let the new owner reconcile. store_failed: roll back and retry. unknown after a pass: nothing proves the outcome yet (delayed visibility looks like absence); the next pass asks again, the effect is never re-sent, and dependents stay blocked. There is no operator action that fails an unknown effect without the downstream's evidence, by design (the operator view below lists them and offers reconcile, which only asks); a connector that can prove absence should set absence_proves_noncommit.
  • Limits. A pass looks at every candidate (a backlog that stays unknown cannot hide a newer one) and does not renew the lease: the caller bounds it with budget_seconds and renews or stops in on_progress. A dispatched row under the current lease is in_flight and is the dispatcher's to settle (it records unknown itself on a settle error that is not a lost lease; the reconciler never abandons it, and expires it to unknown only past in_flight_seconds). A dispatched row with no recorded token (none exist in shipped code; a downgrade through 0125 drops the column) is never abandoned. One connector (document-request) can be reconciled; another needs a verifier and capability record in reconcile.CONNECTORS. The gate runs where the runtime does (the queued-run worker, not preview or evaluation, which refuse effect nodes). A subworkflow's child plan is built separately and is not gated (the legacy effect ledger is not installed there either).

The reconciler loop and the in-flight rule (B05.5d, #997)#

caliber.orchestrator.effect_reconciler.EffectReconcilerTask is the owner-only loop that calls reconcile_pass. It is one of the loops in worker_inventory() (owner_only, with a recovery row in ADR 0002), started and stopped with the others by the lifespan. It is built in the reference profile only (the execution-owner lease exists nowhere else, and a pass cannot act without one), and is on there unless CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_ENABLED=false; leave it on wherever a dispatcher can run, because without it an effect whose settle failed stays blocked until an operator asks.

SettingDefaultBoundsMeaning
CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_ENABLEDtrueflagBuild the loop in the reference profile
CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_INTERVAL_SECONDS151 to 3600, finiteSeconds between passes
CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_BUDGET_SECONDS201 to 600, finiteA pass stops starting lookups after this long; a lookup in progress finishes (its own timeout applies, 30 s by default) and the next pass continues after the last proposal looked at
CALIBER_EFFECT_IN_FLIGHT_MAX_SECONDS900300 to 86400, finiteHow long a dispatch may stay dispatched under the lease that is still current before the loop records it unknown. Must exceed the longest a dispatch can take: the executor's 30 s timeout times at most 5 attempts, its backoff (under 4 s) and the 30 s receipt lookup come to about 3 minutes, which the 300 s floor covers; a connector with a longer timeout needs a larger value
  • Under the lease, never as a secondary. The lifespan binds the loop to role.lease, the lease the ExecutionRoleController holds now. A tick with no lease (a secondary, or the controller dropped it) does nothing but write its own heartbeat. Each pass hands that exact lease to reconcile_pass, so every write compares it in its own transaction. The loop never renews the lease (the controller does, on its own thread); a loop that also renewed would be a second renewer.
  • Lease loss stops it between proposals. Before each proposal the pass checks that the controller still holds the same lease (owner and fencing token) and that no stop was requested; if not, it ends there (lease_changed or stopped) and nothing further is read, asked or written, so nothing new starts after the lease is lost. If the database refuses the lease first (it was taken over before the controller noticed), reconcile_pass raises lease_lost and the pass ends with nothing recorded. The next tick takes whatever lease the controller holds then; a re-acquired lease has a higher token and starts a fresh pass.
  • Bounded. No lock is held across a lookup (each proposal is read, asked about and written in separate transactions), and on PostgreSQL every transaction of the pass carries lock_timeout and statement_timeout of a third of CALIBER_EXECUTION_LEASE_SECONDS, like the controller's own lease calls. A budget-cut pass resumes after the last proposal it looked at, so a backlog of effects that stay unknown can neither starve the rest nor be the only thing ever looked at.
  • Targets are the CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS bindings (the base_url of each (connector, project) that may report a receipt). With none bound the loop still abandons the dispatches of lost leases and expires stuck in-flight ones, and every lookup reports not_bound.
  • Stop. A stop ends the pass at its next proposal and waits up to CALIBER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS for it. A lookup in progress is not interrupted; if it outlasts the grace the stop returns with a warning and that one proposal finishes alone (its writes stay fenced by the lease, so it cannot record anything once the lease is released). The reconciler holds no claims, so there is nothing to give back.
  • Liveness. A caliber_worker_heartbeats row of kind effect_reconciler is written every tick (idle ones too) and inside a long pass; a clean stop removes it. Nothing reads that kind yet: it is a row an operator can query.

The same-token stuck dispatch. abandon_dispatch only helps when the dispatching lease was taken over. When the dispatcher keeps its lease, sends the effect and then cannot record the outcome, the row would stay dispatched under the current token for good. Two rules close that, and neither sends anything (there is no edge from unknown back to dispatched):

  1. The dispatcher records unknown itself. If settle_dispatch fails for any reason other than "someone else owns the row now" (lease_lost, stale_owner, stale_version, illegal_transition), dispatch records unknown in a fresh transaction under the same captured lease, with the reason settle_failed:<code or exception class> (never the message), and then raises the original failure. The move is fenced like the settle: a lost lease, another owner or a row someone else already moved records nothing. It is best effort: if the store is still down it fails too and rule 2 applies.
  2. The loop expires it. A dispatched row whose dispatch_token is the current lease's own and which has been dispatched for longer than CALIBER_EFFECT_IN_FLIGHT_MAX_SECONDS becomes unknown (in_flight_expired, with an effect_in_flight_expired audit row in the same transaction) and is then asked about by key like any other unknown one. A younger row is in_flight and left alone. A row with no recorded token proves nothing and is never expired.

The dispatcher and the loop racing for one row. Both write under the lease row's lock (taken first) and both are conditioned on the version they read, so exactly one wins and the loser records nothing: if the dispatcher settles first the loop finds the row moved; if the loop expires it first, the dispatcher's settle is refused as stale_version (its receipt is rolled back with it), the row stays unknown, and the effect was sent once either way. The outcome is not lost: unknown is settled by a lookup by key, which finds the request for a connector that has one. Set the bound above the longest a dispatch can legitimately take (the transport's timeout times its attempts, plus the receipt lookup), or a slow dispatcher that was about to commit finds its row unknown instead.

Known limits. A connector with no lookup by key (the generic http connector has none) can never be settled by the loop: its unknown rows report not_bound every pass and keep blocking their dependents until a connector with a lookup is bound. Each pass looks at every open row, so a very large backlog of such rows costs a few queries each per pass. The loop is a single sequential worker. Proposals are still created only where a run supplies a governed effect context; see "Governed webhook and API-request nodes".

Operator reconciliation view: legacy claims and proposals, labelled apart (B05.6, #751)#

GET /caliber/system/effects (operator scope) lists two different records of an effect that may need a person, and never mixes them:

effects (source: legacy_ledger, source_version: ledger-v0)proposals (source: effect_proposal, source_version: proposal-v1)
What it isthe queued-run worker's claim ledger (caliber_effect_ledger)the ADR 0003 proposal ledger (caliber_effect_proposals)
Listed by defaultstatus=in_progress (status=any or another status widens it)the open states dispatched, unknown, reconciled (proposal_state=any or one state)
Settled byan operator: POST .../system/effects/{effect_key}/resolve (admin, audited: skip or retry)the reconciler's lookup by key. The operator can only ask now: POST .../system/effects/proposals/{proposal_id}/reconcile
safe_actionsresolve:skip, resolve:retry on an in_progress claim, none otherwisereconcile on an unknown or reconciled row and on a dispatched row with abandoned: true, none otherwise (a dispatched row of the current lease is the dispatcher's until the in-flight bound)

Every row carries source, source_version and its own safe_actions, so a client cannot apply the legacy resolve to a proposal (it is refused, 400, and changes nothing) or read a proposal as a ledger claim. Legacy rows keep exactly the fields they always had (plus the label); the migrations that created the proposal tables leave them untouched and invent no receipt for them. A proposal row has identifiers, state, version, attempt, owner_id, dispatch_token, reason, receipt_id, timestamps, blocks_dependents (true while it is dispatched, unknown or reconciled: nothing that depends on it will run) and abandoned (for a dispatched attempt: true when a newer lease has replaced its dispatching lease and the reconciler will pick it up; false when no newer lease has been acquired, which is the dispatcher's own lease or one that lapsed with nobody to replace it yet; null for any other state, a row with no recorded token, or no lease at all). The proposal response therefore also carries lease (the stored execution-owner lease: owner_id, fencing_token, expires_at, expired, or null), so an operator can tell those two false cases apart. No row carries a payload: no arguments, intent bytes or recorded result (the query selects only the listed columns). The view is operator-scoped and system-wide: it shows every project's rows (each with its project_id, connector, resource and owner_id), like the rest of /system/*; reason is a short code by convention and must never carry a payload (recorders pass fixed codes). Known limit: no index on proposal state/created_at yet, so a very large ledger lists by scan (a follow-up if it grows). Query parameters: source (all by default, legacy or proposal), status, proposal_state, workflow_run_id, limit (1 to 1000, applied to each list; the proposal list reports proposals_truncated when more matched, newest first); proposal_state is only checked when proposals are asked for, and an unknown source or proposal_state is 400. The response also carries sources, a description of each kind (settled_by, safe_actions). SDK: client.system.effects(source="proposal", proposal_state="unknown").

Operator action: reconcile (B05.5d, #997)#

POST /caliber/system/effects/proposals/{proposal_id}/reconcile with {"reason": "<1 to 500 characters>"} (admin scope; SDK client.system.reconcile_effect_proposal(proposal_id, reason=...)). It asks the downstream about one proposal now, which is what the loop does every pass, and it is the only operator action on a proposal. It is deliberately not a way to say what happened:

  • No say-so. The body accepts reason and nothing else (any other key is 400). There is no committed or failed an operator can write: a receipt exists only when the platform read the effect back from the downstream by its key, and failed only when the connector proves absence final (ADR 0003). A 404, a 5xx, an unreadable body, an unreachable downstream or no binding leave the proposal unknown and the answer says so (outcome: unknown, unverified, lookup_failed, not_bound, in_flight); only a stored request that is this proposal's effect settles it (committed, settled: true).
  • Owner-fenced. It runs under the execution-owner lease of the process that serves the request (app.state.execution_role), through reconcile_one, so the lease is compared in the transaction of every write. A process that is not the owner (or whose controller has dropped the lease) answers 409 not_execution_owner and asks nothing; a lease taken over mid-request is 409 lease_lost with nothing recorded. An operator request and the loop asking at once settle the proposal exactly once (the second sees it moved). At most 4 operator lookups run at once per process; the rest get 429 too_many_reconciliations_in_flight and nothing is asked. The route also accepts a dispatched row of the current lease, which safe_actions does not list because it does not always act: younger than CALIBER_EFFECT_IN_FLIGHT_MAX_SECONDS it answers in_flight and changes nothing; older, it records unknown (in_flight_expired) exactly as the loop would and asks.
  • Audited. Every request that reaches the reconciler leaves one effect_reconcile_requested audit row (actor, reason, state before, outcome, state after, owner and fencing token; no payload), whether or not the proposal moved; a lease lost mid-request, or any other failure of the request (recorded by error code or exception class name only), is recorded too. When the lookup settles the proposal, the reconciler's own effect_reconciled row is written in the same transaction as the move. A proposal that is not dispatched, unknown or reconciled is 409 not_reconcilable and nothing is recorded; an unknown id is 404.
  • Why nothing more. A proposal that stays unknown for good (a connector with no lookup by key, a downstream that never shows the request) keeps blocking its dependents. That is the safe state: the alternative, an operator marking it failed, unblocks them on a belief while the effect may have happened. The operator procedure is in the recovery runbook.

Receipt callback: a connector tells the platform it is done (B05.4b, #725)#

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/effects/callbacks/receipt (caliber/src/caliber/routes/system_effects.py) lets a connector say "the effect for this idempotency key is done". It is not a CALIBER session (no identity, no CSRF token, no rate-limit bucket: the connector is the caller) and its only admission control is a signature. The body is exactly {"idempotency_key": "<key>"} and nothing else: the callback is a notification, and the platform asks the downstream itself (the connector's lookup by key) before it records anything.

  • Who may call. CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS is a JSON array of bindings, each {connector, project_id, secret_source, base_url}: the connector, the one project it may act in, where its signing secret is read from (never the secret itself) and the base URL of its downstream. Empty (the default) accepts no callback; a malformed list stops the service at startup; the settings page shows only a count. One connector in one project has one secret; a connector bound to two projects has two. A secret shorter than 16 characters is refused (fail closed). The lookup the platform runs is the connector's plain GET by key (the binding has no authentication field yet, so it suits a downstream that allows it), goes through the egress policy (an internal downstream's host must be in CALIBER_EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS) and is bounded: at most 4 lookups per connector and project at a time (503 busy, retryable).
  • The signature. Headers X-Caliber-Connector, X-Caliber-Project, X-Caliber-Timestamp (whole seconds, canonical: no leading zeros), X-Caliber-Delivery (an id unique per connector and project, 1 to 128 printable characters) and X-Caliber-Signature: v1=<hex>, the HMAC-SHA256 of v1\n<connector>\n<project>\n<timestamp>\n<delivery>\n<hex sha256 of the body> under the binding's secret. The connector, project, timestamp, delivery id and body are all inside the signed string, so a signature made for one connector, project or message is useless for another. A timestamp more than 300 seconds from the server's clock is refused; a captured message replayed inside the window can only make the platform ask the downstream again, and a receipt is recorded once.
  • One refusal. An unknown connector or project, a secret that cannot be read, a bad or malformed signature and a stale timestamp are all the same 401 {"detail": "callback rejected"}: a probe cannot tell them apart. After that, a body that is not exactly the key is 400, and a body over 4 KiB is 413.
  • Scope without leaks. The key is resolved to a proposal of this connector in this project; anything else (a key in another project, another connector's key, a key nobody has) is the same 404 {"detail": "no such proposal"}.
  • What happens. committed already: 200 already_committed. failed: 409 proposal_failed. Not yet dispatched: 409 not_dispatched. dispatched: 202 in_flight (the dispatcher, or the reconciler once the dispatch is abandoned, still owns it). unknown or reconciled: the platform runs the lookup outside any transaction. If the downstream cannot be asked: 502 lookup_failed. If it holds nothing under the key, or something that is not this proposal's effect: 202 unknown, the proposal stays unknown (a missing record is not a failure) and nothing is consumed. If it confirms, one transaction deduplicates the delivery (the inbox of B13.5a), records the verified receipt (B05.4a), moves unknown through reconciled to committed and audits it: 200 committed with the receipt_id.
  • Retryable, never half-consumed. The delivery id is consumed only together with the receipt and the commit; if any of it is refused (409 with the reason code, for example receipt_conflict or stale_version) the transaction rolls back and the same delivery can be sent again. The same delivery id with a different body is 409 inbox_payload_mismatch; the same delivery repeated after success is 200 duplicate (answered from the inbox before any query); a new delivery for an already committed proposal is 200 already_committed. Delivery ids are scoped to the binding (a digest of connector and project), so two projects' connectors never collide or burn each other's ids. A callback that loses a race to the commit is told already_committed, not a failure. Success bodies use the platform's {"data": ...} envelope.
import json
import time

from caliber.effects.callbacks import sign

body = json.dumps({"idempotency_key": proposal_key}).encode()
timestamp = int(time.time())
headers = {
    "X-Caliber-Connector": "document-request",
    "X-Caliber-Project": project_id,
    "X-Caliber-Timestamp": str(timestamp),
    "X-Caliber-Delivery": delivery_id,
    "X-Caliber-Signature": sign(secret, "document-request", project_id, timestamp, delivery_id, body),
}
  • Not here. The lease fencing of a dispatcher's own settle (B05.5a, above) does not apply to this callback, which is not an owner-only path; the callback commits an unknown or reconciled proposal only, never one a dispatcher still holds.

Approved context sources#

A run's context may only come from sources its project has approved (B07, #692). The inventory is caliber_approved_context_sources (caliber/src/caliber/context/sources.py): one row per (project, knowledge base, version), unique. approve_source(session, project_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id, actor) records an approval, revoke_source(...) withdraws it (the row stays, with revoked_at and revoked_by, as evidence) and is_approved(session, project_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id) answers whether it is approved now (False once revoked, for anything never approved and for a source that no longer exists). Admission reads it (B07.1b, #696): under CALIBER_PROFILE=reference every knowledge-base version a run can read must be approved for the run's project (require_approved, called by prepare_admission, so create-run, trigger, retry and the assistant tool all pass through it). That is the versions in the sealed bundle's dependency lock, the versions named on a knowledge-query node that names only version_ids, and the versions read by every child workflow the run calls (each child's own sealed bundle, which must be the one the parent was compiled against). A query whose version_ids arrive on an input port cannot be pinned, so it is refused outright. Otherwise the run is refused with 403, reason_code: source_not_approved in the error body and every unapproved knowledge_base_id@version_id named in the message, and nothing is stored. The role check (resource.execute on the project) comes first, so only a caller who may run the workflow learns what the project has approved. Approval and revocation take effect at the next admission: an idempotent retry of a request that was already admitted still returns that run, and a run already admitted keeps running on what it was pinned to (the load-time check is B07.2, #699). A knowledge base that belongs to another project or to no project can never be approved for this one (only a project's own knowledge bases can), so a workflow pinned to one is refused until it uses one of the project's own. Development does not require approval. The refusal is not audited (it carries no policy decision); the response is the record.

  • A version, not a knowledge base. Approving version 1 approves nothing else; a new build must be approved on its own.
  • Only a project's own, real sources. The knowledge base must belong to the project and the version to that knowledge base. Every miss (unknown id, another project's knowledge base, a version of a different knowledge base) is one source_not_found refusal whose message names no identifier, so a foreign id cannot be probed.
  • Idempotent and race-safe. Approving an approved source returns the existing row; concurrent approvals create one (the unique key decides). Approving a revoked source reactivates the row with the new approver and time. Revoking a source that is not approved is not_approved. The row is read from the database and locked (FOR UPDATE on PostgreSQL) before it changes, so concurrent revocations or reactivations change and audit it once, and never overwrite who revoked it.
  • Completed builds of live knowledge bases only. The version must be completed (the rule that gates activating a version) and the knowledge base not archived; otherwise it is source_not_found. An approval whose version or knowledge base has since been deleted no longer counts (is_approved is false and approved_sources omits it); the row stays as evidence.
  • Audited. Approval and revocation each write an audit row (approve_context_source / revoke_context_source, entity context_source, ids only). The functions do not commit; they do not decide who may approve (the caller's project-role check does).
  • Not a foreign key to the knowledge base. The inventory outlives a deleted knowledge base on purpose; the loader must still check the version exists.

Authorizing a source before it is loaded (B07.2, #699)#

In the reference profile the run's own grant lists the context sources it may read: admission adds the action context.read and one resource per source, knowledge_base:<knowledge_base_id>@<version_id>, for exactly the sources it approved (the bundle's, its query nodes' and its child workflows'). When the worker builds an admitted run's plan it hands the knowledge-query runner a guard (caliber.context.authorize.source_guard_for), and the runner calls it with each version it is about to query, before the retrieval service is touched. The guard runs authorize_source(session, identity, run_manifest, grant_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id):

  1. the run's subject (derived from its stored manifest by identity_for_run) must equal the subject the manifest being checked recorded (identity_mismatch; a guard against mixing manifests, not a second authentication);
  2. the source must still be approved for the project (source_not_approved; a withdrawal after admission lands here and writes an audit row context_read_denied with ids only; no policy question is asked for a withdrawn source);
  3. decide(...) is asked with the manifest's run id, the exact grant id the manifest names, the manifest's typed subject and workload, context.read, the exact source resource and the manifest's purpose: a grant that does not list the source is resource_not_allowed, another run's grant grant_not_found, a member who left not_a_member, a revoked or expired grant is refused, and the decision (allow or deny) is recorded and audited like any other.

Every refusal is a ContextDenied with one fixed message that names no source (<code> (<reasons>): this run may not read that context source); the node fails and the run fails with the stable run error code context_denied (the code and the policy's reasons are in the summary), and nothing was loaded. An authority store that cannot answer is a refusal (authority_unavailable), and a database message is never put in the node's error text. context.read is a project action (owner, editor, reviewer) with policy risk 2. The guard is passed to child workflows the run calls.

run errormeaning and recovery
context_denied with source_not_approvedthe source was approved at admission and withdrawn since: approve it again, or resubmit the run on an approved version
context_denied with authority_denied (not_a_member) / grant_revoked / grant_expiredthe run's subject left the project, or its grant was revoked or ran out: resubmit as someone who may
context_denied with authority_denied (action_not_allowed) or (resource_not_allowed)the run's grant does not list that source (a run admitted before sources were authorized, or a query that reads a version the run was not admitted for): resubmit the run
context_denied with authority_unavailablethe authority store could not answer: nothing was loaded; resubmit when it is back

What it does not do. The guard follows how the run was admitted: it is built when the run's grant carries context.read (or this deployment requires approved sources), so a run admitted with sources stays guarded under any worker configuration. A run admitted before sources were authorized has no context.read and fails where sources are required (resubmit it). A grant holds at most 256 resources, so a run with 256 or more sources is refused at admission (grant_refused). The check is point-in-time: a withdrawal landing between the guard and the query does not stop that one read. Outputs a run already produced (replayed on a resume from a checkpoint) are not re-authorized. Each version queried costs one decision and one audit row (a query naming several versions authorizes each before any is read).

Knowledge reads outside an admitted run (B07.6, #973)#

The reference profile has one governed knowledge-read path. An admitted workflow run supplies the typed run principal, its immutable manifest and its exact grant; the worker passes a SourceGuard to every knowledge-query node, including child workflows. The guard records an explicit context.read decision for each exact knowledge-base version before the retrieval service is called. Foreign projects, revoked memberships or grants, withdrawn approvals, and versions not in the grant therefore fail closed without a retrieval call.

Other paths do not have a run-bound principal and cannot turn a manifest override or an ambient project-visible identity into authority. In CALIBER_PROFILE=reference they refuse before loading knowledge bytes:

surfacereference-profile behaviorrequired principal/authorization
preview, including assistant draft previewgoverned_run_requiredan admitted workflow run; preview is not a run and has no context.read grant
evaluations and deploy gatesgoverned_run_requiredan admitted workflow run; offline replay is not an authorization boundary
refinement and calibrationgoverned_run_requiredan admitted workflow run; the stage/job identity alone is insufficient
assistant query_knowledge_basegoverned_run_requiredan admitted workflow run, not the assistant's project visibility
direct POST /knowledge/querygoverned_run_requiredan admitted workflow run, not the caller's project visibility
exported runtime query and child-workflow querythe default runtime uses the caller-supplied admitted-run SourceGuard; unwrapped custom callbacks return governed_run_requiredthe exact run principal, manifest, grant and context.read decision
knowledge_build workflow nodesgoverned_run_requiredno current workflow-node contract authorizes the source bytes used to build a new version

The refusal is raised before the retrieval or build service is reached. Development and legacy profiles retain their historical behavior; that compatibility is not a reference-profile authorization guarantee. Knowledge-base listing, metadata, build and version-management APIs remain resource-scoped operations; this matrix covers operations that load knowledge content for retrieval or workflow execution.

The context manifest#

What an agent step is given is recorded before the provider sees it (B07.3a, #704): caliber.context.manifest builds a context_manifest v1 record (ADR 0003) and stores it once in caliber_context_manifests, as canonical JSON with its SHA-256 (the record has no digest field: the digest excludes itself), unique per (run, step request, revision). Re-assembling a step is a new revision, never an edit; a revision that skips ahead or repeats is refused. UPDATE and DELETE are refused by database triggers and by the ORM (and, as for run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges).

A manifest lists the segments in the order the provider sees them (position equals the index), each with (a segment's kind must match its source: a knowledge base's text can only be retrieved_text, an instruction or structured-output suffix can only come from a prompt, and a tool specification/result can only come from a tool):

  • a trust tier: instruction only for a system/workflow instruction or structured-output suffix (and every one is); everything else, the user's input, retrieved text, tool output, history and memory, is data. Text a source contains can never be promoted to an instruction by being retrieved;
  • its source (prompt, input, knowledge-base version, tool, memory, history), the retrieval and transform that produced it, and the digest of its content (the content is not stored in the manifest);
  • for payload loaded from a knowledge base or memory, the authorization decision id of the recorded context.read allow that let it be loaded: a segment without one is refused (unauthorized_payload), and storing the manifest checks each id against the recorded decision (an allow, of that action, for this run, of that exact source: knowledge_base:<kb>@<version> or memory:<reference>, decided no later than the manifest). A decision authorizes a read, not a step, so any step of its run may cite it;
  • the omitted and redacted items and the token allocation (budget, used, instruction, data; used is the sum of the segments and may not exceed the budget).

Storing also checks that the run exists and that the record's scope and project are the deployment's and the run's, and stores only canonical bytes. content_digest is a plain SHA-256 of the content, so a short, guessable value (a yes/no, an id) can be confirmed offline by anyone who can read the manifest: treat the record as evidence for the project's members and platform administrators, and do not expose it more widely without a keyed digest.

Reading a manifest back (read_context_manifest) re-checks the digest, the schema (an unknown schema_version is unknown_version, never read as the nearest) and every rule above, so a reordered or relabelled record is caught twice, by its digest and by its positions. Refusals carry a stable code: invalid_manifest, unknown_version, tier_violation, unauthorized_payload, ordering, tokens, authorization_rejected, duplicate_revision, revision_gap, rule_bundle_changed, rule_bundle_unavailable, rule_bundle_mismatch, rule_bundle_unpinned. Nothing here talks to a provider.

Recorded for every agent step (B07.3b, #710). For an admitted run in the reference profile the worker hands the runtime a recorder (caliber.context.assembly.context_recorder_for, built together with the source guard, or alone for a run whose manifest pins a rule bundle), and the runtime calls it with each agent step's initial context (the step's instructions as resolved when it is assembled, its skills, its history and the one input the provider is sent, with the node whose edge delivered it) before any of it reaches the provider, for every agent, every handoff target (a native Agents SDK handoff runs inside the provider call, so every agent the step may reach is recorded first) and in child workflows too. The recorder labels the assembly: the agent's own instructions are the only instruction tier; the history is one history data segment; text a knowledge query delivered straight to the agent is retrieved_text (one segment per version it read, citing the context.read decision the guard recorded when it authorized that version); the run's own input is user_input; any other text is tool_output of the node that delivered it, or of unknown origin (an item a for_each, loop or error_boundary hands an inline agent, text a knowledge query's output reached only through another node), which is still data and is never labelled the run's own input. It builds, validates and stores the manifest (its own short transaction, committed) as revision 1 of a fresh step request. If it cannot (an unknown or unauthorized source, a refused manifest, a database failure) the step does not run: the node fails (a for_each item or an error_boundary does not absorb the refusal), the run ends context_denied and the provider was never called. A document that says "ignore all previous instructions" is therefore recorded as data and reaches the agent as input, never as part of its instructions (scenario V03).

Non-agent model calls covered by B07.6. A knowledge-query node's answer-synthesis call uses the same recorder before the OpenAI or Anthropic provider is called. Its resolved system prompt, bounded history, exact user prompt (including the retrieved answer context), knowledge-base source and context.read decision are recorded against the knowledge node's occurrence and attempt. A missing source decision refuses before the provider is touched. The same boundary is used for each retrieval mode, so multiple synthesis calls become ordered revisions of the same node occurrence rather than an unlinked side channel.

LLM-backed guardrail judges use the same pre-call recorder when they run inside a governed workflow. The criterion and the response/evidence they judge are recorded as data against the guardrail node and attempt; deterministic guardrails do not create a model-call manifest.

Caps and redaction (B07.4, #719). caliber.context.manifest.pack_context(segments, caps=..., redactor=...) is the one pure function that decides what an agent step's context may contain, and build_context_manifest records its result (omitted, redacted and sections=). It redacts every data-tier segment with the PII redactor (the same one the audit log uses, CALIBER_PII_REDACTION_*; an instruction is the operator's own text and is never altered) before the digest is taken, so the manifest hashes what the provider is given and the matched text is never recorded: a changed segment gets one redacted entry (fields: ["content"], reason: "redactor:pattern-1,pattern-3", naming which rules fired); a segment that is nothing but the replacement marker is dropped and listed in omitted as redacted. It caps the retrieved and history sections at the caps the caller passes (parse_section_caps(config.context_section_caps), from CALIBER_CONTEXT_SECTION_CAPS: JSON, default {"retrieved": 4000, "history": 2000}; only those two names are accepted and each cap is a positive integer, else the service refuses to start; a section left out is uncapped): chunks are kept in order while they fit, and the first chunk that does not fit and every later one in that section (they rank below it) is dropped and listed in omitted with reason token_budget and its tokens. The manifest's token_allocation.sections records each capped section's cap_tokens and used_tokens, and the manifest refuses a record where they do not add up to its segments. Example: with a cap of 10 and three retrieved chunks of 8 tokens, the manifest keeps the first chunk and lists two as token_budget; a chunk containing alice@example.com has its digest taken over the text with [REDACTED] in its place (the text itself is never stored). Not yet applied to a live step: the agent-step adapters (B08) call pack_context to decide what the provider receives. The recorder above (B07.3b) records the context as the runtime passes it and does not pack it, so until B08 consumes it no provider input is capped or redacted and the manifests it writes carry no sections; a manifest never claims a cap or a redaction that was not applied. The issue's draft names (allocation, redactions, budget) map onto the shipped v1 record (token_allocation.sections, redacted, token_budget), which is kept so manifests already written stay valid.

The rule bundle at context use (B07.5b, #736). A run admitted with a rule bundle has its path and SHA-256 in the run manifest (see "Admitting a run"); the run manifest is immutable and nothing here writes it. For every agent step the recorder reads the pin from that manifest, never from the current configuration, re-reads the bytes at the recorded path, re-hashes them on every step (nothing is trusted from an earlier step) and compares the hash with the recorded digest; only then are the bytes parsed (caliber.context.rules.rule_bundle_reference). The parse and the manifest entry are cached by the verified digest (a bounded LRU of 8 bundles): a digest is the hash of exactly one byte string, so a hit can only be the bundle those bytes parse to, and the cache never replaces the read and the hash. The step's context manifest then carries a rule_bundle entry: the bundle's bundle_id, version and sha256, and for each selected rule its rule_id, its source_ref (provenance) and the SHA-256 of its text (the rule text itself is not stored). Every rule of the operator-pinned bundle is selected, in bundle order. rule_bundle_reference also hands back the verified in-memory bundle (VerifiedRuleBundle.bundle): the B08 adapters must take rule text from that object and never reopen the path, so the text a provider is given is the text whose digest the manifest cites.

Storing the manifest checks the cited digest against the run manifest read from the database: a run admitted with a bundle cites it in every step, a run admitted without one cites none (a bundle enabled later is never applied to it, and no pin is backfilled). That store check is only the digest comparison; the rest of the entry (id, version, per-rule fields) is not re-derived there, because the store cannot re-read the file. The recorder, which verified the bytes the entry was built from, is the trust boundary for it.

A run that has a rule bundle is recorded even when it has no source guard (no approved sources required, no context.read grant); in that case no knowledge-base text is labelled retrieved_text (no source was authorized) and a query's text is tool_output of its node. Read tool_output there as "the output of this node", not as proof that the text did not come from a knowledge base: with no guard the platform did not authorize or label the source. So a path or configuration change after admission cannot alter what the run uses: the run uses the admitted bytes or is refused.

Size cap. A context manifest is bounded to 1 MiB and every step cites the bundle, so admission refuses a bundle whose citation (the canonical JSON of the entry above) exceeds 256 KiB (262144 bytes): rule_bundle_refused, with the size and the cap in the message and none of the file's content. A citation takes about 116 bytes per rule plus the UTF-8 length of its rule_id and source_ref (a CJK character is 3 bytes). Measured: 1000 rules with 100-character ASCII source refs take 217 KB (admitted); 150 rules with 512-character CJK source refs take 248 KB (admitted); 200 such rules take 331 KB and 1000 rules with 512-character ASCII source refs take 629 KB (both refused at admission, though the loader accepts the files). Shorten the source_ref values or split the bundle. A bundle admitted before this cap that is over it but under the manifest's 1 MiB bound keeps working; one over the bound fails every step with manifest_invalid.

run errormeaning and recovery
context_denied with rule_bundle_changedthe bytes at the pinned path are no longer the admitted bytes (an edit, even a comment or whitespace; a replaced file; a file larger than 1 MiB): the step did not run and no context manifest was written. The run stays failed: restoring the file does not revive it. Resubmit: the new run is admitted against the current CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH and CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_SHA256, so after an intentional edit update both together first (a path with a stale digest is refused at admission)
context_denied with rule_bundle_unavailablethe pinned file is missing, not a regular file, unreadable, or the run manifest's pin is unusable. This includes a pinned path that existed when the run was admitted and is gone on the node that executes it (see "Which path is pinned"). The run stays failed; resubmit once the bundle is readable at the path a new admission will record
rule_bundle_refused at admission (409 manifest_refused)the configured bundle's bytes are missing, changed or invalid, or its citation is over the 256 KiB cap: fix the file or the pinned digest, or shorten the bundle; no run is created
context_denied with rule_bundle_mismatch / rule_bundle_unpinneda context manifest cited another bundle than the run's admitted one, or a bundle for a run admitted without one (the store refuses it; this indicates a defect, not an operator action)

Example. A run is admitted with CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH=/etc/caliber/rules.yaml; an operator then appends a comment to the file. The worker's next agent step ends the run failed with error code context_denied and the summary rule_bundle_changed: the run's pinned rule bundle cannot be used now (digest_mismatch); the provider was never called and the run's manifest is untouched. Deleting the comment does not revive that run: it stays failed. Submitting the same request again creates a new run, admitted against whatever CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH / CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_SHA256 say at that moment (the restored file with the old digest works; an intentionally edited file needs its new digest set together with the path). Changing those settings affects only runs admitted afterwards. The entry records provenance and digests, not the rule text: delivering rule text to the provider is the agent-step adapters' job (B08), as for caps and redaction, so a manifest never claims text was given that was not.

Which path is pinned. Admission records the symlink-resolved absolute path, and the worker that executes the run reads exactly that path. It must therefore exist, with the same bytes, on every node that can execute the run, for as long as the run can still take a step. Mounts that rotate their real directory break this: a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret volume serves rules.yaml -> ..data/rules.yaml where ..data points at a ..data_<timestamp> directory that is replaced and deleted on every update (and a Docker secret or a per-node temporary path differs between nodes). A run admitted before such a rotation records the old directory, which is gone, and its next step is refused as rule_bundle_unavailable.
