The run manifest's pin shape is immutable (#680, #726) and is not changed to work around this. Mount the bundle so its resolved path is stable and identical on every node.

Rollout. An in-place edit or rotation of the bundle file fails every in-flight or waiting run admitted against the old bytes at its next agent step. Use versioned, content-addressed file names (for example rules-<first 12 hex of the sha256>.yaml), publish the new file next to the old one, switch CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH and CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_SHA256 together, and keep the old file in place until the runs admitted against it have drained (finished or failed).

Deploying the rule_bundle field. Adding rule_bundle to the context manifest is a readers-first change: an API pod or worker still running the previous release rejects a stored manifest that carries it (invalid_manifest, the v1 schema is closed). Roll the new release to every pod that reads context manifests before any worker running it can record one for a bundle-pinned run (or drain bundle-pinned runs first); do not mix releases while bundle-pinned runs are in flight.

Model calls outside a live workflow run (for example, offline evaluation and deploy-gate scoring) remain outside this runtime manifest boundary. Token counts are an accounting estimate (four characters a token, and the recorded budget is the larger of the configured one and the total); enforcing a budget on a provider call is B08. Legacy runs and development have no recorder.

Refinement-job creator provenance (B06.1, #731)#

caliber_refinement_jobs.triggered_by is the optional provenance field for the principal that caused a refinement job to be created. It is a VARCHAR(256) and records a declared creator when the creation path has one; it is not an authorization grant and it is not evidence that a candidate may be applied. The apply boundary must still recheck the current project permission, distinct approver and exact candidate digest. A NULL value is therefore unknown provenance, not permission to proceed.

The reference-profile rule for an unknown creator is explicit human review or quarantine before an apply decision. The schema slice itself adds no new runtime refusal code and does not silently rewrite an existing job. Since B06.3 the Apply route enforces it: with the two-person rule on (always, in the reference profile) a job with no recorded creator is refused (apply_creator_unknown) and cannot be applied in place; there is no reviewed-provenance override yet. Recovery is to create a new job through a path that can declare its creator and have a different account apply that; do not infer a principal from timestamps, owners or other mutable fields.

Migration 0131 adds the nullable column with no backfill, so every legacy row reads NULL and old readers remain compatible. Deploy the migration before enabling writers that populate the field. Downgrade removes only the optional provenance value, leaves the job row and all other pipeline state intact, and there is no API/SDK schema change in this slice because RefinementJobSchema does not expose ORM-only columns automatically.

B06.2: authenticated creator writes#

The four producer-owned CaliberRefinementJob constructors now populate triggered_by from the resolved server identity: prompt optimization, skill calibration, workflow calibration, and assistant prompt-promotion proposals. When a request carries a CaliberIdentity, its user_id is authoritative; the route actor is retained only for direct internal callers that do not have a request identity. Prompt, skill, workflow, and assistant metadata are not creator authority, and client-supplied owner or creator values cannot replace the authenticated requester.

This is provenance, not permission: apply still rechecks the current project permission and, under the two-person rule below (B06.3), the distinct approver, and the claim now rechecks both, with the exact candidate digest, inside its own transaction (B06.4, below). Rows written before B06.2 remain explicitly unknown (triggered_by = NULL); with the two-person rule on they cannot be applied in place (apply_creator_unknown), so create a new job via a path that can declare its requester. No new migration or public API/SDK field is required because migration 0131 introduced the column and it remains an ORM-only field.

Apply: a distinct approver (B06.3, #747)#

CALIBER_APPLY_REQUIRE_DISTINCT_APPROVER (apply_require_distinct_approver, default false) is the two-person rule for POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/jobs/{job_id}/apply. With it on:

the job's triggered_bythe authenticated callerresult
a different accountholds caliber.operator and release.apply on the job's projectapplied, as before
the caller (compared trimmed and case-folded, so @Reza is not a second person to @reza)any403, reason_code apply_self_approval
NULL, empty or blank (a legacy job, or a creation path that declared no requester)any403, reason_code apply_creator_unknown

Where the identities come from: the requester is the job row's triggered_by, written from the authenticated request identity when the job was created (B06.2); the approver is the authenticated caller of the Apply request. Neither is read from the request body, query string or model output, and the setting is server configuration, so a client cannot turn the rule off or name a different requester.

The reference profile. The setting must be on: CALIBER_PROFILE=reference refuses to start without it (apply_distinct_approver_disabled, in the table above). The rule is also applied at request time whenever the profile is reference, whatever the flag says, so a process that somehow reached a request in that state still refuses, and an unreadable configuration is treated as the reference profile.

Development compatibility, separately. With the default profile and the flag off, Apply behaves exactly as it did in the alpha: the requester may apply their own candidate and a legacy job with no recorded requester is applied. That is a declared development-only compatibility, not a reference behaviour; a single-operator install that turns the flag on cannot apply its own jobs and needs a second operator.

Refusals are 403 with a static, payload-free message (no job id, account name, candidate text or digest) and a stable reason_code:

{"detail": "the account that requested this candidate cannot apply it; a different authorized person must apply it", "status_code": 403, "reason_code": "apply_self_approval"}
{"detail": "this candidate has no recorded requester, so a distinct approver cannot be verified; re-run the calibration so it records its requester, then have a different authorized person apply it", "status_code": 403, "reason_code": "apply_creator_unknown"}

Both refusals happen after the project-permission check (a non-member still gets 404, a member without release.apply still gets 403 without a reason code) and before the claim, the approval anchor and the promoter call, so a refused Apply changes no job, approval or release state: the job stays candidate_ready. Since B06.4 the refusal is recorded in the audit log (below). The claim repeats the check on the row-locked job with the same helper, and the database enforces the same separation inside the atomic claim (UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'candidate_ready' and the requester, trimmed of ASCII whitespace and lower-cased, is neither NULL, blank nor equal to the caller, trimmed and lower-cased the same way), so a requester that changed after the check, even to a case or whitespace variant of the caller, still cannot claim. The SQL lower-casing is ASCII-only on SQLite; the check before the claim applies the full case-fold. If the server has no configuration object at all, the rule is applied as in the reference profile rather than failing the request.

Recovery. apply_self_approval: ask a different account with release.apply on the project to apply it. apply_creator_unknown: the job has no verifiable requester and there is no reviewed-provenance override yet: the job is refused, never passed. Re-run the calibration through the prompt, skill or workflow path, which records the requester, and have a different account apply the new job. (An assistant promotion proposal also records its requester, but it is created awaiting_approval, not candidate_ready, so it is not a job this route applies.) Do not set triggered_by by hand from timestamps, owners or other mutable fields. The refusal catalogue, with the recovery for the requester and for the operator, is in Apply: refusal catalogue, audit and recovery.

Apply: the claim rechecks everything (B06.4, #753)#

Apply authorises at the start of the request, but the decision that matters is the one at the claim, the write that moves the job from candidate_ready to applying and commits the approval anchor before the promoter runs. Inside that transaction the route now locks the rows the decision rests on and rechecks, on what it locked, in this order:

orderrecheckrefusal
1the job still exists404
2the caller still holds release.apply on the job's project and can still see the job (membership, role, project owner and the agent's project are read after being locked)403, reason_code apply_permission_revoked
3the two-person rule above, when in force, with the same apply_separation_refusal helper as the early check403, apply_self_approval or apply_creator_unknown
4the job is still candidate_ready409, no reason_code (the existing status conflict)
5the candidate about to be promoted is the one that cleared the eval gate409, apply_candidate_changed, or apply_candidate_unverified when no digest was recorded

Lock contention anywhere in the claim transaction (a lock wait that runs out, a deadlock this transaction loses, or on SQLite a busy timeout) is 503 apply_busy (below). After the claim UPDATE, rows 2 and 5 are checked once more before anything is committed (see SQLite, below).

The exact candidate. When the eval gate passes, the stage that moves a job to candidate_ready stores the SHA-256 of the candidate's canonical JSON on the job (caliber_refinement_jobs.candidate_digest, sha256: plus 64 hex digits; migration 0132). The claim recomputes the digest of the candidate it is about to promote and refuses on any difference. The approval anchor's candidate_snapshot, which is what the promoter reads, is taken from that same locked row and checked against the recorded digest once more before anything is committed, so the digest names exactly the content that is promoted even on a database without row locks. The recorded digest also appears in the apply_candidate audit row, so a promoted version can be traced to the exact content that was evaluated. The check applies in every profile: it is an integrity check, not the two-person policy. A job with no recorded digest is refused (apply_candidate_unverified), never trusted.

No gap between check and write. On PostgreSQL the job is locked FOR UPDATE and its agent, project and the caller's membership row FOR SHARE before anything is read for the decision, in that order, and the conditional UPDATE of the claim still carries the status, the recorded digest and (when the rule is on) the requester predicate. A revocation or a candidate edit that is mid-transaction when the claim starts makes the claim wait and then refuse; one that arrives while the claim is in flight waits for the claim to commit, so the apply that passed its checks is the apply that was authorised. Two concurrent applies cannot both claim: the second waits and sees applying. The waits are bounded by a fixed 5 second lock_timeout (not a setting); a wait that runs out, a deadlock in which PostgreSQL aborts this transaction as the victim, or on SQLite a busy timeout is answered 503, reason_code apply_busy, retryable, with nothing decided or written and no audit row.

What SQLite does and does not cover. SQLite has no row locks and ignores the FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE clauses, so the recheck's answer is not held between the recheck and the claim: a grant can be revoked on another connection in that gap. Two things close it. The claim UPDATE is conditional (status, recorded digest, requester), and once it has run, and so holds SQLite's single write lock, the route reads the caller's authority again and verifies the candidate snapshot against the recorded digest before anything is committed; a failure rolls the claim back (apply_permission_revoked / apply_candidate_changed). What remains is the interval after that check and before the commit, during which SQLite's write lock keeps other writers out. This is the development profile; the reference profile requires PostgreSQL, where the row locks above are what is relied on.

Refusals are static and payload-free (no job id, account, digest or candidate text):

{"detail": "the candidate is not the one that was evaluated; nothing was applied, re-run the evaluation and apply the new candidate", "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "apply_candidate_changed"}
{"detail": "your permission to apply candidates in this project is no longer in force; nothing was applied", "status_code": 403, "reason_code": "apply_permission_revoked"}
{"detail": "this candidate has no recorded evaluation digest, so it cannot be verified; nothing was applied, re-run the evaluation so it records one", "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "apply_candidate_unverified"}
{"detail": "this candidate is being changed or applied right now; nothing was applied, retry shortly", "status_code": 503, "reason_code": "apply_busy"}

Audit (#1050). Each of the five refusals listed here, all of which come after the project-permission check (apply_self_approval, apply_creator_unknown, apply_permission_revoked, apply_candidate_changed, apply_candidate_unverified) writes one apply_refused audit row, severity high, on the job, with the caller as actor and {"reason_code": ...} as its only detail. It is written in a transaction of its own after the attempt is rolled back, so the refusal still changes no job, approval or release state, and a failure to write it is logged without turning the refusal into a 500. The existing 404 and role 403 of the early project-permission check, and the status 409, write nothing. There is no rate limit on these rows beyond the platform's request limits: only an authenticated caller holding release.apply can produce one.

Recovery. apply_candidate_changed and apply_candidate_unverified: the content or its evidence is not what was evaluated. Re-run the evaluation (a new candidate, or a request for changes) so the gate records a fresh digest, then apply. Do not edit candidate_digest by hand: the digest is evidence of what was evaluated, and a hand-written one defeats it. apply_permission_revoked: ask a project owner to restore the grant, or have an authorised account apply it.

Upgrade and limits. Migration 0132 is additive, but not safe for a mixed-version rollout: a job that an old process moves to candidate_ready after the upgrade records no digest, and the new Apply refuses it (apply_candidate_unverified, with no override). Drain old writers (the workers that run the eval stages) before migrating, or re-run the evaluation of any job they finish in the window. The migration backfills candidate_digest for jobs that are candidate_ready or applying at upgrade time from their current candidate, since that is the only evaluated candidate such a row can name (a trust-on-upgrade step: an edit made before the upgrade is not detectable); every other row stays NULL, and a job without a candidate stays NULL and is refused at Apply. Rolling back drops only the column. The digest covers the candidate content, not the evaluation results stored beside it, and it is not a defence against someone who can write to the database and rewrite both the candidate and the digest: it catches an edit after the gate by any path that does not also re-record the gate's evidence. The permission recheck covers the project grant and visibility; the caller's platform scopes come from the request's credential as resolved at its start.

Apply: refusal catalogue, audit and recovery (B06.5, #762)#

This is the operator and integrator view of the whole Apply chain: one place for what the two sections above specify piece by piece. It was written from routes/jobs.py (apply_job, _recheck_claim, _verified_claim_snapshot, _refuse_apply), apply.py (the reason codes and their static messages), routes/_job_access.py (the locks and the timeout) and candidate_digest.py. Every body below is the real response of the route under the test client (tests/test_apply_distinct_approver.py and tests/test_apply_claim_recheck.py set up each case), copied from a run, apart from the ids and timestamps that differ on every run.

The request. POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/jobs/{job_id}/apply needs the caliber.operator scope and release.apply (owner or editor) in the job's project. It reads no field of the body: the requester is the job's stored triggered_by and the approver is the authenticated caller, so a body, query string or header that names someone else changes nothing. jobs.apply(job_id) in the SDK posts the same request.

curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" \
  "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/jobs/$JOB_ID/apply"

The setting, by profile#

profileCALIBER_APPLY_REQUIRE_DISTINCT_APPROVERat startupat request time
development (the default)false (the default)startsrule off: the requester may apply their own candidate and a job with no recorded requester is applied (development compatibility only). The candidate digest check still applies
developmenttruestartsrule on
referencetruestartsrule on
referencefalse or unsetrefuses to start with the ConfigError shown below (violation code apply_distinct_approver_disabled)rule on whatever the flag says, if a process ever reached a request in that state
no configuration object on the appn/an/atreated as the reference profile: rule on

The startup refusal is multi-line, one line per violation. With this the only violation it reads:

reference profile refused (1 violation):
- apply_require_distinct_approver is false; set CALIBER_APPLY_REQUIRE_DISTINCT_APPROVER=true for the reference profile [apply_distinct_approver_disabled]

The rule is server configuration, not something a request can switch. A single-operator install that turns it on cannot apply its own jobs and needs a second account that is an operator and holds release.apply.

Order of the checks#

  1. Project gate (load_visible_job): 404 when the job does not exist or the caller cannot see it, 403 (no reason_code) when the caller is a member without release.apply. Nothing is written.
  2. Early two-person check, rule on only: 403 apply_self_approval or apply_creator_unknown. Audited.
  3. The claim transaction starts. On PostgreSQL it sets the 5 second lock_timeout and locks the rows (below). 503 apply_busy if a lock is not granted in time or this transaction is chosen as a deadlock victim (and, on SQLite, if the write lock is not granted within the busy timeout, which surfaces at the claim UPDATE or the commit rather than here). Nothing is decided or written.
  4. On the locked rows (when the recheck passes but the claim UPDATE still matches no row, the answer is the uncoded 409 it changed while being claimed): 404 if the job is gone, 403 apply_permission_revoked if the caller no longer holds release.apply or can no longer see the job, the two-person check again (rule on), 409 when the status is not candidate_ready, then the digest check: 409 apply_candidate_unverified or apply_candidate_changed.
  5. The conditional UPDATE (status candidate_ready, the recorded digest and, rule on, the requester predicate) claims the job; then permission and digest are checked once more before the commit.
  6. The claim and the born-approved approval anchor commit, then the promoter runs (intent first).

Permission is checked before separation on purpose: a caller whose grant is gone gets the permission refusal, never a separation code that would confirm who requested the job. The status 409 is checked before the digest 409, so a job that is already applied or applying is a plain status conflict whatever its candidate is.

Refusal catalogue#

reason_codeHTTPauditedwhat it meansrequesteroperator
(none)404nothe job does not exist, or the caller is not a member of its project (the response never says which)check the job id and the X-CALIBER-Project headeradd the caller to the project if they should act on it
(none)403nothe caller is a member without release.apply (a viewer or reviewer): project role 'viewer' cannot perform release.applyask a project owner for the editor or owner rolegrant the role
apply_self_approval403yesthe caller is the account that requested the job (compared trimmed and case-folded, so @Reza is not a second person to @reza)ask a different account that is an operator with release.apply to apply itnothing to repair; do not edit triggered_by, and do not turn the rule off under the reference profile
apply_creator_unknown403yesthe job has no recorded requester (a legacy job: triggered_by is NULL or blank), so a distinct approver cannot be verified; there is no overridestart a new calibration (it records its requester) and have a different account apply the new jobthe old job cannot be applied in place; do not infer a requester from timestamps or owners
apply_permission_revoked403yesthe early checks passed, then the caller's grant went away before the claim: membership removed or deactivated, role lowered, the agent moved to another project, or the project's ownership changedwait for the grant to be restored, then apply againrestore the grant, or have another authorised account apply it
(none)409nothe job is not candidate_ready (already applied, applying, running, and so on): job 'RFN-A' cannot be applied: current status is 'applying' (expected 'candidate_ready'). Also, rarely, job 'RFN-A' cannot be applied: it changed while being claimed: the conditional claim UPDATE matched no row although the locked read passed (a race SQLite leaves open), and the recheck that follows found no more precise refusalread the job; do not retry while it is applying; after it changed while being claimed, read the job and apply again if it is still candidate_readyan applying job is in flight or is settled by the release reconciler; the janitor returns a stranded one to candidate_ready
apply_candidate_unverified409yesthe gate recorded no digest for the job (written by a process that predates migration 0132, or not digestible), so the candidate cannot be verifiedask for another passsend the job back for another pass (POST /jobs/{job_id}/request-changes) or start a new calibration, so the gate records a digest; see "Finding unverified jobs" below
apply_candidate_changed409yesthe candidate about to be promoted is not the one that cleared the eval gate (edited since, emptied, or not digestible)ask for another passfind out who edited it, then send the job back (request-changes) or recalibrate so the new candidate is evaluated and its digest recorded
apply_busy503noanother transaction held a lock this claim needed, so nothing was decided: on PostgreSQL a row lock was not granted within 5 seconds (SQLSTATE 55P03, another claim or a membership, project, agent or candidate edit holds it), or this claim was the victim of a lock-order deadlock (40P01); on SQLite another connection held the write lock for the whole busy timeout (30 s, database is locked)retry shortly; the SDK does not retry a POST for youif it persists, on PostgreSQL look for a long-open transaction on caliber_refinement_jobs or the agent, project or membership rows (pg_stat_activity) and for writers that take those rows in another order (pg_stat_database.deadlocks counts the deadlocks); on SQLite find the process holding the database file

The 404 and the role 403 write nothing because they are the project gate that every job route shares and they are answered before the claim; the status 409 and the 503 are not a decision about the caller or the candidate. The five coded refusals that are a decision about this caller and this candidate are audited (#1050).

Real bodies#

A different account applies a candidate that cleared the gate (200; this is the response of a simulated promoter, so simulated is true, and the approval id and the timestamp change on every apply):

{"data": {"job_id": "RFN-A", "status": "applied", "promotion": {"artifact_ref": "prompt://support-agent/v-fake", "rotated_at": "2026-10-31T19:39:30.111843+00:00", "details": {"alias": "prod", "approval_id": "AP-95e24f7c"}, "bundle_size": 1, "bundle_results": [{"agent_id": "support-agent", "artifact_type": "prompt", "artifact_ref": "prompt://support-agent/v-fake"}]}, "simulated": true}}

The same job applied a second time (409, no reason_code):

{"detail": "job 'RFN-A' cannot be applied: current status is 'applied' (expected 'candidate_ready')", "status_code": 409}

A member who is only a viewer (403, no reason_code), and a caller who is not a member (404):

{"detail": "project role 'viewer' cannot perform release.apply", "status_code": 403}
{"detail": "refinement job 'RFN-A' not found", "status_code": 404}

The requester applies their own job with the rule on (403); a different account can then apply the same job, because the refusal changed nothing:

{"detail": "the account that requested this candidate cannot apply it; a different authorized person must apply it", "status_code": 403, "reason_code": "apply_self_approval"}

The bodies of the other coded refusals (apply_creator_unknown, apply_candidate_changed, apply_candidate_unverified, apply_permission_revoked and apply_busy) are the ones shown in the two sections above. None of them holds a job id, an account, a digest or candidate text, and a test asserts that none of those strings is in a body.

From the SDK the status picks the exception and reason_code names the case; it is None for the uncoded 404, 403 and 409:

from caliber_sdk import CaliberConflictError, CaliberPermissionError, CaliberServerError

try:
    caliber.jobs.apply(job_id)
except CaliberPermissionError as exc:
    if exc.reason_code in {"apply_self_approval", "apply_creator_unknown"}:
        ...  # a different authorised account must apply it
    elif exc.reason_code == "apply_permission_revoked":
        ...  # the grant is gone; ask a project owner
    else:
        raise  # the role 403 (no reason_code)
except CaliberConflictError as exc:
    if exc.reason_code in {"apply_candidate_changed", "apply_candidate_unverified"}:
        ...  # send the job back for another pass; do not retry the same job
    else:
        raise  # the status 409
except CaliberServerError as exc:
    if exc.reason_code != "apply_busy":
        raise
    ...  # retry after a short wait: nothing was decided

What is audited#

Each of the five refusals marked audited in the catalogue writes one apply_refused row, in a transaction of its own after the attempt is rolled back. A refused attempt changes no job, approval or release state (a test asserts that the job is still candidate_ready, the promoter was not called and no approval row exists). The row is:

columnvalue
actionapply_refused
actorthe caller who was refused
entity_type, entity_idrefinement_job, the job id
severityhigh
details{"reason_code": "apply_self_approval"}: the code only, never a digest, the requester or candidate text

Read them with GET /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/audit-log?action=apply_refused (admin scope; entity_id, actor and since also filter it). A refusal that cannot be recorded is logged and is still the typed refusal, never a 500. An applied job's apply_candidate row carries the evaluated candidate_digest, and a failed promotion writes apply_failed. Not audited: the project gate (404 and the role 403), the status 409 and apply_busy.

The candidate digest#

The digest binds an Apply to the exact candidate the gate cleared. It is sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits (71 characters) of the candidate's canonical JSON (sorted keys, no insignificant whitespace, ASCII only; NaN and Infinity have no form), so key order and storage format do not matter. It is written by the three stages that move a job to candidate_ready (the prompt and skill eval stage, the workflow deploy gate and the workflow calibration gate), recomputed by the claim from the locked row, and compared once more against the snapshot the promoter reads.

coverednot covered
everything in the job's candidate object (content, rationale, diff summary, promotion type, and any other key)eval_results and diagnosis beside it, and the job columns the promoter also reads: bundle_targets, skill_name, artifact_type, agent_id
the content that reaches the promoter, because the approval anchor's candidate_snapshot is verified against the digest before the committhe live registry at apply time (the promoter's own conflict check and the release operation handle that)
nothing in a refusal: the digest is never written to a refusal row or a responsesomeone with database write access who rewrites both candidate and candidate_digest

It is an integrity check, not the two-person policy, so it applies in every profile and whether or not the flag is on. candidate_digest is an ORM-only column: it is not in the API or the SDK models.

Locks, order and the timeout#

On PostgreSQL the claim transaction takes, in this fixed order: the job FOR UPDATE, then its agent, the agent's project and the caller's membership row in that project, each FOR SHARE. Concurrent applies do not serialise on the shared locks; any writer of those rows (a revocation, a role change, a candidate edit, an ownership transfer, an agent move) waits for an in-flight claim, and a claim waits for an uncommitted one. The wait is bounded by SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 5000 (5 seconds, fixed, not a setting). A wait that runs out (SQLSTATE 55P03) rolls the transaction back and answers 503 apply_busy with nothing written and no audit row, and so does a deadlock in which PostgreSQL picks this claim as the victim (SQLSTATE 40P01). The mapping wraps the whole claim transaction, from the locks to the commit of the claim and its approval anchor (_lock_contention_is_busy), not only the lock statements. Any other database error is not mapped and propagates as a server error. The claim commits before the promoter runs, so the locks are never held across the provider call and the waits are short; a database error after that point is the promotion's own failure path, not apply_busy.

For developers: a transaction that takes more than one of these rows must take them in the same order (job, agent, project, membership). The opposite order can deadlock against Apply: PostgreSQL aborts one of the two transactions with DeadlockDetected (SQLSTATE 40P01), and either side can be the victim. When Apply is the victim it answers 503 apply_busy like a lock timeout (is_lock_contention recognises both), with nothing written; the other transaction, if it is yours, continues, so a writer that must not be retried should expect the deadlock error itself. An Apply that answers 500 is not one of these lock cases (a serialization failure, SQLSTATE 40001, is deliberately not mapped and also answers 500): check the job's status before retrying, because an error after the claim committed can leave the job applying for the release reconciler. The busy 503s (apply_busy, approval_busy) carry Retry-After: 1.

SQLite and PostgreSQL#

guaranteePostgreSQL (required by the reference profile)SQLite (development)
two concurrent appliesthe second waits on the job lock and sees applyingthe conditional UPDATE matches no row for the second
a grant revoked while an Apply is in flightthe revoking write waits for the claim, or the claim waits and refuses: no gapnot closed by locks: the route reads the caller's authority again after the claim UPDATE, while SQLite's single write lock is held, and rolls back with apply_permission_revoked; between that check and the commit only the write lock protects it
a candidate edited after the gatethe job lock makes the edit wait, or the claim refusethe snapshot the promoter reads is verified against the recorded digest after the claim UPDATE and before the commit (the UPDATE's predicate matches the candidate_digest column, not the candidate content, so an edit to the content is caught by the snapshot check)
apply_busyyes, on a lock timeout or a deadlock victimyes, on a busy timeout: SQLite has no row locks to wait for, so database is locked (30 s) surfaces at the claim UPDATE or the commit and is mapped to apply_busy
a lock-order deadlock (a transaction that takes the rows in another order)PostgreSQL raises DeadlockDetected (SQLSTATE 40P01) in one of the two transactions, either side can be the victim; a victim Apply answers 503 apply_busynot applicable
allowed under CALIBER_PROFILE=referenceyesno (sqlite_database refuses startup)

The permission recheck covers the project grant and the job's visibility. The caller's platform scopes (caliber.operator) come from the credential as resolved at the start of the request.

Deploying migration 0132#

Migration 0132 adds the nullable candidate_digest column and backfills it for jobs that are candidate_ready or applying from their current candidate. It is additive for the schema and not safe for a mixed-version rollout of the writers.

  1. Stop every process that can move a job to candidate_ready, as step 1 of Upgrading already asks (the server and the workers), so no old writer is running after the migration.
  2. Run caliber-migrate. The new release reads the column on every job query, so it must not start before this, and the old release must not write jobs after it.
  3. Start the new release on every node.

A job an old process moves to candidate_ready after 0132 has no digest, and the new Apply refuses it with apply_candidate_unverified; there is no override, by design. The same holds for a job finished by an older release that is running again after a code rollback (the column stays and the old release does not fill it). The backfill is trust-on-upgrade: an edit made to a waiting candidate before the upgrade cannot be detected, because the current content is the only evaluated candidate the row can name. Rolling back the migration drops only the column.

Finding unverified jobs (read-only, on the CALIBER database):

SELECT job_id, agent_id, status FROM caliber_refinement_jobs
WHERE status = 'candidate_ready' AND candidate_digest IS NULL;

Each row needs another evaluation pass: POST /jobs/{job_id}/request-changes (a reviewer, editor or owner with the operator scope; it returns the job to running at the candidate stage, and the gate that follows records a fresh digest) or a new calibration. Never write candidate_digest by hand.

How this relates to the workflow approval chain#

Apply is not the workflow approval chain, and the two rules are set separately:

Applyworkflow protected-effect approval
what is decidedpromoting a refinement job's candidate (POST /jobs/{job_id}/apply)a protected effect proposed by a workflow step (caliber_runtime_approval_requests)
recorda born-approved CaliberApprovalRequest (caliber_approval_requests) minted by Apply as the rollback and provenance anchora request bound to one proposal's intent_hash, with expiry, supersession and a policy digest (below)
second personCALIBER_APPLY_REQUIRE_DISTINCT_APPROVER, apply_separation_refusal: trimmed and case-folded, an unknown requester is refusedCALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL, assert_distinct_actor: exact comparison, an unknown initiator is not compared
rechecked at committhe caller's current project permission and the exact candidate digest, inside the claimthe exact intent, evidence, policy, expiry, supersession and downstream version, at the dispatch boundary

The reference profile requires both settings. An Apply never decides a workflow approval request, and a workflow approval never applies a job.

Approval requests: bound to the exact intent (B06.1, #706)#

A protected effect is approved by a person, and the approval has to say what it approves. create_approval_request (caliber/src/caliber/workflows/approval_requests.py) records a pending row in caliber_runtime_approval_requests that is bound to one effect proposal and to what the approver is shown (ADR 0003 approval_request; migration 0127). It runs in the caller's transaction and never commits. The decision routes answer it by naming its runtime_approval_id (B06.4, #735, below); the dispatcher consumes the decision. A request has a lifetime and is replaced by a newer one for the same step (see "Expiry" and "Supersession", B06.2, #712).

  • What is bound. proposal_id, the proposal's full intent_hash (sha256: and 64 hex digits, the digest every consumer reuses), its expected_resource_version (the downstream version the approval is valid for, or NULL), the evidence_hash of what the approver is shown, the policy_digest, requested_by and expires_at (now + ttl_seconds, UTC). The record is validated against approval_request.v1.json before the row is stored (risk_class is the proposal's effect class; every response is allowed: approve, reject, request_changes). Values are read from the stored proposal, never from the object the caller holds.
  • The node's own policy. The caller passes the node's ApprovalPolicy (required). It is stored as the request's policy_snapshot exactly as the decision route reads it back (ApprovalPolicy.from_snapshot), so a node that needs caliber.admin with a quorum of two, or a deployment that allows self-approval, is enforced as configured. policy_digest is computed (policy_digest(policy): sha256: and the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the snapshot) and cannot be supplied. It pins the policy as requested, not the approvers a quorum accumulates in the same snapshot afterwards. A policy the runtime cannot honour (unknown role, a count below 1, escalate or auto_reject, a non-boolean flag) is bad_field.
  • Only a proposed proposal. Any other state (already approved, dispatched, committed, failed, unknown or reconciled) raises ApprovalRequestError("proposal_not_proposed"), a ValueError whose message is that code; nothing is stored. A proposal that does not exist is proposal_not_found. A malformed evidence_hash (not sha256: and 64 lowercase hex digits), a requested_by that is blank, has leading or trailing whitespace, is over 256 characters or holds a control, zero-width or bidirectional character, a ttl_seconds that is not an integer from 1 to 31 536 000, or a now the expiry cannot be computed from (a date at the end of year 9999, not a datetime) is bad_field, and the message names the field. The one-year ceiling is a policy choice (a request open longer is a caller's mistake), not a configuration value or a storage limit.
  • Expiry (B06.2, #712). expires_at = requested_at + ttl_seconds. The ttl is the caller's argument; a deployment's default is CALIBER_APPROVAL_TTL_SECONDS (approval_ttl_seconds, default 86400, 1 to 31 536 000), which the caller reads with configured_ttl_seconds(config). A change affects only requests created afterwards. Expiry is computed, never stored: nothing sweeps a request into an expired status, so a request that expires stays pending (or approved) in the list, and refusing it writes nothing. The rule is approval_refusal(status=, superseded_by=, expires_at=, now=) (approval_policy.py, database-free). The clock is the application's (datetime.now(timezone.utc), the same clock that wrote expires_at), not the database's: one request is never judged by two clocks, and a test can fix it. The window is half open, [requested_at, expires_at): at expires_at itself the request is already expired, so it is never usable one tick longer than its ttl (one microsecond earlier it is not). Servers that share a database need synchronized clocks, as for every other deadline here; a clock that runs behind lets a request live that long past its expiry. A request with no expires_at (a legacy, node-level one) never expires.
  • Supersession (B06.2, #712). In the transaction that inserts a request, every other live bound request for the same (workflow_run_id, node_id) becomes status = "superseded" with superseded_by set to the new request's id: a request that is pending, or approved and not yet consumed (consumed_at unset), whether it names the same proposal or a later one of the node (a changed intent or version). It is atomic with the new request: if the caller rolls back, the older one is live again. Left alone: a request for another node or another run, a legacy request (it binds no intent a change could void), a rejected one, a consumed one, and one already superseded (its superseded_by is never rewritten, so superseded requests form a chain). Only status and superseded_by move; the binding the approver saw and any decision already recorded stay on the row, unusable. The requests a call replaced are those whose superseded_by is the returned request's id. The newer request is the one whose creator took the run lock later (commit order), not the one with the later requested_at.
  • Refusal codes (reason_code of the 409; the vocabulary of docs/architecture/approval-ux-contract.md, which replaces the approval_expired and approval_superseded the plan named). superseded when the request was replaced (status is superseded or superseded_by is set), expired when the clock is at or past expires_at. Superseded is reported first, so a replaced request that is also expired says it was replaced (the current request is the thing to decide).
  • Locking. Creators take the run row, then the proposal row, both FOR UPDATE (a no-op on SQLite, whose write transaction is exclusive), in that order. The run lock is what makes supersession safe: creators for different proposals of one node lock different proposal rows, so without it each would read the other's request as absent and leave two live ones. Creators for one proposal and the proposal's own state transition serialize on the proposal row: a proposal moving to approved either commits before the creator reads it (the creator refuses) or waits for the creator's transaction. The requests being superseded are read FOR UPDATE, predicate included, so a decider or a consumer that holds one finishes first and a request it consumed is not overwritten. Whatever decides or consumes a request must lock that request's row FOR UPDATE and re-run approval_refusal on what it read before writing (taking the run row first if it takes both). All locks last until the caller commits or rolls back, so a caller keeps its transaction short; the run lock also briefly holds up other writers of that run's row.
  • The binding is a database fact. A row is either legacy (every binding column NULL) or fully bound, never half-bound in either direction (ck_runtime_approval_bound); the three hash and digest columns are exactly 71 characters (ck_runtime_approval_digest_length); and a BEFORE UPDATE trigger (SQLite and PostgreSQL) refuses any change to proposal_id, intent_hash, evidence_hash, policy_digest, expected_resource_version, expires_at and requested_by: a request cannot be re-bound to another intent, nor a legacy row bound after the fact. status, the decision columns, policy_snapshot, superseded_by and consumed_at still move. PostgreSQL also enforces the proposal foreign key (SQLite does not enforce foreign keys in this repository).
  • Decision versus commit. The decision routes (approve and reject) record an explicit decision for a request that has a proposal_id, but never consume it. For a bound request they answer 409 with a reason_code and a static message that carries no id, hash, requester or approver, and write nothing, for already_consumed, superseded, expired, approval_not_current and already_decided (B06.2/B06.4, above and below). This is intentional: the HTTP decision is not effect consumption. At the dispatch boundary B06.3's approval_valid_at_commit rechecks the exact stored proposal, evidence and policy pins, expiry, supersession, consumption, and the current downstream version before any connector call. It then calls the B03.4 identity path, which invokes decide with the run manifest's original subject, workload, purpose, run id and grant id. The actual approver is checked separately against the current required platform scope, active project membership/approval role and separation-of-duties policy; the approver is never substituted into the run's grant. The dispatcher in B04.1 consumes the still-locked request only after this validator succeeds. The validator returns stable intent_mismatch, expired, superseded, role_revoked and stale_version codes (plus self_approval, not_approved, already_consumed, not_found and authority_unavailable for their distinct failure states), and does not call a downstream connector. The default selection (no runtime_approval_id) ignores bound rows, so a legacy node-level request is never shadowed by a newer bound one. The list endpoint still shows bound rows (with their status; it does not yet expose expires_at or superseded_by, which the approvals UI, #743, adds). A request that expires is not turned into a proposal state (the proposal stays proposed, so ask again).
  • Legacy rows stay valid. A node-level approval that guards no proposal keeps NULL in every new column and is decided exactly as before.
  • Migration. 0127 adds nine nullable columns, a foreign key, two checks, an index and the trigger (on PostgreSQL a function pinned to the schema); no backfill. Downgrade drops the trigger and function, the checks, the index and the columns; a legacy request is untouched and a bound one is lost. It needs 0126 (B05.5b) to be applied first. B06.2 adds no migration: expires_at, superseded_by and consumed_at are already in 0127 (the trigger lets status and superseded_by move), so there is no schema change, rollback or deployment step beyond the new optional setting CALIBER_APPROVAL_TTL_SECONDS. 0134 (B11.3c, #1061) adds one nullable column, commit_decision_id (the policy decision the dispatcher's commit check recorded in the claim that consumed the request), and two triggers that make it write-once and settable only by consumption (see the causal-links section); it adds the column in place, so the 0127 trigger is kept, and it does not backfill. Downgrade drops the triggers, their functions and the column.
  • Distinct actors. The separation-of-duties rule of record_approval is now assert_distinct_actor(actor, initiated_by, *, allow_self) (approval_policy.py): it raises ApprovalPolicyError ("the account that triggered this run cannot approve it; a second person must decide ...") when the actor is the initiator, unless allow_self (CALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL) is set; an unknown initiator is not compared. actor_provenance.require_distinct_actors and the assistant service's author/reviewer checks are not delegated to it: they raise another error type, compare objects or other parties and have no allow_self, so sharing one function would change behaviour their callers pin.
from caliber.workflows.approval_policy import ApprovalPolicy
from caliber.workflows.approval_requests import ApprovalRequestError, create_approval_request

try:
    request = create_approval_request(
        session,
        proposal=proposal,
        policy=node_policy,  # the node's ApprovalPolicy; stored as the snapshot, digested into policy_digest
        evidence_hash=evidence_digest,  # "sha256:" + 64 hex digits
        requested_by="editor_a",
        ttl_seconds=86400,
    )
except ApprovalRequestError as refused:
    # refused.code is "proposal_not_proposed", "proposal_not_found" or "bad_field". For proposal_not_proposed the proposal has already
    # moved on: read its state, do not ask again for the same intent. Nothing was stored, so there is nothing to undo.
    ...
session.commit()  # the caller owns the transaction; the proposal row stays locked until then

Deciding such a request through the API (the same answers for approve and reject). A live request that the caller may decide answers 200 and records the decision (approve answers status: pending with remaining_approvals until the node's quorum is met). The refusals write nothing:

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/workflow-runs/{run_id}/approval/approve   {"runtime_approval_id": "<bound request>"}

# replaced by a newer request for the step (B06.2). Recovery: decide the current request of the step; list the run's approvals and take the
# newest one that is `pending`.
409 {"detail": "this approval request was replaced by a newer request and can no longer be decided; decide the current request for this step",
     "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "superseded"}

# at or past expires_at (B06.2). Recovery: ask for a new approval of the step (create a new request, which also replaces this one); the
# proposal is unchanged and still `proposed`.
409 {"detail": "this approval request has expired and can no longer be decided; ask for a new approval of the step",
     "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "expired"}

# already consumed by the dispatcher; the decision is terminal and cannot be changed (a late reject does not fail the run).
# Recovery: none needed; read the proposal's state (`dispatched`, `committed`, `unknown`) and let the reconciler settle it.
409 {"detail": "this approval decision was already consumed by dispatch",
     "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "already_consumed"}

# approved or rejected already (an approval waits for the dispatcher to consume it). Recovery: none; resume the run (POST .../resume) if it is
# still parked behind an approval.
409 {"detail": "this approval request already holds a decision and cannot be decided again; an approval is consumed when its effect is dispatched",
     "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "already_decided"}

# the request belongs to another node than the one the run waits at. Recovery: decide the request of the node the run is waiting at.
409 {"detail": "this approval request is not for the step the run is waiting at",
     "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "approval_not_current"}

# a lock is held too long (PostgreSQL lock_timeout, 5 s), the decision lost a deadlock (40P01) or SQLite stayed busy (database is locked): nothing was decided or held. Recovery: retry shortly.
503 {"detail": "this approval is being decided or dispatched right now; nothing was decided, retry shortly",
     "status_code": 503, "reason_code": "approval_busy"}

# the caller requested this approval (or started the run) and self-approval is not enabled: a second person must decide.
403 {"detail": "the account that triggered this run cannot approve it; a second person must decide (set CALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL=true for a single-operator install)"}

What the dispatcher answers when it later claims the decision (EffectRefused.code; the approval stays unconsumed and no backend is called): not_approved (not decided yet, rejected, or fewer recorded approvers than the quorum), already_consumed, expired, superseded, role_revoked (an approver's scope, project role or membership changed since they decided, so the quorum is no longer met), self_approval (an approver is now the run's initiator or the requester), intent_mismatch, stale_version, lease_lost / stale_owner (the captured execution-owner lease is no longer the held one). Recovery for each is to ask again (a new request) or to let the current owner retry; a retry after the claim committed is already_dispatched and sends nothing.

Creating a replacement, with the deployment's window:

from caliber.workflows.approval_requests import configured_ttl_seconds, create_approval_request

request = create_approval_request(
    session,
    proposal=changed_proposal,  # a later proposal of the same node; the older live request becomes superseded
    policy=node_policy,
    evidence_hash=evidence_digest,
    requested_by="editor_a",
    ttl_seconds=configured_ttl_seconds(config),  # CALIBER_APPROVAL_TTL_SECONDS, default 86400
)
session.commit()  # the older request's status and superseded_by are written in the same transaction

For a decision endpoint that only needs the lifecycle code, the pure rule remains:

from caliber.workflows.approval_policy import approval_refusal

code = approval_refusal(
    status=row.status, superseded_by=row.superseded_by, expires_at=row.expires_at, now=datetime.now(timezone.utc)
)  # "superseded", "expired" or None; call it on the row read FOR UPDATE, in the transaction that acts on it

The B06.3 commit validator is the producer-owned boundary used by the dispatcher:

from caliber.workflows.approval_policy import approval_valid_at_commit

checked = approval_valid_at_commit(
    session,
    approval_id=approval.runtime_approval_id,
    proposal_id=proposal.proposal_id,
    approver_scopes=current_approver_scopes,
    current_resource_version=downstream_version,  # required for versioned targets; omission fails closed
    evidence_hash=current_evidence_hash,
)
# Keep the run, proposal and approval locks until the same transaction consumes
# approval and claims dispatch. No connector is called by this function.

The approval panel: what the approver sees and what the console obeys (B06.5, #743)#

A person deciding a bound request has to see what they are approving. The console shows it in an inline approval panel under Recovery Diagnostics of a run (ApprovalDecisionPanel, opened by BoundApprovalReview) for every bound request that is pending, or approved and not yet consumed. A legacy node-level request (no proposal_id) keeps the plain Approve and Reject buttons it always had; for a bound one those header buttons are not shown, because they would approve it unseen. The panel reads one record, GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/approvals/{approval_id} (caliber.workflows.approval_view), and decides nothing itself.

Who may read it. The access of reading the run (a run you cannot see is 404) plus the project read role, evaluated now. A caller who fails either, an approval of another run and an unknown id all get the same 404. A caller who also holds the project approve action (owner or reviewer) sees the effect and who requested it; anyone else with read access sees the pins, the state and the quorum, proposal is null and binding.requested_by is null (deliberate: the view is a project-read surface and shows any reader a request's state, as the list route already showed its status and who decided; the decision routes still tell a caller who may not decide nothing about the state, because they check authority before state). The SDK reads it as client.workflows.runs.approval(run_id, approval_id), untyped like approvals(). The list route (GET .../approvals) gains optional proposal_id, expires_at, superseded_by and consumed_at, so the console can tell a bound request from a legacy one; an older client ignores them. They follow the view's rule: filled only for a caller with the project read role, null for anyone else (the rest of the list is unchanged).

What it returns.

FieldContent
bindingproposal_id, intent_hash, evidence_hash, policy_digest, expected_resource_version, expires_at, requested_by, superseded_by, consumed_at; null for a legacy request
proposalconnector, connector_version, effect_class (the risk class: read only, reversible write, irreversible write or data export), resource, state, and the shape of the arguments: each top-level name (only when it is a plain identifier, otherwise unnamed) and the kind of its value, at most 50
policy, quorumthe node's required_role, approval_count, timeout_behavior, allow_self_approval; who approved so far, how many are required and how many remain
stateopen, or why the request cannot be decided now, most final first: already_consumed, superseded (with superseded_by), expired, rejected, run_not_waiting (a rejection and a cancellation both clear the run's current node, so they are named before the node is compared), approval_not_current (another node's request of a waiting run), already_decided
allowed_responsesthe decisions the routes accept now: approve and reject. request_changes is in the contract but has no route, so it is not offered
callerthe authenticated principal, and for approve and reject whether it is allowed now and, when not, the first reason: the request's state, a disabled deployment switch (queue_disabled, approvals_disabled, and for an approval checkpointing_disabled, which the routes check first and answer with a plain 409), project_role_required, insufficient_scope, self_approval or duplicate_approver

No argument value ever leaves the server. The arguments are the one place a secret or a personal datum can sit, the platform's other operator views never load them, and the intent_hash binds every value, so the panel shows names, kinds and counts and says that the values are pinned by the digest. Showing values needs a connector-owned preview that redacts, which does not exist yet; the console does not guess at one. Nothing in a response is logged by the console, and a refusal message is chosen from the reason_code the server sent, with values from the view, never from response text.

The server decides, the console renders. caller is computed with the decision routes' own rules (the project approve action, the node's required_role scope, the requester and run-initiator rule, one approval per person) and the panel only disables a button from it (aria-disabled, with the reason attached through aria-describedby, so the button stays focusable and the reason is read). The route re-derives everything under its locks, so a stale panel cannot approve what the server would refuse. A decision sends {runtime_approval_id, reason} and nothing else; who decides is the authenticated principal.

Refusals, with the text the panel shows and the recovery (the decision route's 409 codes arrive as reason_code; the ability reasons arrive in the view):

CodeWhere it comes fromPanel text (abridged)Recovery
expiredview state, 409 on decide"This request expired at 2026-11-01 14:30 UTC. Nothing was done. Ask the requester to send it again."ask for a new request
supersededview state, 409"A newer request replaced this one (RAP-...). Open the newer request."decide the newer request (linked when it is on the page)
already_decidedview state, 409"This request already holds a decision ... waiting for the system to act on it."nothing; dispatch consumes it
already_consumedview state, 409"This approval was already used to run the action."ask for a new request if needed again
approval_not_currentview state, 409"This request is not for the step the run is waiting at."decide the run's current request
run_not_waitingview state"This run is no longer waiting for approval ..."none
approval_busy503 on decide"This request is being decided or dispatched right now. Nothing was decided. Wait a moment, then press the button again."press again; the buttons stay live
self_approvalview ability"You started this run, so you cannot approve it. A second person must decide."a second person decides; Reject stays available
duplicate_approverview ability"You already approved this step. It needs 2 different approvers; 1 more is needed."another approver decides
queue_disabled, approvals_disabled, checkpointing_disabledview ability"Deciding approvals is switched off for this deployment ..."an administrator enables the switch (checkpointing_disabled blocks only Approve)
insufficient_scope, project_role_requiredview ability"This step needs the caliber.approver role and your account does not hold it ..."ask for the role
a network failure or any other 5xxdecide"We could not confirm whether your decision was recorded ... check it before deciding again."the panel refetches; it never retries by itself, because a retry would answer duplicate_approver

Not built, stated plainly. The contract's stale_version, intent_mismatch, fenced_owner and role_revoked messages are in the panel and render when a reason_code of that name reaches it, but today the platform refuses those only at dispatch (effect.approval.commit_check span, EffectRefused), never as the answer to a decision, and the view cannot read them back: there is no persisted commit-time refusal to show (the causal-links route says as much). The view does not carry the target's current state, a before-and-after preview (both need a connector query operation), requested_by_type (the platform has no principal type yet; the requester's id is shown), evidence_url (there is no evidence package yet) or the policy decision's reason codes. request_changes and a intent_hash in the decision body are not implemented in the routes. Approving the last required approval does not resume the run: the run stays waiting_approval until someone with the operator role resumes it, and the panel says so.

What the browser checks cover. The Playwright spec asserts roles, accessible names and descriptions, keyboard order, focus and the announced text with role and name queries and an accessibility-tree snapshot. The repository has no axe integration, so there is no automated colour-contrast or rule-engine audit of the panel; contrast follows the console's existing slate, amber and red palette and has not been measured.

Configuration, migration and rollback. No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. The view is read-only and the list fields are optional additions. Rolling back is reverting the change; a console without it ignores the new list fields and keeps the plain buttons.

Agent steps: a request, a result, and no effects (B08.1a, #713)#

An agent step is one bounded unit of model work in a workflow node. Two control records (ADR 0003) describe it, and caliber.contracts.agent_step is the gate in front of both: it validates a record and refuses it before anything is dispatched. This page is the contract; the adapters that produce results (B08.1b onwards), the limit enforcement (B08.3) and the token reservation (B08.4) build on it and are not part of it.

  • agent_step_request v1 names the step (step_request_id, workflow_run_id, node_id, the durable occurrence_id and the attempt), what it was given (run_manifest_digest and context_manifest_digest, each 64 lowercase hex digits), the one grant_id it runs under and its limits: max_turns, max_tool_calls, max_tokens (integers, zero allowed) and a deadline (RFC 3339 with an offset, ASCII digits, at most nine fractional digits, no leap second; StepLimits.deadline_at is the aware datetime, and nothing reads the clock). The platform enforces the limits, not the adapter. Every identifier is not blank and has no control character or lone surrogate, the rule the effect proposal applies.
  • The step and its id. The platform allocates one step_request_id for one (run, node, occurrence, attempt) tuple; the context manifest of the step carries the same id. A result must repeat the id and the tuple: one whose tuple matches but whose id differs, or whose id matches but whose tuple differs, is refused.
  • agent_step_result v1 answers it: the same five identifying fields, a stop_reason (completed, proposed_action, max_turns, max_tool_calls, max_tokens, deadline, refused, error), the provider's usage and at most one proposed_actions element, present exactly when the stop_reason is proposed_action. Optional: usage_source (provider when absent, estimated, unknown) and error_code (a short lowercase token, only with error or refused).
  • One proposed action per step, in v1. A logical effect is keyed by (run, node, occurrence), so a second action would share the first's key. The array stays so a later version can carry more, but only after it adds a per-action identity.
  • A step proposes; it never says anything happened. The result has no state, receipt or approval field and every schema is closed, so a result that claims a commit (state: committed, a receipt_id, stop_reason: committed) is refused like any other unknown field or value. An action becomes a recorded proposal only through caliber.effects.records, and committed there still needs a verified receipt.
  • What the model says is a claim, not a fact. Everything in a result is model output. In particular a proposed action's effect_class and connector_version are untrusted: a model can call an irreversible write read, and a read can be approved by policy alone. ProposedAction.bound_to(inventory_effect_class) returns the action carrying the platform's class (from the protected-effect inventory) and raises ClaimMismatch (code claim_mismatch) when the claim differs; the platform calls it (caliber.effects.step_proposal, B08.2) before record_proposal, and an action that is not platform_bound is never recorded.
  • One action shape for the step and the proposal. A proposed action is effect_class (read, reversible_write, irreversible_write, export), target (connector and resource), connector_version, args and expected_resource_version: the names and meaning they have in the proposal record. ProposedAction.intent is the very caliber.effects.records.Intent of that proposal and ProposedAction.intent_hash its sha256: digest, so what a step proposed, what an approver is shown and what a receipt answers are one digest. An action is immutable (args is a read-only deep view; intent and record() are fresh copies, so nothing handed out can make the stored arguments disagree with the digest) and equal to another exactly when their canonical intents are ({"a": True} is not {"a": 1}). Parsing builds each intent, so args that are too deep (more than 64 levels), too large (the intent is at most 256 KiB) or not plain JSON are refused here too, not later at the store.
  • Usage and the token reservation. usage.total_tokens is what a budget settles against: it may not be less than prompt_tokens + completion_tokens, and cached_prompt_tokens may not exceed prompt_tokens. When a call failed or the provider gave no usage, report usage_source estimated or unknown rather than figures that look genuine. A refused or malformed result does not release the step's token reservation: the reservation ledger charges the whole reservation for it.
  • Integers are integers. 1.0 is not an integer for these two kinds; attempt: 1.0 is refused, not coerced.
from caliber.contracts import ContractValidationError, UnsupportedSchemaVersion
from caliber.contracts.agent_step import parse_step_request, parse_step_result

request = parse_step_request(request_record)  # raises before any provider or tool is touched
try:
    result = parse_step_result(result_record, request)  # the request is required: a result is read as its answer
except UnsupportedSchemaVersion:
    ...  # a newer writer: refuse the step and upgrade this reader first, never read it as v1
except ContractValidationError as refusal:
    print(refusal.errors)  # the violations, by path and rule; nothing was dispatched
else:
    for action in result.proposed_actions:
        bound = action.bound_to(inventory_effect_class)  # the platform's class, or ClaimMismatch
        print(bound.intent_hash)  # submit as a proposal; the effect is still unperformed

Refusals are quiet. For these two kinds a refusal names the field and the rule, never the offending value, an unexpected property name or an unbounded amount of text: at most 20 violations are listed, an unsupported version is named only when it is a short plain token (else by its type), and a record of more than 1 MiB of JSON text (1048576 characters) is refused before it is validated. Other record kinds keep their messages. Refusals and what to do (ContractValidationError.errors, sorted by path):

the record hasrefused asrecover by
schema_version: "v2" (or anything but v1)UnsupportedSchemaVersion: agent_step_result schema_version v2 is not supported; supported: v1upgrading the reader before the writer (ADR 0003, readers before writers)
a field it does not define (state, receipt_id, a typo)<record>: additional properties are not allowed (proposed_actions/0: ... inside an action; the property is not named)removing the field; a step reports no state
stop_reason: "committed"stop_reason: is not one of ['completed', 'proposed_action', ...]reporting completed or proposed_action; a commit is the proposal's, with a receipt
effect_class: "write"proposed_actions/0/effect_class: is not one of ['read', 'reversible_write', 'irreversible_write', 'export']using one of the four classes of the connector inventory
an action with no targetproposed_actions/0: 'target' is a required propertynaming the connector and the resource
two or more actionsproposed_actions: violates maxItems 1proposing one effect per step; the next is the next occurrence
proposals with stop_reason: "completed", or proposed_action with noneproposed_actions: must equal [] or proposed_actions: violates minItems 1stopping with proposed_action exactly when there is a proposal
attempt: 1.0, a blank or control-character identifierattempt: must be of type integer, node_id: does not match the required patternintegers and printable identifiers
a total below the partsusage/total_tokens: is less than prompt_tokens + completion_tokensreporting the provider's total (or usage_source: "estimated")
a result for another stepstep_request_id: names another step than the request's, although run, node, occurrence and attempt are the same (or <field>: differs from the request's, although step_request_id is the same)applying only the result of the request that was asked
an action whose class the platform does not holdClaimMismatch: the step claimed effect_class 'read'; the platform's is 'irreversible_write'proposing nothing: the step's claim is discarded, the platform's class governs

A result that is refused is the end of that step's use of it: nothing was proposed, recorded or dispatched, and the retry is the same occurrence_id with the next attempt. A parse_* call is pure: it does not read the clock, so the deadline and the other limits are checked by the platform around the provider call (B08.3), not here.

Agent step adapters: the boundary every provider answers through (B08.1b, #720)#

caliber.workflows.agent_step is the seam between the agent-step contracts above and a model provider. It adds no route, no table and no setting. It defines what an executor must do to take part in governed execution and how the platform treats the answer; the limits (B08.3), the token reservation (B08.4) and turning a model's tool call into a recorded proposal (B08.2) build on it.

  • AgentStepAdapter (caliber.workflows.runtime.AgentStepAdapter is the same protocol) is run_step(request: AgentStepRequest, step_input: AgentStepInput) -> AgentStepResult, a plain function (an async def is refused). AgentStepInput carries the agent, its input_text and history, the handoff_agents it may hand off to and read_tools: the callables of the tools the platform classified read in the protected-effect inventory (filter_read_tools(tool_callables, is_read) applies one classification, fails closed, and is what the platform uses for the step and for each handoff target). That is the only set of tools an adapter may run. Every name must be a tool bound to the agent, a tool the model calls that is not in the set is proposed (B08.2), never run, and an adapter cannot invoke a protected tool because it was never given one. Each handoff target is a StepHandoffTarget(agent, read_tools) holding only its read-class callables: the runtime's own handoff maps, which carry every callable of the target, are refused by type. Construction copies read_tools, history and the handoff targets into read-only containers, so neither side can change what the other holds. An adapter repeats the request's step_request_id and its run, node, occurrence and attempt; it never says an effect happened (the result has no field for that) and answers a provider failure with a typed result, not an exception.
  • run_agent_step(adapter, request, step_input) is the one entry the platform calls, and it trusts nothing the adapter does:
    1. the request is validated first (parse_step_request(request.record())) and step_input.agent must be the request's node; either failure raises ContractValidationError and the adapter is not called;
    2. an object without run_step, or whose run_step returns a coroutine (closed, never awaited), is refused (adapter_unsupported);
    3. what the adapter returns must be exactly an AgentStepResult holding exactly the contract's types (no subclass of the result, StepUsage or ProposedAction, no str or int subclass in a field, a tuple of actions): a subclass can override record() or answer differently each time it is read, so none is asked anything. The platform then takes one plain snapshot of the record (a JSON round trip, no hook, no NaN) and reads only that snapshot through parse_step_result(snapshot, request): schema, every proposed action's intent, and that it answers this step. No method of an adapter-supplied object runs after the snapshot, the platform returns a result it rebuilt, and ProposedAction.platform_bound is false on every action (an adapter cannot mark a claim as bound);
    4. an exception, a timeout, a return that is not a result, or a result that fails step 3 becomes an error result with a fixed error_code. No exception text and no provider payload is placed in a result or a log line; the exception's class name and the step id are logged, and a result dropped as malformed logs the usage numbers it reported. BaseException (KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, asyncio.CancelledError, GeneratorExit) propagates.
  • Refusals and failures keep the reservation. A refused or error result the boundary creates carries zero usage with usage_source: "unknown": "the provider may have been called and nothing is known", never "nothing was used". The ledger charges the whole reservation for each of them, and for any BaseException that escapes it leaves the reservation open at its whole ceiling, because the provider call may have happened. NOT_CALLED_CODES (adapter_unsupported, adapter_not_integrated) mark a body that never ran, but the ledger does not infer "not called" from a result an adapter could write itself: the platform decides before it reserves (an executor that is not an adapter, and a step before_work_stop stops, reserve nothing), and every reservation it does take is kept.
  • Timeouts. The boundary maps TimeoutError (asyncio.TimeoutError is the same class from Python 3.11) to adapter_timeout and nothing else; it does not know a provider's exception types. A provider adapter (#727-#730) catches its SDK's timeouts (openai, anthropic, httpx) and returns failure(request, ADAPTER_TIMEOUT) itself.
  • FakeWorkflowExecutor is the scripted adapter (FakeWorkflowExecutor(step_script=[...])): deterministic, offline, no clock, no network, and it never runs a protected tool. An entry is a ScriptedStep (answered with the request's identity; read_tool_calls run named tools through read_tools only, and a name outside it is refused tool_not_read_class and not run), an exception (a staged provider failure the adapter returns as error: adapter_timeout for a TimeoutError, else provider_error) or a callable returning a raw agent_step_result record (read with parse_step_result like provider output, so a claimed commit or another step's result is malformed_result, returned by the adapter itself). Entries are used in order, one per caller even under concurrency, and a script that runs out refuses with script_exhausted; with no script every step completed with usage estimated from the input. fake.step_requests lists the requests it was asked.
  • The provider executors are integrated for governed execution (B08.openai-agents #728, B08.openai-chat #729, B08.openai-responses #730 and B08.anthropic #727). Each executor's run_step uses the shared typed step contract while its run_agent path remains unchanged. The OpenAI Agents adapter loads the optional SDK lazily, runs only read tools, and returns protected calls as unbound proposals; its ordinary tests use a deterministic SDK stub and never call a live provider.
  • Conformance harness. caliber.testing.agent_step_conformance (re-exported by caliber/tests/agent_step_conformance.py) is what a provider adapter's tests plug into, and the conformance suite (B08.5 #769) runs every rule against each of the four provider adapters. An adapter supplies a driver that builds it with its provider transport stubbed to a scenario and whose stub calls ctx.provider_called() each time the provider would be called. run_scenario checks, through run_agent_step: the stub was reached; the asked step is answered; a protected-tool canary (behind the agent's tool binding and ctx.tool_registry, never in read_tools) is never run; a proposal is built from the staged tool call and stays an unbound claim, and a model that lies about the effect class is a ClaimMismatch at bound_to; a read tool runs through read_tools; completes reports exactly the stubbed usage with source provider and a max_* stop keeps it; and each of a provider error, a timeout, unreadable output, a claimed commit and another step's result is a bounded error whose code is the adapter's own (adapter_timeout and malformed_result where they apply; the platform's adapter_error, adapter_unsupported, adapter_not_integrated and script_exhausted never pass) and that the adapter itself, called directly, returned rather than raised. The planted payload is in neither the result nor any log record (loggers lowered to DEBUG). A driver may not declare completes, proposes_protected_tool or claims_commit unsupported. An adapter that reads a clock against the request's deadline needs its driver to inject a fake one (the harness' default deadline, 2026-10-26T09:10:00Z, is in the past), and budget_exhausted stages one turn that spent the budget (StepUsage(900, 100, 1000, 1, 0)). Each provider adapter's test file under tests/conformance/ is its driver; each declares another_steps_result unsupported (no provider's response carries the identity of the step it answers).
from caliber.workflows.agent_step import AgentStepInput, ScriptedStep, run_agent_step
from caliber.workflows.runtime import FakeWorkflowExecutor

fake = FakeWorkflowExecutor(step_script=[ScriptedStep("proposed_action", (action,)), TimeoutError()])
result = run_agent_step(fake, request, AgentStepInput(agent=agent, input_text=text, read_tools=read_only_tools))
if result.stop_reason == "proposed_action":
    bound = result.proposed_actions[0].bound_to(inventory_effect_class)  # the platform's class, or ClaimMismatch

Failures the boundary returns (all stop_reason error unless noted). Every result the boundary creates has usage_source: "unknown", no proposal and the asked step's identity; an adapter's own failure keeps the usage it reports. Recovery is always the same shape: the occurrence is retried as the next attempt, after the reservation of this one is settled (B08.4):

the adapterresultrecover by
has no Agents SDK installedrefused, provider_unavailableinstall the optional Agents SDK extra; the legacy run_agent path remains available
has no run_step, or an async def onerefused, adapter_unsupportedpassing an AgentStepAdapter with a plain run_step
raises (a provider error, anything else)adapter_errorreading the server log (the exception's class and the step id, never its text) and retrying as the next attempt
times out (TimeoutError)adapter_timeoutthe call's outcome is unknown: retry as the next attempt; the reservation is kept
returns a result for another step, a record with an unknown field (state, receipt_id), stop_reason: "committed", two actions, a bad effect class, usage that contradicts itself, a subclass or a non-plain value, or a non-resultmalformed_resultnone for this output: it was dropped (its usage numbers are in the log); check the adapter's transcription of the provider output
