No double counting. The boundary keeps no state between calls: each call has its own counter and reads only its own result. A retry is the next attempt of the same occurrence with the full limits, and a resumed step that finds its recorded proposal asks nobody and reports no usage. Adding the usage of several attempts to one budget is the reservation ledger, not this check.

For the conformance suite. before_work_stop(request, clock=...) is the pre-work check the reservation calls first (a step it stops needs no reservation); the stop reasons are caliber.workflows.agent_step.LIMIT_STOPS. The conformance harness (caliber.testing.agent_step_conformance) gains FakeStepClock, fixed_clock, limits_changes and stop_before_work, and every run_scenario runs on a fixed clock (StepContext.clock); caliber/tests/test_agent_step_bounds.py runs the five executors over tripwire clients through stop_before_work, and the conformance suite (turn_limit, tool_call_limit, token_limit, deadline_limit, limits_before_work, adapter_cannot_raise_limits) runs the four provider adapters against every limit.

Not covered, so not claimed: the platform cannot observe a provider's turns or tokens, only what the adapter reports, so for those two the check bounds what is recorded and stops the proposal, while an adapter's own in-loop checks bound what is spent (a lying adapter can under-report tokens; the reservation charges a conservative figure unless a trusted result says less). A blocking provider call is not interrupted. The usage of a stopped step is in its result and in the run error text, and its charge is persisted by the reservation ledger.

Token reservations: reserved before the call, charged conservatively, settled once (B08.4, #761)#

The platform cannot observe a provider's tokens, only what the adapter reports, and a crash, a timeout or a refused result leaves nobody knowing what was charged. So a governed step's ceiling is reserved first, a charge is lowered only on a figure the platform believes, and nothing is ever released on a guess. caliber.budget.step_reservation holds the ledger (table caliber_step_token_reservations, migration 0133); the interpreter reserves in _run_governed_step, immediately before run_agent_step, and settles right after it returns. It is not a second budget authority for later milestones: the per-run figure below is the Beta per-step ledger, and the persistent budgets of M08 extend this table rather than add another.

The reservation. One row per (workflow_run_id, node_id, occurrence_id, attempt) (unique, and the step's step_request_id is stored with it). Its reserved_tokens is the step's limits.max_tokens after the B08.3 ceilings, and it is taken before the adapter is called, in one transaction under the run's row lock (FOR UPDATE, the first lock of the run, proposal, request order every writer of a run uses; on SQLite, which has no row lock and whose driver reads outside a transaction, the same section starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE): two workers asking together are serialized, so the sum of what a run has reserved or been charged plus the new ceiling can never pass the run's budget. Past it the step is refused with a typed, payload-free run error and the adapter is never called:

governed agent step token reservation refused: token_budget_exhausted (budget=39999 committed=0 requested=40000)
SettingDefaultAcceptedMeaning
CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS20000001 to 1000000000The most tokens one run's governed steps may reserve and be charged in total. Reaches a live step through GovernedStepContext.run_token_budget (the producer passes config.agent_run_max_tokens); a context that names none is bounded at this default, never unbounded. A ceiling larger than the whole budget refuses every step.
CALIBER_AGENT_RESERVATION_GRACE_SECONDS3001 to 86400, finiteHow long past its step's deadline an open reservation is left before the execution owner finalizes it as abandoned.

A value outside its bounds stops the service at startup, naming the setting; the context and the reservation functions refuse a budget that is not an integer in those bounds (a boolean is not a count).

Idempotent, and a replay is not a second call. A duplicate request for the same step returns the same reservation (created false) and never reserves twice, whatever the budget is by then. A step that is handed a reservation it did not create (a restarted run and the one that was never stopped both reach it, or the same attempt runs again after a crash) is refused with governed agent step token reservation refused: reservation_replayed and its adapter is not called: the earlier call may have spent, and the platform will not call the provider again on that strength. A retry of the node is the next attempt and takes its own reservation, so the attempts of one occurrence add up against the run. A step the platform stops before work (before_work_stop: no turn or token, a deadline already past) and an executor that is not an adapter reach no provider and reserve nothing, so nothing is ever released for them. There is no release.

What is charged. charge_for decides, from the stored ceiling and the result, never from a caller's copy:

the resultchargebasis
a figure above the reservation (an overrun), from any sourcethe figure, in full (the overage included)reported
a step that ran to an answer, usage_source provider (or absent: the contract reads that as the provider), a non-zero total at or below the reservationthe reported total; the unused part goes back to the runreported
refused, error, an estimated or unknown source, a zero total, a malformed or inconsistent usage, no resultthe whole reservationconservative

Believing a figure can only lower a charge when the result is one the platform trusts; believing a figure above the reservation can only raise it, so that is always done. What this does not do: it cannot verify a provider's number. The adapters are the platform's own code and report the provider's usage; this ledger refuses to let a result that carries no usable figure shrink a charge, and stores what the adapter said (reported_tokens, usage_source, stop_reason and a fixed-token error_code, never free text) for audit.

Settled once. settle_step_tokens is a compare-and-set from reserved to settled on the stored row: a retry, a duplicate, a settlement racing the janitor finds a final row, changes nothing and gets that row back, so a charge is never written twice and never lowered after the fact. A store that fails to settle leaves the reservation open, which counts at its whole ceiling (it can only overcharge); the step still goes on with the result in hand, the failure is logged by exception class only.

Open counts in full; nothing is released. A reservation is reserved from the moment it is taken. An exception out of the adapter that is not a result, a cancellation, a KeyboardInterrupt or a worker that is killed leaves it open at its whole ceiling, because the provider may have been called. There is no operator action that lowers a charge: nothing the platform can check would back it (the same rule as for effect proposals). A run that needs more budget gets a larger CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS.

Abandoned, owner only. After each pass the execution owner's effect reconciler loop (the same lease, compared in the transaction that writes) runs abandon_stale: a reservation still open past its step's deadline plus CALIBER_AGENT_RESERVATION_GRACE_SECONDS moves to abandoned at its whole reservation, oldest first and bounded per pass. The run's total does not move; the row only stops being open. A worker that returns after that finds a final row and its settlement changes nothing, including an overrun: a step that returns usage above its reservation after the sweep abandoned it (more than the step's deadline plus the grace) keeps the abandoned charge, the reservation, and the overage is not recorded (very unlikely: a provider timeout is capped at the remaining step deadline). The sweep runs only where the reconciler loop does (the reference profile, with CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_ENABLED on, its default); elsewhere, or with it off, open rows stay open and keep counting in full, which is safe. A process that does not hold the lease changes nothing.

Final means final. The ORM refuses every edit and delete of a reservation. The database refuses the same: CHECK constraints keep every figure non-negative, a conservative charge equal to the reservation, a reported charge equal to the reported figure, an abandoned row conservative, and a final row complete; a trigger refuses any UPDATE of a settled or abandoned row and any change to the identity and the reserved figures of an open one, and refuses DELETE (PostgreSQL also TRUNCATE, and revokes both from PUBLIC).

Migration and rollout. 0133 only adds the table and its guards (nothing else references it and nothing reads it before the code that writes it). Run it before the new code serves: a process on the new code with no table refuses a governed step with governed agent step token reservation refused: store_failed and never calls its adapter. Rolling back the code leaves the table unread; downgrading the migration drops the table and loses the charges counted against runs, so never do it where they matter.

the stepresultrecover by
would take the run past its budgettoken_budget_exhausted, nothing reserved, adapter not calleda larger CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS (a new run: a finished run's budget is its own)
runs again on an attempt that holds a reservation (a node retry in the same process, or a process-level re-execution)reservation_replayed, adapter not calleda node retry is the next attempt and reserves afresh; after a crash the attempt counter restarts at 1, so the resumed governed node is refused and the run fails: start a new run (see the known limit below)
the store cannot reservestore_failed, adapter not calledthe database; nothing was reserved
the worker died or was cancelled mid-callthe reservation stays reserved, counted in full, then abandoned after the gracenothing: it is already charged; see the recovery runbook

Known limit: crash recovery of a governed step is terminal (follow-up #1073). The attempt counter (_STEP_ATTEMPT) restarts at 1 on every process-level re-execution of a run. After a crash between the reservation and the settlement (or between the settlement and the recording of the proposal) the resumed governed node reaches the same (run, node, occurrence, attempt), finds the reservation, and is refused with reservation_replayed: the run fails and only a new run proceeds. That fails closed and avoids a second provider spend under one reservation, but it means a governed step cannot be resumed after a crash. The follow-up is to persist or derive the attempt so a legitimate resume reuses or supersedes the open reservation safely.

Deleting a workflow whose runs hold reservations is refused with 409 (cannot delete workflow: its runs have step token reservations), like run manifests and effect proposals.

Reading it back: caliber.budget.step_reservation.run_token_usage(session_factory, run_id) returns what a run has counted and how many reservations are open and final. No route lists reservations yet.

For the conformance suite (#769). reserve_step_tokens(session_factory, request, run_budget_tokens=...) returns a StepReservation (created, state, reserved_tokens, charged_tokens, charge_basis) or raises ReservationRefused whose code is one of token_budget_exhausted, reservation_replayed, request_invalid, budget_invalid, run_not_found, reservation_mismatch; settle_step_tokens(session_factory, reservation, result) returns the final row; charge_for(reserved, result) is the pure rule; abandon_stale(session_factory, lease, grace_seconds=...) is the owner janitor. The scenario tests/egi_scenarios/test_v08_timeout_retry.py::test_budget_refuses_before_call and the PostgreSQL races in tests/egi_scenarios/test_b08_token_reservation.py are the oracle; tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_governed_plan.py runs each provider adapter through the reservation (charged as reported for honest usage, the whole reservation for every other result, no second provider call on a replay).

Adapter conformance suite: the rules every provider adapter passes (B08.5, #769)#

The governed agent step has one boundary (run_agent_step) and four provider adapters behind it. The conformance suite is the evidence that an adapter holds its side of that boundary, and it is the same suite for every adapter: the four that ship (OpenAI chat completions, OpenAI Responses, the OpenAI Agents SDK and Anthropic Messages) and any adapter written elsewhere. It adds no route, table, setting or migration; it calls no provider, reads no real clock and needs no provider SDK.

Two modules ship with the package (caliber.testing, test support like the fault barriers) so that an adapter outside this repository can run what the repository runs:

  • caliber.testing.agent_step_conformance: the per-scenario harness that B08.1b introduced (moved here from tests/, which re-exports it), with its protected-tool canaries, fixed clock and StepContext;
  • caliber.testing.adapter_conformance: the rules, the provider script language, AdapterUnderTest, and the report.

Run it for the shipped adapters. The real executor classes over canned transports, every rule, offline:

cd caliber && pytest tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_conformance.py     # 4 adapters x 40 rules
pytest tests/conformance/test_suite_fails_against_broken_adapters.py         # the suite fails when an adapter is broken
pytest tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_governed_plan.py                 # the same adapters under the interpreter
pytest tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_openai_agents_real_sdk.py        # the Agents adapter on the installed SDK

Run it for your adapter. An adapter is any object with run_step(request, step_input) -> AgentStepResult (AgentStepAdapter). The suite needs one function from you, build(script, probe): it returns a fresh adapter whose provider transport plays script, an ordered list of what your provider does on its first, second, ... call (Reply, Fault, Garbage). The transport calls probe.provider_called(tools=[...], sent="...") each time the provider would be called (tools, the names the request offers the model, and sent, the request's text, are optional; the rules offered_tools_are_the_agents_own and read_tool_failure_is_class_only are reported unsupported without them), and the adapter reads time from probe.clock (the fake the rules move; an adapter that reads the real clock cannot be tested for a deadline). Something your transport cannot express raises Unsupported(reason): that passes for a rule marked optional (invalid_argument_text, read_tool_failure_is_class_only, offered_tools_are_the_agents_own) and fails for every other.

The complete example below is a correct adapter for a made-up provider and the build that stages the suite's scripts on it. It is the file tests/conformance/toy_adapter.py, which tests/conformance/test_example_third_party_adapter.py runs exactly as the last lines of the example say, and checks that the code quoted here is the file's. Every rule passes against it.

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json
import logging
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Any

from caliber.contracts.agent_step import (
    AgentStepRequest,
    AgentStepResult,
    ProposedAction,
    StepUsage,
)
from caliber.contracts.registry import ContractValidationError
from caliber.effects.records import ProposalError
from caliber.testing.adapter_conformance import (
    MALFORMED_USAGE,
    AdapterUnderTest,
    Call,
    Fault,
    Garbage,
    ProviderProbe,
    ProviderUsage,
    Reply,
    Script,
    fault_exception,
)
from caliber.workflows.agent_step import (
    ADAPTER_TIMEOUT,
    MALFORMED_RESULT,
    PROVIDER_ERROR,
    AgentStepInput,
    StepDeadlineReached,
    StepToolBudgetExceeded,
    answer,
    failure,
)

logger = logging.getLogger("acme_adapter")

_ENVELOPE = {"connector", "connector_version", "effect_class", "resource", "args"}
_OPTIONAL = {"expected_resource_version"}


class _Unreadable(Exception):  # noqa: N818 - what the provider sent cannot be read; never carries its text
    pass


@dataclass
class _Tally:
    prompt: int = 0
    completion: int = 0
    turns: int = 0
    tool_calls: int = 0
    estimated: bool = False

    def usage(self) -> StepUsage:
        total = self.prompt + self.completion
        return StepUsage(self.prompt, self.completion, total, self.turns, self.tool_calls)

    @property
    def source(self) -> str:
        return "estimated" if self.estimated else "provider"


def _count(value: object) -> int:
    if type(value) is not int or not 0 <= value <= 2_147_483_647:
        raise _Unreadable
    return value


class ToyAdapter:
    """One governed step against a provider callable; the example every rule of the conformance suite is run on."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        provider: Callable[[list[dict[str, Any]], list[str]], Any],
        *,
        now: Callable[[], datetime],
    ):
        self._provider = provider
        self._now = now

    def run_step(  # noqa: PLR0911, PLR0912 - one loop, one exit per way a step can end
        self, request: AgentStepRequest, step_input: AgentStepInput
    ) -> AgentStepResult:
        tally = _Tally()
        read_tools = dict(step_input.read_tools)
        messages = [*step_input.history, {"role": "user", "content": step_input.input_text}]
        while True:
            if (limit := self._limit_reached(request, tally)) is not None:
                return self._stop(request, limit, tally)
            try:
                reply = self._call_provider(messages, sorted(read_tools))
            except (TimeoutError, asyncio.TimeoutError):
                return failure(request, ADAPTER_TIMEOUT)
            except Exception as exc:
                return self._provider_failed(request, exc)
            try:
                calls = self._read_reply(reply, tally, step_input)
                if reply.get("finish") == "length" or self._over_budget(request, tally):
                    return self._stop(request, "max_tokens", tally)
                protected = [call for call in calls if call["name"] not in read_tools]
                if protected:
                    return self._propose(request, protected[0], tally, step_input)
                if not calls:
                    return answer(
                        request, "completed", usage=tally.usage(), usage_source=tally.source
                    )
                for call in calls:
                    if self._tool_limit_reached(request, tally):
                        return self._stop(request, "max_tool_calls", tally)
                    tally.tool_calls += 1
                    try:
                        result = self._run_read_tool(read_tools[call["name"]], call["arguments"])
                    except StepToolBudgetExceeded:
                        return self._stop(request, "max_tool_calls", tally)
                    except StepDeadlineReached:
                        return self._stop(request, "deadline", tally)
                    except Exception as exc:
                        # The model is told which kind of failure it was; the message is the tool's, not the model's.
                        result = json.dumps({"_error": type(exc).__name__})
                    messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": str(result)})
            except _Unreadable:
                return failure(request, MALFORMED_RESULT)

    @staticmethod
    def _stop(request: AgentStepRequest, reason: str, tally: _Tally) -> AgentStepResult:
        return answer(request, reason, usage=tally.usage(), usage_source=tally.source)

    def _limit_reached(self, request: AgentStepRequest, tally: _Tally) -> str | None:
        """A limit that forbids another provider call: turns, tokens, then the deadline."""
        limits = request.limits
        if tally.turns >= limits.max_turns:
            return "max_turns"
        if tally.prompt + tally.completion >= limits.max_tokens:
            return "max_tokens"
        if self._now() >= limits.deadline_at:
            return "deadline"
        return None

    @staticmethod
    def _over_budget(request: AgentStepRequest, tally: _Tally) -> bool:
        """The response just read took the step past ``max_tokens``: whatever it asked for is not acted on."""
        return tally.prompt + tally.completion > request.limits.max_tokens

    @staticmethod
    def _tool_limit_reached(request: AgentStepRequest, tally: _Tally) -> bool:
        return tally.tool_calls >= request.limits.max_tool_calls

    def _call_provider(self, messages: list[dict[str, Any]], tools: list[str]) -> Any:
        return self._provider(messages, tools)

    @staticmethod
    def _provider_failed(request: AgentStepRequest, exc: Exception) -> AgentStepResult:
        # Only the exception's class is logged: its text is the provider's, and may quote the prompt.
        logger.warning("provider call failed (%s)", type(exc).__name__)
        return failure(request, PROVIDER_ERROR)

    @staticmethod
    def _run_read_tool(tool: Callable[..., Any], arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> Any:
        return tool(**arguments)

    def _read_reply(
        self, reply: Any, tally: _Tally, step_input: AgentStepInput
    ) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        """The reply's tool calls (name and decoded arguments); its usage is added to ``tally``."""
        if not isinstance(reply, Mapping):
            raise _Unreadable
        usage = reply.get("usage")
        if usage is None:
            tally.estimated = True
            tally.prompt += len(step_input.input_text.split())
            tally.completion += len(str(reply.get("text") or "").split())
        elif isinstance(usage, Mapping):
            tally.prompt += _count(usage.get("prompt"))
            tally.completion += _count(usage.get("completion"))
        else:
            raise _Unreadable
        tally.turns += 1
        names = {binding.local_name for binding in step_input.agent.tools}
        calls = []
        try:
            for raw in reply.get("tool_calls") or []:
                text = raw["arguments"]
                arguments = json.loads(text) if isinstance(text, str) else text
                if not isinstance(arguments, dict) or raw["name"] not in names:
                    raise _Unreadable
                calls.append({"name": raw["name"], "arguments": arguments})
        except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
            raise _Unreadable from None
        return calls

    def _propose(
        self,
        request: AgentStepRequest,
        call: dict[str, Any],
        tally: _Tally,
        step_input: AgentStepInput,
    ) -> AgentStepResult:
        """The model's protected call as one unbound proposal: its claims are kept exactly as it made them."""
        del step_input
        envelope = call["arguments"]
        if not _ENVELOPE <= set(envelope) <= _ENVELOPE | _OPTIONAL:
            raise _Unreadable
        try:
            action = ProposedAction(
                connector=envelope["connector"],
                connector_version=envelope["connector_version"],
                effect_class=envelope["effect_class"],
                resource=envelope["resource"],
                args=envelope["args"],
                expected_resource_version=envelope.get("expected_resource_version"),
            )
        except (ProposalError, ContractValidationError, TypeError, ValueError):
            raise _Unreadable from None
        return answer(
            request,
            "proposed_action",
            usage=tally.usage(),
            proposed_actions=(action,),
            usage_source=tally.source,
        )

def toy_provider(
    script: Script, probe: ProviderProbe
) -> Callable[[list[dict[str, Any]], list[str]], Any]:
    """The made-up provider the suite's scripts are played on."""
    remaining = list(script)

    def provider(messages: list[dict[str, Any]], tools: list[str]) -> Any:
        probe.provider_called(tools=tools, sent=json.dumps(messages, default=str))
        if not remaining:
            raise RuntimeError("the script has no reply left")
        item = remaining.pop(0)
        if isinstance(item, Fault):
            raise TimeoutError(item.text) if item.kind == "timeout" else fault_exception(item)
        if isinstance(item, Garbage):
            return ["not", "a", "reply", item.text]
        return _wire(item)

    return provider


def _wire(reply: Reply) -> dict[str, Any]:
    wire: dict[str, Any] = {
        "text": reply.text,
        "tool_calls": [_wire_call(call) for call in reply.calls],
        "finish": "length" if reply.cut_off else "stop",
    }
    if reply.usage is MALFORMED_USAGE:
        wire["usage"] = {"prompt": "many", "completion": "some"}
    elif isinstance(reply.usage, ProviderUsage):
        wire["usage"] = {"prompt": reply.usage.prompt, "completion": reply.usage.completion}
    return wire


def _wire_call(call: Call) -> dict[str, Any]:
    text = call.arguments if isinstance(call.arguments, str) else json.dumps(call.arguments)
    return {"name": call.name, "arguments": text}


def toy_subject() -> AdapterUnderTest:
    """The conformance subject for :class:`ToyAdapter`: ``build`` returns a fresh adapter over a provider playing the script."""
    return AdapterUnderTest(
        name="toy",
        build=lambda script, probe: ToyAdapter(toy_provider(script, probe), now=probe.clock.now),
    )


import pytest

from caliber.testing.adapter_conformance import RULES, check_rule, conformance_report

SUBJECT = toy_subject()  # for your adapter: AdapterUnderTest(name="acme", build=your_build)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("rule", RULES, ids=lambda rule: rule.id)
def test_acme_conforms(rule):
    check_rule(SUBJECT, rule.id)  # raises ConformanceFailure naming the adapter, the rule and what was seen


print(conformance_report(SUBJECT).render())  # one table: PASS / FAIL / UNSUPPORTED per rule, then a verdict

What every run checks, whatever the rule. A rule plays its script twice: through the platform's entry (run_agent_step) and by calling the adapter alone on a fresh copy, because an adapter may not rely on the boundary to catch its mistakes. Both runs must satisfy: the result is a schema-valid agent_step_result that answers the asked step; no protected tool ran (a canary sits behind the protected tool's binding and in the unfiltered tool registry); the provider payload planted in the script (SECRET_MARKER) is in no result, log record (every logger, every level, extra= fields included), warning, stdout or stderr; and the adapter returned a typed result instead of raising. (The nine rules that come from the per-scenario harness, from completes to claims_commit, check the result, the canaries and the log records, which is what that harness has always checked.) Log capture cannot see a logger created during the run that turns propagation off, or output that bypasses logging, warnings and the standard streams.

RuleWhat it demands
completesA final answer completes the step and reports exactly the provider's usage
read_tool_callA read tool the model calls runs through read_tools, and usage sums over turns
proposes_protected_toolA protected tool call is one unbound proposal built from the model's call, never executed
model_lies_about_effect_classA claimed effect class is passed through unchanged, so binding it to the platform's class is refused
budget_exhaustedA response the provider cut off is a limit stop that keeps the provider's usage
provider_errorA provider error is a typed error result carrying no provider text
provider_timeoutA provider timeout is adapter_timeout
unreadable_outputOutput the adapter cannot read is malformed_result
claims_commitOutput that claims an effect happened is malformed_result, never a proposal
hostile_model_textHostile model text is inert: nothing is carried into the result, a log or a tool
extra_fields_rejectedA proposal that carries a field the contract does not have is malformed, never a proposal
oversized_arguments_refusedProposal arguments larger than the intent's limit are malformed, never recorded
deep_arguments_refusedProposal arguments nested deeper than the intent's limit are malformed
lone_surrogate_refusedA lone surrogate in a proposal is malformed: it cannot be canonicalised or stored
invalid_argument_textTool arguments that are not a JSON object are malformed for a proposal, and never crash the adapter
unknown_tool_not_runA tool the agent does not have is never run, and the step is not completed
connector_version_claimA claimed connector version is passed through, so the platform can refuse it
read_tools_authoritativeOnly the callables the platform classified read are run, whatever the binding says
one_proposed_actionTwo protected calls in one response are at most one proposal, and the second never runs
proposal_ends_stepA proposal ends the step: the provider is not asked again after it
handoff_not_followedA governed step never follows a handoff: the target's tools are not run
read_tool_failure_is_class_onlyA read tool that raises never crashes the adapter, and its message is not handed to the provider
offered_tools_are_the_agents_ownThe model is offered only tools the agent has: no handoff, no target's tool
invalid_request_refusedA request that is not a valid step, or not for this agent, never reaches the adapter
limits_before_workA step with no turn, no token or no time left never reaches the adapter or its provider
turn_limitThe adapter asks the provider for no more turns than the limit, and a stopped step proposes nothing
tool_call_limitNo read tool runs past max_tool_calls, and the step stops instead of going on
token_limitA step over max_tokens stops with the provider's usage kept and proposes nothing
deadline_limitA step past its deadline asks for nothing more, runs no tool and proposes nothing
adapter_cannot_raise_limitsThe platform holds a step to the limits it set, whatever the adapter was told
honest_usage_is_charged_as_reportedUsage the provider reported is reported as the provider's, so it is charged as spent
missing_usage_not_fabricatedA response without usage is reported estimated or unknown, never as genuine figures
malformed_usage_charged_wholeUnreadable usage never lowers the charge, and no proposal rides on it
asyncio_timeout_is_adapter_timeoutA timeout raised by asyncio itself is adapter_timeout, on every supported Python
no_hidden_retryA failed provider call is not retried: the provider is called once, and the retry is the platform's
cancellation_propagatesCancellation and interruption reach the caller, so the reservation stays open (the call may have spent)
errors_are_payload_freeA failure is a fixed code: no provider text, argument or tool name reaches a result or any output
deterministicThe same step against the same provider answers identically, proposals included
fresh_state_per_stepAn adapter carries nothing from one step to the next: each answers its own request
input_isolationThe adapter gets its own copy of the request and its tools, and changes none of what it was handed

The platform enforces some of this whatever an adapter does, and the suite says so rather than pretend otherwise. The limits are held by the boundary (before_work_stop, the tool meter, _enforce_limits): an adapter that overruns still has its proposal dropped and the typed stop returned. What an adapter alone decides is what it spends: whether it stops asking the provider once a limit is reached. A rule therefore asserts both: the result through the platform and the adapter's own answer when called alone, and the provider calls it made. adapter_cannot_raise_limits is the one limit rule with no "alone" half: its point is that the boundary holds an adapter to the limits it set although the adapter was told otherwise.

A subject may declare the stops it cannot make. AdapterUnderTest(unbounded_in_loop=...), from proposal, tool_calls, tokens and deadline, is for an adapter whose SDK offers no hook between provider calls for that stop: the rules then do not demand the adapter's own stop (the spend past the limit is bounded by the token reservation only). The declaration is the subject's own, so it is public: the report prints it on its second line (cannot stop asking the provider at: ...), and it is read in the pull request or the CI log like any other line of the report. It relaxes only those spend checks, never a rule. No shipped adapter declares any. The OpenAI Agents SDK takes max_turns for the run and tool_use_behavior (a function; present since openai-agents 0.0.7 and run here on 0.20 and 0.24, where the SDK requires the function to return its own ToolsToFinalOutputResult, which the adapter uses) for everything else: after each turn's tools the adapter's function ends the run for a proposal, the tool-call limit, the token budget or the deadline, before the model is asked again. test_agent_adapter_openai_agents_real_sdk.py runs that on the installed SDK with a scripted model, so the emulation the conformance suite uses cannot drift from what the SDK does. (Separately and before this change: the adapter already builds FunctionTool(needs_approval=..., timeout_seconds=...), which openai-agents 0.0.7 does not accept, so the declared minimum >=0.0.7 is stale for the adapter as a whole; follow-up.)

The suite has been shown to fail. tests/conformance/broken_adapters.py holds 38 deliberately broken adapters, each the reference adapter with exactly one defect (it runs a protected tool, strips a claimed receipt_id and proposes anyway, forgets usage on a cut-off, fabricates figures for a response without usage, retries a provider call, swallows a cancellation, misses an asyncio timeout, logs the model's text or the provider's exception, hands a tool's exception message to the provider, offers a handoff target, ignores a limit, carries the first step's result into the second, rewrites the limits of the request it was handed), and test_suite_fails_against_broken_adapters.py requires that each fails the rule written for it for a reason the rule states, and that the intact adapter passes all 40. The rules the boundary decides (limits_before_work, adapter_cannot_raise_limits, invalid_request_refused and the copy half of input_isolation) are shown to fail against a boundary with that enforcement removed.

Inside a governed plan (test_agent_adapter_governed_plan.py, SQLite, the real interpreter and reservation ledger): for each shipped adapter, a protected call is one recorded proposal charged as reported with the protected tool's mutation counter at zero; a lying effect class records nothing; a provider error, a timeout, unreadable, missing or malformed usage, and a claimed commit are each charged the whole reservation (conservative) and carry no provider text into the run error or the log; a replayed step is refused with reservation_replayed and its provider is not reached again; a step past the run's budget never reaches the provider; a timed-out attempt keeps its reservation, and its retry is reserved again and calls the provider once; a cancelled step leaves its reservation open and counted in full; and a governed agent with a handoff is refused before any adapter runs.

A failure reads like this (a reference adapter that retries a failed provider call; 3 of its 40 rules failed). The output is what the suite prints, and test_example_third_party_adapter.py runs it again and requires these lines:

adapter conformance: RetriesTheProviderOnce
  FAIL        provider_timeout                     scenario provider_timeout: expected adapter_timeout, got provider_error
  FAIL        asyncio_timeout_is_adapter_timeout   an asyncio timeout (through the platform): expected an error with no proposal, got completed with 0 proposed
  FAIL        no_hidden_retry                      an error (through the platform): expected an error with no proposal, got completed with 0 proposed
DOES NOT CONFORM (3 failed)

Findings the suite produced, and what was done.

  • The OpenAI Agents adapter read a read tool the platform refused for the deadline (StepDeadlineReached) as a tool failure, so a step that ran past its deadline ended error / malformed_result instead of deadline. It no longer does.
  • The OpenAI Agents adapter let the SDK ask the model again after a proposal, a refused tool, a spent budget or a passed deadline, because it chose tool_use_behavior="run_llm_again"; the extra model calls were bounded only by the reservation. It now passes a function that ends the run at those points (an earlier version of this section called the SDK unable to do that: wrong, the SDK has the hook).
  • The chat and Responses adapters handed a failing read tool's exception message (Type: message) to the provider as the tool result; the Agents and Anthropic adapters sent the class name only. The governed paths of the chat and Responses adapters now send the class name only (_execute_model_tool_call(..., error_detail=False)); the ungoverned loops are unchanged.
  • The Anthropic adapter recognised only the builtin TimeoutError; on Python 3.10, where asyncio.TimeoutError is a different class, an asyncio timeout became provider_error instead of adapter_timeout. It now recognises both, and a rule (asyncio_timeout_is_adapter_timeout) raises a real asyncio.wait_for timeout at every adapter.
  • The harness' direct call of the adapter was not checked for logs; it is now.

Not covered, so not claimed. The suite proves an adapter's behaviour over its stub of the provider, not the provider's: it cannot show that a real client is configured as its stub is, that a provider's tokens are what it reported, or that a model cannot be talked into a harmful proposal (a proposal is only ever the model's claim, which the platform binds and an approver reads). another_steps_result (a provider that answers another step's identity) cannot be staged through a provider script and stays in the per-scenario harness. The Agents and Anthropic adapters and the boundary emit no spans; the chat and Responses adapters run a read tool through a shared helper that opens a tool span carrying the model's arguments and the tool's output (the ungoverned loops do too), and no span is checked: the checked outputs are the result, log records, warnings, stdout and stderr. A read tool that raises ends an Agents step malformed_result but lets the other adapters' model recover: both are allowed (the rule requires only that the message is not handed to the provider and that nothing crashes), and the Agents policy is pinned by its own test. FakeWorkflowExecutor is the platform's scripted adapter (its entries are structured, so a hostile model cannot be staged through it) and has its own tests (tests/test_agent_step_adapter.py); the suite covers the four provider adapters, not five. Run it without python -O: the harness uses assert and the suite refuses to run without them.

Policy decisions#

caliber.policy.decisions.decide(...) (B03.3, #671; migration 0117, table caliber_policy_decisions) answers "may this run do this action on this resource, for this purpose, right now?" with a typed PolicyDecision and records it, allow or deny, immutably (ADR 0003 policy_decision v1 plus the run, subject and workload it was asked about; there are no foreign keys, so a decision about a grant that does not exist is still evidence).

  • Exact identity, no fallback. The caller supplies run_id, grant_id, the Subject and the Workload. A different run, an unknown grant, another subject (user, authentication method or project) and another workload each deny, and nothing is looked up by recency.
  • One reason, a fixed order: grant_not_found, subject_mismatch, workload_mismatch, grant_revoked, grant_expired, not_a_member, action_not_allowed, role_not_allowed, resource_not_allowed (the run grant checks, including the current membership and role), then the policy's own: policy_version_mismatch (the grant was issued under another policy version), purpose_not_allowed, explicit_deny, unknown_action_risk and risk_above_ceiling. An unavailable store is authority_unavailable. An allow carries no reason codes.
  • Explicit maps, never ordering. Each action has an explicit risk number in the policy (every action in resource_access.PROJECT_ACTIONS must have one; a test fails otherwise), compared with the policy's ceiling. policy-v1 has a ceiling of 4 (risk equal to the ceiling is allowed). Risk 5 means "a person, never a run": project administration (archive, restore, members, ownership transfer) and every approval or acceptance (resource.approve, release.approve, release.quality_signoff, change_request.accept), so no grant can make a run approve its own work (Beta keeps a human accountable owner and human protected-action approval, ADR 0004). Explicit denies are exact (action, resource) pairs. A Policy is read-only and type-checked.
  • Replayable. input_hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of every input (run, grant, subject, workload, action, resource, purpose and the live scopes) plus the policy's own digest; the clock is not an input. The same inputs under the same policy hash identically.
  • Transactions. A decision is flushed, never committed. For initial admission the run, its grant and the decision share one uncommitted transaction and the caller commits only after an allow; a denial rolls all of it back. If an decision cannot be recorded, the answer is a deny with persisted = False (an allow becomes authority_unavailable; a deny keeps its reason and gains authority_unavailable), and PolicyDecision.allowed is true only for a recorded allow. A decision never touches the run manifest. The record is written in a savepoint, so a failed record never poisons the caller's transaction. Consumers must know: a denied initial admission rolls its decision row back with the transaction, so evidence of a denial must be written separately (the audit record of B03.5, or a decision made in its own transaction), and on SQLite (development only) a savepoint that is the first write of a transaction commits it, so call decide after the run and grant writes.
  • Callers must not leak identity mismatches. decide records the specific reason (subject_mismatch and workload_mismatch reveal that a grant exists). It is server-internal: any layer that answers a client (HTTP, the admission API) must collapse identity and grant-lookup failures into one uniform refusal. purpose is stored verbatim: it names why, never context or payload.
  • Malformed input is a bug, not a decision. A blank, oversized or control-character id, action, resource or purpose, a naive now, or a non-Subject raises DecisionInputError and records nothing.
  • Immutable. Triggers refuse UPDATE and DELETE (TRUNCATE too on PostgreSQL) and the ORM raises ImmutableRecordError; as with run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges.
  • Audited (B03.5, #688). Every recorded decision also writes one audit-log row through audit.record, in the decision's own savepoint, so the two exist together: action is policy_allow (severity standard) or policy_deny (severity high, or standard when every reason is ordinary lifecycle: grant_expired, grant_revoked, not_a_member), actor the subject, entity_type policy_decision, entity_id the decision id, and details the run, grant and workload ids, the action, resource and purpose, the result, the reason codes, the policy version and the input hash. The run's input, context and any secret are never in it (and the audit log's redactor runs over it anyway). If the decision and its audit row cannot be written (the store is down) the answer is an unrecorded deny (authority_unavailable) and one structured error log line carries the decision, run, grant, action and result; nothing is allowed that is not on record. At initial admission the decision's own rows are rolled back with the refused run (nothing about a refused run is stored), so the denial's audit row is written afterwards in its own short transaction from the decision's ids and reasons (admission.record_denial; a failure there is logged and never changes the refusal).

Recovery: grant_*, not_a_member, role_not_allowed, action_not_allowed and resource_not_allowed are as in the grant table above; policy_version_mismatch means the run must be admitted again under the current policy; purpose_not_allowed and explicit_deny are policy decisions to change deliberately, not retry; risk_above_ceiling means the action cannot be done by a run (use the human-approval path or a person); unknown_action_risk means the policy lacks a risk for the action and must be extended; subject_mismatch and workload_mismatch are always a bug or an attack: fix the caller.

Release evaluation: the evaluator executes queued attempts (B10.2, #707)#

POST /projects/{project_id}/releases/{release_id}/evaluate queues one caliber_workspace_release_evaluations row (queued) per attempt. WorkspaceReleaseEvaluator (caliber/src/caliber/orchestrator/workspace_release_evaluator.py) is the owner-only loop that picks them up. It reuses the service's own queue and lease (claim_workspace_release_evaluation); there is no second queue.

It is still opt-in. With the feature and worker flags enabled, the evaluator claims a row, resolves the release's own immutable revision pins, runs the configured EvalProvider, and completes the attempt. If the lease expires, the next owner records the abandoned attempt and claims a new fenced attempt; provider run identifiers observed before a crash remain attached to the evaluation and are deduplicated.

  • One claim per tick, oldest first. Every CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_INTERVAL_SECONDS (default 5, from 0.5 to 3600) it claims the queued row with the oldest requested_at (ties by id). The row becomes running with started_by, started_at, heartbeat_at and a lease of CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_LEASE_SECONDS (default 300, from 1 to 86400; inf and nan are refused when the settings load). A row that is not queued (running under another claimer, succeeded, failed) is never touched. GET .../evaluations/{evaluation_id} shows it.
  • The claim identity. claimed_by (and started_by) hold workspace-release-evaluator-<pid>-<id>, followed by :t<token> when the claim was fenced (the fencing token of the execution-owner lease it was made under; no suffix outside the reference profile). That is how the token is kept without a migration: an attempt claimed by owner 1 reads ...:t1, one claimed after a takeover ...:t2. The evaluator passes this identity and the attempt number to the service's heartbeat and complete calls (it is the worker_id of ClaimedEvaluation), and may read the token back from the row.
  • Pinned execution. Before the provider call the worker loads only the release's revision_id and its CaliberWorkspaceRevisionResource rows. It requires one candidate, one evaluation dataset, and one evaluation judge pin; optional baseline pins are also revision-local. Each registered adapter resolves and snapshots its exact resource again, and a changed resource digest, missing adapter, missing pin, provider mismatch, or digest mismatch blocks the release without calling the provider. The request carries the exact dataset version and judge configuration; it never follows an unrelated workflow/run manifest or a mutable alias.
  • Result provenance and settlement. The provider result records a SHA-256 evidence digest containing the plan and input digests, candidate/baseline scores, example count, thresholds, and provider/simulated provenance. A score below the pinned aggregate threshold becomes no_go; an unavailable plan/provider or invalid result becomes a retryable blocked outcome. Completion uses the same release lock version captured before provider work, so a concurrent transition cannot be overwritten.
  • Evidence-bound gate digest (B10.3, #714). A provider must return one per-example result row for every pinned dataset example. The worker persists the canonical gate_evidence block on the evaluation attempt before settling the release. It contains the complete rows, a dataset digest derived from example_id/input/expected/weight/tags, the scored-result digest, per-scorer valid-row/weight denominators, candidate/baseline aggregates, thresholds and provider provenance. evaluation_evidence_sha256 is the digest of that exact block and can be recomputed without a provider call. A missing row set or row-count mismatch blocks settlement and writes no gate evidence.
  • Durable attempt history and recovery (B10.4, #721). The parent evaluation row remains the idempotent public queue/status record. Each claim also creates one row in caliber_workspace_release_evaluation_attempts, keyed by (evaluation_id, attempt_number), with its worker identity, lease, status and provider run identifiers. When a lease expires, the old attempt becomes orphaned and the next claim increments the attempt number; the old row and any run identifiers are never overwritten. A provider run observed before settlement is recorded immediately, so a crash after an external call remains auditable. Completion, heartbeat and run-recording operations are fenced to the current attempt; a stale worker cannot settle the recovered release. Only the current attempt can become the authoritative completion, and all parent/provider run identifiers are merged without duplicates.
  • Matching successful gate evidence (B10.5, #732). Manual quality/final decisions and automatic/break-glass release paths accept only a release-local evaluation row with status=succeeded whose canonical evidence recomputes to the release-bound digest and matches the evaluation's plan and input digests. The evidence must preserve provider and simulated/real provenance, satisfy the recorded aggregate criteria, and contain no critical-failure or waiver bypass. Missing, stale, tampered, non-passing, or out-of-scope evidence fails closed; break-glass does not waive a failed critical gate.
  • Adapter refusal (B10.6, #740). A release operation that names a resource type with no registered adapter returns HTTP 409 with the stable payload {"reason":"adapter_unavailable","adapter":"<resource type>","disabled_by":"profile"}. Deployments that construct the registry from an environment-controlled feature may set disabled_by to that exact CALIBER_* variable instead. The refusal is emitted before an operation lock or durable operation is created, so the recovery is to enable/register the named adapter and retry the same intent; it is not evidence that an external effect was attempted. When the release-candidate feature itself is off, the existing route gate still returns HTTP 404 reason_code=feature_disabled and names CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES.
  • Owner-only and fenced. It runs only in the process holding the execution-owner lease (see above), and in the reference profile each claim is made in a transaction that first runs assert_fenced with the exact lease the owner captured. A process whose lease was taken over, expired or cannot be checked claims nothing and records nothing; the log says workspace release evaluator is no longer the execution owner (<reason>); nothing claimed. On PostgreSQL the fenced claim sets lock_timeout and statement_timeout to a third of CALIBER_EXECUTION_LEASE_SECONDS (at least 100 ms), the same bound the lease calls use. Two claimers racing for one row cannot both win (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL and a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'queued'); the loser claims nothing that tick and the next tick takes the next row.
  • Opt-in, and dormant while the feature is off. The evaluator is built only when CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES=true and CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_ENABLED=true (default false). Setting the second without the first logs a warning at startup and does nothing; with the feature off the release routes keep answering 404 feature_disabled. When it does start it logs a WARNING that the worker is enabled and an INFO for each completed evaluation. CALIBER_BACKGROUND_TASKS_ENABLED=false stops it like every loop. A manually constructed worker without its provider and adapter registry is claim-only test/dry-run mode; the server always supplies both dependencies.
  • A clean stop gives the claims back. On shutdown or when the lease is lost the controller stops the loops; stop() then marks this process's own still-running attempt history as requeued and sets the parent claim back to queued, clearing claimed_by, started_by, started_at, heartbeat_at and lease_expires_at in one compare-and-set statement on its own claim identity. It never touches a row another worker owns, and it works after the lease is gone. A crash, a kill or a stop that outlives CALIBER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS leaves the attempt running until the next owner observes the expired lease and records it as orphaned.
  • Liveness is write-only for now. Every tick, idle ones included, writes a caliber_worker_heartbeats row of kind workspace_release_evaluator; a clean stop removes it and a replaced evaluator's stale row is reaped after a few poll intervals. Nothing reads that kind yet (/readiness queue health reads the workflow_run kind only), so it is a row an operator can query, not a probe.
  • No row content in logs or errors. The log carries evaluation and release ids, the attempt number, the claim identity and the lease refusal reason, never the plan or input digests.

Known limits. An idle tick still writes a heartbeat row and runs one indexed SELECT. A tick still running when the stop grace ends is abandoned (a thread cannot be cancelled) and can claim a row after the requeue. A queued row whose claim keeps failing with an unexpected error is retried first on every tick, so it holds up the rows behind it.

Inspecting recovered attempts (a crashed or killed process, or an expired stop grace, left an attempt running). The next owner recovers these automatically after lease_expires_at is in the past. Inspect both the parent queue row and its immutable attempt history:

SELECT evaluation_id, workspace_release_id, claimed_by, lease_expires_at
FROM caliber_workspace_release_evaluations
WHERE status = 'running' AND claimed_by LIKE 'workspace-release-evaluator-%';

SELECT evaluation_id, attempt_number, worker_id, status, provider_run_ids, authoritative,
       completed_at, error_code
FROM caliber_workspace_release_evaluation_attempts
WHERE status IN ('running', 'orphaned', 'requeued')
ORDER BY evaluation_id, attempt_number;

Rollback. Unset CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_ENABLED (or set it false) and restart: a clean stop of the old process requeues its claims, and a new process claims nothing. If the old process did not stop cleanly, recover only expired rows with the SQL above. There is no migration and nothing else to undo.

Reserved tool names and refused paths (#641)#

The protected-effect inventory (docs/architecture/protected-effect-paths.md) classifies a built-in tool by its name, and the tool registry is unique only on (name, version). So a tool someone registers as grep_files could be taken for the built-in. Registration therefore refuses every name a built-in owns, and the inventory trusts a tool's name only when the tool really is CALIBER's own.

Reserved names. The sixteen tools CALIBER seeds: read_text_file, list_folder_files, grep_files, regex_search, grok_parse, sandbox_python, list_workdir_files, read_workdir_file, get_file_metadata, write_workdir_file, create_artifact, extract_document, memory_search, memory_list, list_entities and memory_add. The comparison is stricter than the resolver's exact match: case and surrounding spaces are ignored, and so are a tool. prefix and a .vN suffix, so Grep_Files, grep_files and tool.grep_files.v2 are all reserved. A name that merely contains one (grep_files_v2, my_grep_files) is free. The rule applies in every profile, to every owner, module and version. The names of the trusted connectors (document_request, document-request, http, registered_tool, openapi_http, openapi-http, mcp, mcp-tool; see Trusted connector admission) are reserved the same way, with a message that names the connector instead of a built-in tool.

Where it is enforced. POST /tools, POST /openapi-integrations/{id}/tool-drafts/{draft_id}/publish and the Aria publisher (AssistantPublisher, for a tool draft). Nothing is written when a name is refused. CALIBER's own seeding is unaffected.

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/tools   {"name": "grep_files", "version": "1.0", ...}
409 {"detail": "reserved_tool_name: tool name 'grep_files' is reserved for the built-in CALIBER tool
     'grep_files', which the protected-effect inventory classifies by name; register your tool under a
     different name", "status_code": 409}

The OpenAPI publish route answers the same 409; recover by publishing the draft again with another name in the request body. A tool draft Aria publishes under a reserved name is not registered: the draft ends as publish_failed and the publish report carries "success": false, "code": "reserved_tool_name" and the same message. Recover by asking Aria for a new tool draft under a different name and publishing that one.

A tool registered under a built-in's name before this rule is not migrated or rewritten. It is neutralised by two things only: the identity check and an audit. A registry row counts as CALIBER's own only when every field the seed writes matches (workflows.builtin_tools.is_builtin_tool): the name, the owner @caliber, the version 1.0, a callable named like the tool, and that tool's own module (BUILTIN_TOOL_MODULE_BY_NAME, which the seed also reads, so the two cannot drift). effects.inventory.effect_class_for_registry_tool classifies every other row as irreversible_write, the fail-closed class, and tool_disposition_for_registry_tool routes it through the dispatcher instead of trusting it. The audit: every time the tool list seeds the built-ins, each row that holds a reserved name without being the seed's own row is logged once per process at ERROR and gets one audit record (action flag_reserved_tool_name, entity type tool, severity high, with blocks_seed). blocks_seed: true means the row is at version 1.0 under the exact built-in name, so the registry (unique on name and version) cannot hold the real built-in: it was never seeded and is missing from the list until the squatter is archived and renamed, or deleted by an operator. To rename such a tool, register it again under a new name, point the workflows that use it at the new name, then archive the old one (a registered tool cannot be renamed in place).

The owner is part of that identity, so PATCH /tools/{id} refuses (409 reserved_tool_owner) to give a registered tool the owner @caliber, unless the row already matches the seed in every other field. That exception exists to repair a built-in whose owner was edited away: until it is set back the row is untrusted (fail-closed) and the audit flags it; a row that differs from the seed in name, version, module or callable can never be made trusted by editing its owner.

Where trust comes from at run time. The dispatch call sites (B07 #524, B08 #526, the B04 tasks) must pass the registry row's own name, owner, module, callable and version, read from the database for the tool being run. They must never pass a manifest binding's local_name or resolved_name, and IRToolBinding and ToolRegistryEntry carry no owner on purpose: the IR is written into generated exports field by field, so an owner there would be data an export author controls. A test fails when production code passes a constant or a **kwargs expansion to these lookups.

Refused until explicitly supported. The inventory now marks two paths refuse for the reference profile, so the dispatcher (B04.7, #774) will refuse them with unsupported_in_reference_profile:

inventory rowpathwhy
EP-055the host-file tools read_text_file, list_folder_files, grep_files, regex_searchthey read any host path, with no confine_to_file_root, and return what they read to the model provider (an export)
EP-114the write tools of the first-party PostgreSQL MCP server (create_table, insert_rows, update_rows, delete_rows, execute_sql, create_vector_table, upsert_vectors, create_graph, drop_graph, create_vertex, create_edge, cypher_query)they create tables and write rows with no guard of their own; its read tools (list_tables, describe_table, run_query, similarity_search) run in a read-only transaction and are not refused

effects.inventory.tool_disposition(name, caliber_defined=...) answers refuse or dispatch for a tool, on the same trust rule as effect_class. The DB MCP write tools are not registry rows, so tool_disposition_for_registry_tool answers dispatch for those names (a registry row is never the first-party server); their refusal rests on the MCP server's identity, which the MCP route now establishes from the server record (tool_disposition_for_mcp_tool, Governed MCP tools): a workflow tool node or MCP node reaching one of these tools on the first-party server is refused with unsupported_effect_path under the reference profile (the development profile classifies it by the administrator's policy; the first-party server is recognised from its stdio launch or an operator-attested managed sidecar host). The switch that raises unsupported_in_reference_profile for every refused row is #774. The four host-file tools are already refused by a workflow tool node in a manifest-backed plan (see "Governed registered tools"); until #774 lands, model-chosen tool calls still run the host-file tools if a workflow uses them, so do not wire the four host-file tools into a reference workflow. The first-party database server's write tools are refused through a workflow under the reference profile (B04.5), but a deployment that does not need the server should still not register it.

Configuration, migration and rollback. No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. Rolling back is reverting the change; rows already refused were never written.

Not enforced yet#

ADR 0001 describes the whole reference shape; this table is what the process checks today. Not checked:

  • The shape itself: one tenant and region, MLflow addressed by MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, an S3-compatible object store, at least two projects, and one real model provider next to the scripted adapter. Readiness reporting for MLflow and the object store is #535. The PostgreSQL version and the pgvector extension are checked by the migrations (migration 0060) and the migration-parity CI job, not by the profile.
  • Origin rules (#533). ADR 0001 names them, but #533 has no allowed-origins task yet; that rule is not scheduled.
  • Run-time refusal of the refuse inventory rows, including the host-file tools and the DB MCP write tools (#774; see "Reserved tool names and refused paths"), the trusted-connector set (#534), the full attack pack (#535), a single execution owner (#536) and the Apply separation-of-duties flag (#589).
  • A governed effect context outside the worker's own graph (#1051, #1068): the worker binds one for an admitted reference-profile run, but synchronous version runs, evaluation, gate and Aria previews, and the sub-workflows of a worker run have no owner lease and bind none, so the reference profile refuses their protected nodes (and an agent in them that can reach a mapped tool) and the development profile runs them on the legacy guarded path; see "Profiles and a missing governed context".
  • A verifier for the generic workflow connectors (#1055, #1051): a webhook, API-request, registered-tool, OpenAPI or MCP node is refused no_authoritative_verifier in the reference profile because no connector other than document_request has a lookup by key; only a governed agent step reaches a backend end to end. Model-chosen calls of an agent that is not governed (B04.6, #768) are not routed.
  • Cookie flags: auth_session_cookie_secure is not checked.
  • The database role: whether the application connects as a role without UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on caliber_run_manifests (see "Run manifests are written once").

A configuration that passes this page is the minimum for the reference profile, not the whole of it.
